p.seg: Tàibó, the former ruler of Wú,
was a descendant of Hòujì.
Hòujì’s mother,
Jiāng Yuán, a daughter of the Tái clan,
was the primary consort of Emperor Dì Kù.
While young and not yet pregnant,
she went out to travel in the wilds,
where she saw the footprints of a giant and observed them.
Her heart felt joyful,
she delighted in their shape,
and consequently she stepped on and trod in them.
Her body was moved,
as if she were sensed by someone.
Afterward she became pregnant,
and fearing the calamity of being accused of illicit behavior,
she then performed sacrifices to seek guidance.
It was said that though she had no child,
by treading in the footprints of Shàngdì,
Heaven nonetheless granted her one.
Jiāng Yuán thought the child strange and abandoned him in a narrow alley,
but passing oxen and horses swerved to avoid him.
She then abandoned him in the forest,
but happened upon many woodcutters.
She then placed him on the ice in a marsh,
but many birds covered him with their feathers.
Thus Hòujì managed to survive.
Jiāng Yuán believed he was divine,
so she took him in and raised him.
When he grew up, he was named Qì.
As a child, he loved planting trees, grain, millet, mulberry, hemp, and the five cereals.
He assessed the suitability of the five soils,
green, red, yellow, and black,
and the hills, waters, high lands, and low lands.
Ritual millet, common millet, panicled millet, and grain;
hemp, wheat, beans, and rice;
for each, he understood their principles.
When Yáo encountered the great flood,
the people were adrift.
They lived on high ground.
Yáo recruited Qì
and had him teach the people to live in the mountains,
creating plots according to the land
and refining the techniques of planting.
After more than three years,
travelers no longer had the look of hunger or exhaustion.
He then appointed Qì as the Nóngshī,
enfeoffed him at Tái,
gave him the title Hòujì,
and the surname Jī.
Hòujì went to his state as a feudal lord.
When he died,
his son Bùkū was established.
Encountering the decline of the Xià dynasty,
he lost his office
and fled to live among the Róng and Dí.
His grandson was Gōngliú.
Gōngliú was compassionate and benevolent;
when walking, he would not tread on living grass,
and he steered his carriage to avoid reeds and rushes.
Gōngliú avoided Xià Jié among the Róng and Dí,
changing the local customs,
and the people were transformed by his governance.
When Gōngliú died,
his son Qìngjié was established.
Eight generations later, Gǔgōng Dǎnfù was obtained.
He cultivated the works of Gōngliú and Hòujì,
accumulated virtue and practiced righteousness,
and was admired by the Dí people.
The Xūnyù Róng became envious and attacked him.
Gǔgōng served them with dogs, horses, oxen, and sheep,
yet their attacks did not stop.
He served them with furs, silks, gold, jade, and heavy treasures,
yet their attacks still did not stop.
Gǔgōng asked:
“What is it you desire?”
They said:
“We desire your land.”
Gǔgōng said:
“A gentleman does not use that which supports life to harm those who are supported.
It is for the sake of the state that one might perish.
If it becomes a harm to one’s person,
I will not dwell in it.”
Gǔgōng then leaned on his staff and left Bīn,
crossed Mount Liáng, and settled at Qízhōu.
He said:
“How is that ruler any different from me?”
The people of Bīn—fathers, sons, and brothers—led one another,
carrying the elderly and leading the young,
lifting their pots and steamers to follow Gǔgōng.
After staying for three months,
the outer and inner city walls were completed.
In one year, it became a town;
in two years, it became a capital city;
and the population was five times what it was at the beginning.
Gǔgōng had three sons:
the eldest was named Tàibó,
the second was named Zhòngyōng—
Yōng was also known as Wúzhòng—
and the youngest was named Jìlì.
Jìlì married a woman of the Tàirèn clan,
and they gave birth to a son named Chāng.
Chāng had the auspicious signs of a sage.
Gǔgōng knew Chāng was a sage
and wished to pass the state down to reach Chāng.
He said:
“He who will raise the royal enterprise,
will it not be Chāng?”
Consequently, he renamed him Jìlì.
Tàibó and Zhòngyōng observed the situation and understood the intent.
They said:
“‘Lì’
means ‘Successor.’”
They knew Gǔgōng wished to pass the state to Chāng.
When Gǔgōng fell ill,
the two men used the pretext of gathering medicinal herbs at Mount Héng.
They then went to Jīngmán,
cut their hair and tattooed their bodies,
wore the clothing of the Yídí,
showing they were unsuitable for succession.
When Gǔgōng died,
Tàibó and Zhòngyōng returned.
After the funeral rites were finished,
they went back to Jīngmán.
The people of that land made him their lord and served him.
He called himself Gōuwú.
Someone among the people of Wú asked:
“What does it mean to be Gōuwú?”
Tàibó said:
“Because I was the eldest son (Bó), I dwelt in the state,
but I am one who has severed his lineage.
The one who should be enfeoffed
is Wúzhòng.
Therefore I call myself Gōuwú;
is that not appropriate?”
The Jīngmán people considered him righteousness,
and more than a thousand households followed and joined him,
together establishing him as Gōuwú.
Within a few years,
the people became prosperous and wealthy.
They encountered the decline of the late Yīn dynasty.
The lords and kings of the Central States frequently used military force.
Fearing it would reach Jīngmán,
Tàibó built a city,
three lǐ and two hundred paces in circumference,
with an outer wall of over three hundred lǐ.
Located in the northwest corner,
it was named Gùwú.
The people all farmed within its walls.
When Gǔgōng was ill
and about to die,
he ordered Jìlì to yield the state to Tàibó,
but Tàibó yielded three times and would not accept it.
Therefore it is said:
“Tàibó yielded the world three times.”
Thereupon Jìlì assumed the administration,
cultivated the enterprises of the former kings,
and maintained the way of benevolence and righteousness.
When Jìlì died,
his son Chāng was established,
titled Xībó.
He followed the methods of Gōngliú and Gǔgōng,
focusing his efforts on caring for the elderly,
and the world turned to him.
Xībó brought about great peace;
Bóyí came from the seashore to join him.
When Xībó died,
the Crown Prince Fā was established.
He employed Zhōu and Zhào to attack Yīn.
Once the world was at peace,
he then claimed the title of King,
posthumously honored Gǔgōng as Tàiwáng,
and posthumously enfeoffed Tàibó in Wú.
When the ancestor Tàibó died,
he was buried in the plain of Méilǐ.
Zhòngyōng was established;
this was Wú Zhòngyōng.
When Zhòngyōng died,
his son Jìjiǎn succeeded him.
Jiǎn’s son was Shúdá.
Dá’s son was Zhōuzhāng.
Zhāng’s son was Xióng.
Xióng’s son was Suì.
Suì’s son was Kēxiāng.
Xiāng’s son was Qiángjiūyí.
Yí’s son was Yúqiáoyíwú.
Wú’s son was Kēlú.
Lú’s son was Zhōuyáo.
Yáo’s son was Qūyǔ.
Yǔ’s son was Yíwú.
Wú’s son was Qínchǔ.
Chǔ’s son was Zhuān.
Zhuān’s son was Pōgāo.
Gāo’s son Jùbì was established.
At this time,
Duke Xiàn of Jìn destroyed Běiyú in Zhōu,
as the Duke of Yú had facilitated Jìn’s attack on the Guó clan.
Bì’s son Qùqí succeeded him;
Qùqí’s son Shòumèng was established,
and Wú became increasingly powerful.
claimed the title of King.
From the generations of Tài Bó to Shòumèng,
they occasionally had communications and court audiences with Zhōngguó,
and the state thus became a hegemon.
In the first year of Shòumèng,
he went to the court of Zhōu,
traveled to Chǔ,
and observed the rites and music of the feudal lords.
Duke Chéng of Lǔ met with him at Zhōnglí,
and he inquired deeply about the rites and music of Zhōugōng.
Duke Chéng explained all the rites and music of the former kings for him,
and consequently sang the melodies of the three dynasties.
Shòumèng said:
"I reside among the Yí and Mán barbarians,
where our custom is merely to wear our hair in a mallet-shaped bun.
How could we have such refinement?"
He then sighed and left, saying:
"Alas!
Such are the rites!"
In the second year,
the exiled Grand Master Shēngōng Wūchén of Chǔ arrived in Wú,
was appointed as an envoy,
taught the people of Wú archery and charioteering,
and led them to attack Chǔ.
King Zhuāng of Chǔ was enraged,
and sent Zǐfǎn to lead the army,
who defeated the Wú army;
from then on, the two states became enemies.
Thus Wú began to communicate with Zhōngguó
and became an adversary to the other lords.
In the fifth year,
they attacked Chǔ
and defeated Zǐfǎn.
In the sixteenth year,
King Gòng of Chǔ resented Wú for attacking him on behalf of Wūchén,
so he raised an army to attack Wú,
reaching Héngshān before returning.
In the seventeenth year,
Shòumèng appointed Wūchén’s son Hú Yōng as Chancellor,
and entrusted him with the government of the state.
In the twenty-fifth year,
Shòumèng became ill and was about to die.
He had four sons:
the eldest was named Zhūfán,
the next was named Yújì,
the next was named Yúmèi,
and the next was named Jìzhá.
Jìzhá was virtuous,
and Shòumèng wished to establish him.
Jìzhá declined, saying:
"The rites have ancient systems;
how can we discard the rites of the former kings
and act upon the private feelings between father and son?"
Shòumèng then commanded Zhūfán, saying:
"I wish to pass the state to Zhá;
do not forget my words."
Zhūfán said:
"The Tàiwáng of Zhōu knew of the sagacity of Xībó,
so he set aside the eldest and established the youngest,
and the Way of Kings flourished.
Now you wish to grant the state to Zhá;
I will truly go and plow in the fields."
The King said:
"In the past, the virtue practiced by Zhōu reached all within the four seas,
but now you are in a small state in the land of the Jīngmán barbarians;
how can you achieve the legacy of the Son of Heaven?
Furthermore, if you do not forget the words of your predecessor,
you must grant the state in succession until it reaches Jìzhá."
Zhūfán said:
"How would I dare not follow your command?"
Shòumèng died,
and Zhūfán, being the eldest legitimate son, took charge of affairs
and handled the government of the state.
In the first year of Zhūfán, King of Wú,
after the mourning period ended,
he yielded to Jìzhá,
saying:
"Before the former King passed away,
he was often uneasy at dawn;
observing his expression,
his intent was on Jìzhá.
Furthermore, for three mornings he sighed mournfully and commanded me, saying:
'I know of the virtue of Noble Son Zhá.'
He wished to set aside the eldest and establish the youngest,
but found it difficult to speak the words aloud.
Nevertheless,
my heart has already consented.
But the former King could not bear to carry out his private plan
and entrusted the state to me.
How would I dare not follow his command?
Now the state
is your state.
I wish to fulfill the righteousness of the former King."
Jìzhá declined, saying:
"That the eldest legitimate son should head the state
is not the private matter of a former King,
but the system of the ancestral temples and the altars of grain and soil.
How can it be changed?"
Zhūfán said:
"If it can be applied to the state,
what does the former King's command matter?
The Tàiwáng changed the succession to Jìlì;
the two elder brothers came to the Jīngmán lands,
and thus established a state,
and the Way of Zhōu was fulfilled.
Our predecessors spoke of it incessantly,
and it is what you have studied."
Zhá declined again, saying:
"In the past, when the Duke of Cáo died,
the son of a concubine remained while the legitimate heir was gone;
the feudal lords and the people of Cáo acted unrighteously and established him over the state.
Zǐzāng heard of this,
and went away singing as he returned home.
The Lord of Cáo was afraid
and intended to establish Zǐzāng.
Zǐzāng left
to fulfill the Way of Cáo.
Although I, Zhá, am untalented,
I wish to adhere to the righteousness of Zǐzāng;
I will truly avoid the position."
The people of Wú insisted on establishing Jìzhá,
but Jìzhá would not accept and went to plow in the fields,
so the people of Wú let him be.
Zhūfán was arrogant and self-indulgent,
and was disrespectful toward the ghosts and gods,
looking up to heaven and seeking death.
When he was about to die,
he commanded his younger brother Yújì, saying:
"You must ensure the state reaches Jìzhá."
He then enfeoffed Jìzhá at Yánlíng,
and titled him "Yánlíng Jìzǐ."
In the twelfth year of Yújì,
King Líng of Chǔ gathered the feudal lords to attack Wú,
and they besieged Zhūfāng
and executed Qìng Fēng.
Qìng Fēng had often performed sacrifices for Wú,
which was why Jìn and Chǔ attacked him.
Yújì, King of Wú, was enraged and said:
"Qìng Fēng came to Wú in desperation,
and we enfeoffed him at Zhūfāng
to show that we do not resent a scholar."
He immediately raised an army to attack Chǔ,
taking two cities before leaving.
In the thirteenth year,
Chǔ resented Wú for attacking them because of Qìng Fēng,
their hatred remained unresolved,
so they attacked Wú.
When they reached Gānxī,
Wú struck them,
and the Chǔ army was defeated and fled.
In the seventeenth year,
Yújì died,
and Yúmèi was established.
In the fourth year,
he died.
He wished to grant the position to Jìzhá,
but Jìzhá declined
and fled,
saying:
"I will not accept the position;
that is clear.
Previously, the former lords gave commands,
but I have already adhered to the righteousness of Zǐzāng,
keeping my person pure and my conduct clean,
looking up to the lofty and treading the noble path,
dwelling only in benevolence.
As for wealth and honor to me,
they are like the autumn wind passing by the ear."
He then fled back to Yánlíng.
The people of Wú established Yúmèi's son Zhōuyú,
who was titled King Liáo of Wú.
In the second year,
King Liáo sent Noble Son Guāng to attack Chǔ
to avenge the previous execution of Qìng Fēng.
The Wú army was defeated and lost their boats;
Guāng was afraid,
so he stayed behind,
but eventually recovered the King's boat and returned.
Guāng wished to plot the assassination of King Liáo,
but had no one with whom to deliberate.
He secretly sought out virtuous men,
and thus appointed a skilled physiognomist as an official of the Wú market.
In the fifth year,
the exiled minister of Chǔ, Wǔ Zǐxū, came to seek refuge in Wú.
Wǔ Zǐxū
was a man of Chǔ,
named Yuán.
Yuán’s father was Shē,
and his elder brother was Shàng.
Their ancestor was named Wǔ Jǔ,
who served Chǔ Zhuāng Wáng with upright admonitions.
For three years after the Wáng ascended the throne,
he did not attend to the state’s affairs,
but indulged in wine
and wallowed in music and sex.
In his left hand he held a lady from Qín,
and in his right hand he embraced a woman from Yuè.
Sitting amidst bells and drums, he issued an order:
“If anyone dares to admonish me,
they shall die!”
Thereupon, Wǔ Jǔ stepped forward to admonish him, saying:
“There is a great bird
perched in the courtyard of Chǔ.
For three years it has neither flown nor chirped.
What kind of bird is this?”
Thereupon Zhuāng Wáng said:
“This bird does not fly,
but once it flies, it will soar to the heavens.
It does not chirp,
but once it chirps, it will startle everyone.”
Wǔ Jǔ said:
“If it neither flies nor chirps,
it will be targeted by hunters.
When the bowstring and arrow are suddenly released,
how can it soar to the heavens or startle everyone?”
Thereupon, Zhuāng Wáng cast aside his ladies from Qín and Yuè,
stopped the music of bells and drums,
employed Sūnshū Áo,
entrusted him with the state’s affairs,
and subsequently became hegemon of the world,
with his prestige subduing the Zhūhóu.
When Zhuāng Wáng died,
Líng Wáng ascended the throne.
He built the Zhànghuá Terrace
and climbed it with him.
The Wáng said:
“The terrace is beautiful!”
Wǔ Jǔ said:
“I have heard that a ruler considers being clothed in favor to be beauty,
bringing peace to the people to be joy,
being able to listen to be hearing,
and reaching far to be vision.
I have not heard that the height of wood and earth, the carvings of decorations, the clear sounds of metal and stone, or the mournful cries of strings and pipes are considered beauty.
Previously, Zhuāng Wáng built the Bàojū Terrace;
its height was only enough to observe the state’s atmosphere,
and its size was only enough to accommodate feast vessels.
The timber did not interfere with defense,
its use did not trouble the government offices,
the people did not neglect their seasonal tasks,
and officials did not change court routines.
Now, Your Majesty has been building this terrace for seven years;
the people of the state are resentful,
the wealth and resources are exhausted,
the annual harvests are ruined,
the common people are troubled,
the Zhūhóu are angry and resentful,
and the Qīngshì are slandering and mocking.
Is this what previous kings called prosperity or what a ruler considers beauty?
I am truly foolish
and do not know what you mean.”
Líng Wáng immediately dismissed the workers and removed the decorations,
and no longer toured the terrace.
Because of this,
the Wǔ family served as loyal ministers of Chǔ for three generations.
Chǔ Píng Wáng had a Tàizǐ named Jiàn.
Píng Wáng appointed Wǔ Shē as the Tàizǐ Tàifù
and Fèi Wújì as the Shǎofù.
Píng Wáng sent Wújì to arrange a marriage for the Tàizǐ from Qín.
The woman from Qín was beautiful.
Wújì reported to Píng Wáng, saying:
“The woman from Qín is peerless in the world;
Your Majesty should take her for yourself.”
The Wáng then took the woman from Qín as his consort
and favored her,
and she gave birth to a son, Zhēn.
He instead sought a woman from Qí for the Tàizǐ.
Wújì then left the Tàizǐ to serve Píng Wáng.
He deeply worried that once Píng Wáng died and the Tàizǐ ascended the throne,
he would harm him.
Therefore, he again slandered Tàizǐ Jiàn.
Jiàn’s mother, a woman of the Cài clan, was not favored.
The Wáng then sent the Tàizǐ to guard Chéngfù
and prepare the border troops.
Before long,
Wújì day and night spoke of the Tàizǐ’s faults,
saying:
“Because of the woman from Qín, the Tàizǐ
cannot help but harbor resentment.
I hope Your Majesty will be on guard.
The Tàizǐ is at Chéngfù leading troops,
communicating with Zhūhóu externally;
he will enter to cause a rebellion.”
Píng Wáng then summoned Wǔ Shē and questioned him.
Shē knew of Wújì’s slander
and thus admonished him:
“Why does Your Majesty alone distance your own flesh and blood because of a slandering and treacherous minor official?”
Taking advantage of a banquet,
Wújì spoke again, saying:
“If Your Majesty does not restrain him now,
his plot will succeed,
and Your Majesty will be captured.”
Píng Wáng was greatly enraged
and consequently imprisoned Wǔ Shē,
and sent the Chéngfù Sīmǎ Fèn Yáng to kill the Tàizǐ.
Fèn Yáng sent someone ahead to warn the Tàizǐ:
“Leave quickly!
Otherwise, you will be executed.”
In the third month,
the Tàizǐ fled to Sòng.
Wújì spoke to Píng Wáng again:
“Wǔ Shē has two sons,
both of whom are worthy.
If they are not executed,
they will become a cause for worry for Chǔ.
You can use their father as a hostage to summon them.”
The Wáng sent a messenger to tell Shē:
“If you can bring your two sons here, you will live;
otherwise, you will die.”
Wǔ Shē said:
“I have two sons.
The elder is named Shàng,
and the younger is named Xū.
Shàng is a person of compassion, warmth, benevolence, and trustworthiness;
if he hears that I am summoning him,
he will surely come.
Xū is a person who in his youth loved literature
and in his adulthood became practiced in martial arts.
In literature, he can govern a state;
in martial arts, he can stabilize the world.
He holds to principles and maintains his integrity,
enduring disgrace and bearing shame.
Even if wronged, he does not struggle,
and he can accomplish great things.
He is a man of foresight;
how can you get him to come?”
Píng Wáng, regarding Wǔ Shē’s praise of his two sons,
immediately sent an envoy driving a carriage with four horses,
with sealed letters and official seals,
to Xǔ to summon the sons Shàng and Xū.
The order said:
“Congratulations to the two sons.
Your father Shē, because of his loyalty, trustworthiness, compassion, and benevolence,
has escaped difficulty and been granted a pardon.
Píng Wáng is inwardly ashamed of imprisoning a loyal minister
and outwardly embarrassed by the shame before the Zhūhóu.
He has instead treated Shē as the Guóxiāng
and enfeoffed the two sons as Hóu.
Shàng is granted the title of Hóngdū Hóu,
and Xū is granted the title of Gài Hóu.
The distance between them is not far, just over three hundred lǐ.
Shē has been imprisoned for a long time
and worries about and misses his two sons;
therefore, he sent me to present the seals to you.”
Shàng said:
“My father has been bound for three years.
My heart is filled with grief;
my food has no flavor,
and I have often suffered from hunger and thirst.
Day and night I am moved to thought,
worrying that my father would not live.
Only now that my father has obtained a pardon,
how could I dare to be greedy for the seals?”
The messenger said:
“Your father was imprisoned for three years.
The Wáng has fortunately pardoned him now
and has nothing to reward him with but to
enfeoff his two sons as Hóu.
Once you say the word, we should arrive;
what is there to explain?”
Shàng then went in to report to Zǐxū, saying:
“Our father has fortunately escaped death,
and his two sons are to be Hóu.
The messenger is at the door
with the seals for the enfeoffment;
you can see the messenger.”
Zǐxū said:
“Shàng, please sit calmly,
and let me cast a divination for you, elder brother.
Today is the jiǎzǐ day,
and the time is at sì.
The branch harms the day below,
and the qì is not received.
The ruler is deceiving his minister,
and the father is deceiving his son.
If you go now, you will surely die;
what Hóu will there be?”
Shàng said:
“It is not that I am greedy for the title of Hóu,
but I desire to see our father!
To see him once and then part,
even if I die, it will be as if I lived.”
Zǐxū said:
"Shàng, do not go yet;
our father is keeping me alive.
Chǔ fears my bravery,
and the situation is such that they dare not kill him.
If you mistakenly go,
you will surely die and not escape."
Shàng said:
"The love between father and son
is a grace that comes from within;
I hope for a chance to see him
to bring comfort to myself."
Thereupon Zǐxū sighed and said:
"If we are both executed with our father,
how will we be known to the world?
If the grievance and enmity are not removed,
the shame and humiliation will grow daily.
If you go from here,
I shall depart from here."
Shàng wept and said:
"If I were to live,
I would be mocked by the world;
if I grow old upon this earth,
where would I even go?
If I cannot seek revenge,
I shall ultimately be a useless thing.
You possess both civil and military talents
and are brave in strategy and planning;
the revenge for our father and brother,
you can achieve it.
If I can return,
it will be by Heaven's blessing.
If I should end up buried,
it is also what I desire."
Xū said:
"Shàng, go then;
I shall depart and not look back.
Do not let us face disaster together;
though you might regret it, how could you change it later!"
He then wept and took his leave,
going together with the messenger.
Chǔ obtained Zǐshàng,
seized him and imprisoned him.
They again sent people to pursue and capture Zǐxū.
Xū then strung his bow, held his arrows, and left Chǔ.
When Chǔ pursued him,
they saw his wife,
who said:
"Xū has fled;
he has gone three hundred lǐ."
The messenger caught up to him in a deserted wilderness;
Xū then drew his bow and aimed an arrow, intending to harm the messenger;
the messenger fell prostrate and fled.
Xū said:
"Report to your Píng Wáng:
if he wishes for his state not to be destroyed,
release my father and brother.
If you do not do so,
Chǔ shall become a ruin."
The messenger returned to report to Píng Wáng,
and when the King heard this,
he immediately dispatched a great army to pursue Zǐxū.
Reaching the river,
they lost track of his location;
failing to capture him, they returned.
Zǐxū traveled to the Great River,
looking up to Heaven and weeping as he walked through the forests and marshes,
saying:
"The King of Chǔ is unprincipled
and has killed my father and brother;
I wish to rely on the feudal lords to exact my revenge!"
Hearing that Tàizǐ Jiàn was in Sòng,
Xū wished to go there.
When Wǔ Shē first heard of Zǐxū's escape,
he said:
"The ruler and ministers of Chǔ are about to suffer the miseries of war!"
Shàng reached Chǔ and joined his father;
they were both executed in the marketplace.
Wǔ Yún fled to Sòng
and met Shēn Bāoxū on the way,
saying to him:
"The King of Chǔ killed my father and brother;
what should be done about it?"
Shēn Bāoxū said:
"Alas!
If I were to teach you to take revenge on Chǔ,
then I would be disloyal.
If I were to teach you not to take revenge,
then I would be without concern for a friend.
You should go on your way;
I cannot say another word."
Zǐxū said:
"I have heard that for the revenge of one's parents,
one should not live under the same sky or tread the same earth;
for the revenge of a brother,
one should not share the same territory or border;
for the revenge of a friend,
one should not share the same neighborhood or village.
Now I shall avenge the crime of Chǔ
to wash away the shame of my father and brother."
Shēn Bāoxū said:
"If you can destroy it,
I can preserve it.
If you can endanger it,
I can stabilize it."
Xū then fled to Sòng.
Sòng Yuán Gōng was untrustworthy within his state,
and the people of the state disliked him.
The Grand Master of the Huà Shì clan plotted to kill Yuán Gōng;
the people of the state joined with the Huà Shì clan
and consequently caused a great rebellion.
Zǐxū then fled together with Tàizǐ Jiàn to Zhèng,
and the people of Zhèng treated them with great courtesy.
Tàizǐ Jiàn also went to Jìn.
Jìn Qǐng Gōng said:
"Since the Prince is already in Zhèng,
Zhèng trusts the Prince.
If the Prince can act as an internal ally to destroy Zhèng,
I will enfeoff the Prince with Zhèng."
The Prince returned to Zhèng,
but before the matter was accomplished,
he happened to desire to favor one of his followers;
the follower knew of the plot
and thus informed Zhèng.
Zhèng Dìng Gōng and Zǐchǎn executed Tàizǐ Jiàn.
Jiàn had a son named Shèng;
Wǔ Yún and Shèng fled to Wú.
They reached Zhāoguān;
the pass officials wanted to seize them.
Wǔ Yún then lied, saying:
"The reason the superiors are searching for me
is for a beautiful pearl.
Now I have already lost it,
and I am going to retrieve it."
The pass officials therefore let him go.
He and Shèng departed;
pursuers were behind them,
and they nearly failed to escape.
They reached the river;
in the river, there was an old fisherman in a boat coming from downstream and sailing against the current.
Zǐxū called out to him
and said:
"Fisherman, ferry me across!"
He called thus twice,
and the fisherman wished to ferry him.
It happened that there was someone nearby watching them,
so he sang:
"The sun and moon are bright, yet the time has already raced by;
I have an appointment with you at the edge of the reeds."
Zǐxū immediately stopped at the edge of the reeds.
The fisherman sang again:
"The sun has already set, and my heart is grieved and sorrowful;
the moon has already raced by, why have you not crossed?
The matter grows increasingly urgent, what should be done?"
Zǐxū entered the boat;
the fisherman knew his intent
and so ferried him across the thousand-fathom ford.
After Zǐxū had crossed,
the fisherman looked at him
and saw that he had the look of hunger.
He then said to him:
"You wait for me under this tree;
I will bring provisions for you."
After the fisherman left,
Zǐxū doubted him
and hid himself within the deep reeds.
After a while,
the old man came,
carrying wheat rice, salted fish soup, and a vessel of liquid.
He searched for him under the tree,
but did not see him,
so he sang and called out to him, saying:
"Man in the reeds,
man in the reeds,
are you not a scholar in distress?"
He called thus twice,
and Zǐxū then emerged from the reeds and answered.
The fisherman said:
"I saw you had the look of hunger,
so I brought provisions for you;
why did you have suspicions?"
Zǐxū said:
"My life belonged to Heaven,
but now it belongs to you, elder;
how could I dare have suspicions?"
After the two of them finished eating and drinking,
as they were about to part,
Xū unfastened his sword worth a hundred pieces of gold to give to the fisherman:
"This is the sword of my former lord;
inside there are the seven stars,
and its value is worth a hundred pieces of gold;
I give this to you in return."
The fisherman said:
"I have heard the laws of Chǔ:
whoever captures Wǔ Xū
shall be granted fifty thousand dàn of grain
and the noble rank of Zhíguī.
Why would I seek to take a sword worth a hundred pieces of gold?"
He then declined and would not accept it,
saying to Zǐxū:
"You must leave quickly,
do not stay,
for you are about to be captured by Chǔ."
Zǐxū said:
"May I ask your surname and name, old sir?"
The old fisherman said:
"Today is a time of great peril,
and two rogues have met each other;
I am what is called one who ferries a rogue of Chǔ.
When two rogues understand each other,
their form is manifested in silence;
what use is a surname and name?
You shall be the man in the reeds,
and I shall be the old fisherman;
when you attain wealth and honor, do not forget me."
Zǐxū said:
"I agree."
Having departed,
he warned the old fisherman, saying:
"Cover your jar of broth,
do not let it be exposed."
The fisherman agreed.
Zǐxū walked several paces
and looked back at the fisherman;
the fisherman had already overturned his boat and drowned himself in the middle of the river.
Zǐxū remained silent.
He then proceeded to Wú,
falling ill midway
and begging for food in Lìyáng.
It happened that he met a woman washing silk by the Lài River;
there was rice in her basket.
Zǐxū met her
and said to her:
"Madam,
may I have a meal?"
The woman said:
"I live alone with my mother,
and at thirty I am unmarried;
rice cannot be given."
Zǐxū said:
"Madam, in relieving one on a desperate road with a little rice,
what cause for suspicion is there?"
The woman knew he was no ordinary person
and so she consented.
She opened her basket,
fed him rice and jarred broth,
and knelt to give it to him.
Zǐxū ate twice and then stopped.
The woman said:
"Sir, you have a journey of distant flight ahead;
why not eat your fill?"
When Zǐxū had eaten and was leaving,
he again said to the woman:
"Cover your jar of broth, madam,
and do not let it be exposed."
The woman sighed and said:
"Alas!
I have lived alone with my mother for thirty years,
guarding my purity and virtue,
unwilling to marry.
How was it appropriate to provide a meal to a man
and violate the rites and etiquette?
I cannot endure this.
Sir, you may go."
As Zǐxū walked on,
he looked back at the woman;
she had already thrown herself into the Lài River.
Alas!
To hold so firmly to purity and virtue—
she was indeed a heroic woman!
When Zǐxū arrived in Wú,
he let down his hair and feigned madness,
went barefoot and smeared his face,
begging for food in the marketplace.
The people of the market watched him,
but none recognized him.
The next day,
an official of the Wú market who was an expert in physiognomy saw him
and said:
"I have observed many people,
but I have never seen such a man as this.
Is he not a fugitive official from a foreign state?"
He then reported to King Liáo of Wú
and described his appearance in detail:
"The King should summon him."
King Liáo said:
"Bring him in with you."
Prince Gōngzǐ Guāng heard of this
and privately rejoiced, saying:
"I have heard that Chǔ killed the loyal official Wǔ Shē;
his son Zǐxū
is both brave and wise.
He will certainly seek revenge for his father
and has come to enter Wú."
He secretly desired to support him.
The market official then entered with Zǐxū to see the King.
King Liáo marveled at his grand appearance:
his body was ten feet tall,
his waist was ten spans around,
and the space between his eyebrows was one foot wide.
King Liáo spoke with him for three days,
and no one could match his eloquence.
The King said:
"He is a man of talent."
Zǐxū knew the King favored him;
every time he entered to speak with him,
he displayed a brave and vigorous spirit,
gradually mentioning his grudge
with a look of urgent intensity.
King Liáo understood this
and wished to raise an army for him to seek revenge.
The Prince plotted to kill King Liáo
and feared Zǐxū might become close to the King first and hinder his plot,
so he slandered him:
"Wǔ Xū's advice to attack Chǔ
is not for the sake of Wú,
but merely because he wishes to avenge his own personal grudge;
Your Majesty should not use him."
Zǐxū knew Prince Gōngzǐ Guāng wanted to harm King Liáo,
so he said:
"That Guāng has internal ambitions;
he cannot yet be spoken to regarding external affairs."
He went in to see King Liáo
and said:
"I have heard that feudal lords do not raise armies and use troops against a neighboring state for the sake of a common man."
King Liáo said:
"Why do you say this?"
Zǐxū said:
"Feudal lords focus on governance;
they do not raise armies based on impulsive whims to rescue or avenge.
Now Your Majesty has taken possession of the state and established authority;
to raise troops for a common man
is not righteous.
I certainly do not dare follow the King's command."
The King of Wú then desisted.
Zǐxū retired to farm in the countryside
and sought a brave man to recommend to Prince Gōngzǐ Guāng,
wishing to ingratiate himself.
He then found the brave man Zhuān Zhū.
Zhuān Zhū
was a man of Tángyì.
When Wǔ Xū was fleeing from Chǔ to Wú,
he met him on the road.
Zhuān Zhū was just then fighting with someone;
about to engage his opponent,
his rage had the spirit of ten thousand men,
making him truly unstoppable;
yet when his wife called out once, he immediately returned.
Zǐxū marveled and asked about this:
"How is it that your rage was so great,
yet you turned back at the sound of a single woman?
Is there an explanation for this?"
Zhuān Zhū said:
"Look at my bearing;
do I seem like a fool?
Why are your words so insulting?
He who can submit beneath one person
will surely rise above ten thousand people."
Zǐxū then observed his features:
a high forehead and deep-set eyes,
a tiger's chest and a bear's back;
he was one who would face any difficulty.
Knowing he was a brave man,
Zǐxū secretly befriended him,
wishing to make use of him.
When Prince Gōngzǐ Guāng was forming his plot,
Zǐxū presented him to the Prince.
Once Guāng had Zhuān Zhū, he treated him with ritual respect.
Prince Gōngzǐ Guāng said:
"Heaven has sent you, sir, to help me regain my lost roots."
Zhuān Zhū said:
"When the former King Yúmèi died
and Liáo was established,
it was his rightful portion.
For what reason does the Prince wish to harm him?"
Guāng said:
"The previous ruler Shòumèng had four sons:
the eldest was called Zhūfán,
who was my father.
The next was called Yújì,
the next was called Yúmèi,
and the next was called Jìzhá.
Jìzhá was a man of virtue.
As Shòumèng was about to die,
he passed the throne to the eldest
so that it would eventually reach Jìzhá.
He considered that Jìzhá was on a mission
and was abroad among the feudal lords, not yet returned.
When Yúmèi died,
the throne was vacant;
the one who should have been established was the legitimate heir of the eldest brother.
After the eldest brother's line,
that means myself.
Now how can Liáo stand in my place?
My power is weak and I have no help in the administration;
without using a man of great strength,
how can I fulfill my ambition?
Even if I take the throne,
when Jìzǐ returns from the east,
he will not depose me."
Zhuān Zhū said:
"Why not have a close minister calmly speak at the King's side,
explaining the mandate of the previous king,
so as to subtly suggest your intent
and let him know to whom the state should return?
Why must you privately prepare swordsmen,
and thus cast aside the virtue of the late king?"
Guāng said:
"Liáo is habitually greedy and relies on strength;
he knows the profit of advancing
but does not see the wisdom of yielding.
Therefore, I seek a man who shares my concerns,
wishing to combine my strength with his;
only you, Master, can interpret this righteousness."
Zhuān Zhū said:
"Your words are very revealing;
what is the Prince's intent?"
Guāng said:
"It is not so.
These are words for the sake of the state;
petty people cannot carry them out,
so I entrust my life to you."
Zhuān Zhū said:
"I wish for the Prince to command me."
Gōngzǐ Guāng said:
"The time is not yet right."
Zhuān Zhū said:
"Whenever one wishes to kill a ruler of men,
one must first seek what he likes.
What does the King of Wú like?"
Guāng said:
"He likes flavors."
Zhuān Zhū said:
"What flavor does he find sweet?"
Guāng said:
"He is fond of the taste of roasted fish."
Zhuān Zhū then departed
and went to Tàihú to learn how to roast fish.
In three months, he mastered its flavor
and sat peacefully waiting for the Prince to command him.
In the eighth year,
Liáo sent Gōngzǐ Guāng to attack Chǔ,
and he greatly defeated the Chǔ army,
subsequently welcoming the mother of the former Crown Prince Jiàn from Zhèng.
The ruler of Zhèng sent Jiàn’s mother pearls, jade, hairpins, and earrings,
wishing to resolve the fault of killing Jiàn.
In the ninth year,
Wú sent Guāng to attack Chǔ,
and he captured Jūcháo and Zhōnglí.
The reason why Wú and Chǔ attacked each other was
that originally,
the girls of the Chǔ border town of Píliáng
and the maidens of a Wú border town were raising silkworms
and quarreled over the mulberry leaves on the border.
The two families attacked each other,
and the state of Wú could not prevail,
so they further attacked each other,
destroying the Wú border town.
Wú was angry,
and therefore attacked Chǔ, took the two towns, and left.
In the winter of the twelfth year,
King Píng of Chǔ died.
Wǔ Zǐxū said to Báigōng Shèng:
"King Píng has died,
and my ambitions are not fully realized.
However, as the state of Chǔ still exists,
why should I worry?"
Báigōng remained silent and did not respond,
and Wǔ Zǐxū sat and wept in his room.
In the thirteenth year,
in spring,
Wú wished to take advantage of the Chǔ funeral to attack them.
They sent Gōngzǐ Gàiyú and Zhúyōng with troops to surround Chǔ,
and sent Jìzhá to Jìn
to observe the changes among the feudal lords.
Chǔ dispatched troops to cut off the rear of the Wú army,
and the Wú troops could not return.
Thereupon, Gōngzǐ Guāng's heart was stirred.
Wǔ Xū knew that Guāng saw the opportunity,
so he persuaded Guāng, saying:
"Now the King of Wú attacks Chǔ,
and his two brothers are leading the troops;
it is unknown whether it will bring good or ill fortune.
The matter of Zhuān Zhū
is urgent at this moment.
Opportunity does not come twice;
it must not be lost."
Thereupon, the Prince saw Zhuān Zhū and said:
"Now the two brothers are attacking Chǔ,
and Jìzǐ has not yet returned.
At this time,
if we do not seek it, what will we gain?
The time must not be lost,
and moreover, I, Guāng, am the true heir to the king."
Zhuān Zhū said:
"Liáo can be killed.
His mother is old,
his son is weak,
and his brothers are attacking Chǔ,
with Chǔ cutting off their rear.
Currently, Wú is outwardly troubled by Chǔ
and inwardly empty of straightforward ministers;
thus, there is nothing they can do to me."
In the fourth month,
Gōngzǐ Guāng concealed armored soldiers in a cellar
and prepared a banquet to invite King Liáo.
Liáo told his mother:
"Gōngzǐ Guāng has prepared a banquet for me and come to invite me;
can I expect no malicious intent?"
His mother said:
"Guāng's spirit is discontented,
and he often has an expression of shame and resentment;
you must be cautious."
King Liáo then wore three layers of Tángtiě armor
and ordered guards to be stationed along the road,
from the palace gate to the gate of Guāng's house.
To the left and right of the steps and mats were all King Liáo's relatives,
and those sitting, standing, or attending all held long halberds crossed.
When they were merry with wine,
Gōngzǐ Guāng feigned a foot ailment,
entered the cellar to wrap his foot,
and ordered Zhuān Zhū to place the Yúcháng sword inside a roasted fish and present it.
When he arrived before King Liáo,
Zhuān Zhū split open the roasted fish,
and then thrust the dagger.
The standing halberds were crossed and pressed against Zhuān Zhū's chest;
his chest was broken and his breastbone split open,
but the dagger remained as before
and was used to stab King Liáo,
piercing through the armor to his back.
Once King Liáo was dead,
those to his left and right killed Zhuān Zhū together.
The crowd of soldiers was in turmoil;
Gōngzǐ Guāng unleashed his armored soldiers
to attack Liáo's followers
and destroyed them all.
He then established himself,
and this was King Hélǘ of Wú.
He then enfeoffed Zhuān Zhū’s son
and appointed him as a Guest Minister.
Jìzhá returned from his mission,
and upon arriving in Wú,
Hélǘ offered him the throne.
Jìzhá said:
"If only the previous ruler’s sacrifices are not abolished,
the people are not deprived of a master,
the state is upheld,
and the country does not collapse,
then he is my ruler;
whom should I resent?
I mourn the dead and serve the living
to await the Mandate of Heaven.
It was not I who caused the disorder;
I follow the one who is established,
for this is the way of the predecessors."
He ordered a wailing at Liáo's tomb
and returned to his position to wait.
The two men, Gōngzǐ Gàiyú and Zhúyōng, who were leading troops and had been besieged in Chǔ,
heard that Gōngzǐ Guāng had killed King Liáo and established himself,
so they surrendered to Chǔ with their troops,
and Chǔ enfeoffed them in Shū.
In the first year of Hélǘ,
he began to appoint the worthy and employ the capable,
bestowing favors and practicing kindness,
so that he became known for benevolence and righteousness among the feudal lords.
Benevolence had not yet been fully bestowed
and favors had not yet been fully practiced,
and he feared the people of the state would not follow him
and the feudal lords would not trust him.
He then appointed Wǔ Zǐxū as a Xíngrén,
treating him with the etiquette due a guest,
and consulted with him on the governance of the state.
Hélǘ said to Zǐxū,
"I wish to strengthen the state and become a hegemon;
by what means can this be achieved?"
Wǔ Zǐxū advanced on his knees,
wept, bowed his head, and said:
"I, your servant,
am a fugitive from the state of Chǔ;
my father and brother were abandoned and killed,
their bones remain unburied,
and their souls receive no blood offerings.
I bore guilt and suffered humiliation,
coming to entrust my life to the Great King.
I am fortunate not to have been executed;
how would I dare participate in state affairs?"
Hélǘ said:
"If not for you, Master,
I would not have escaped the service of a captive.
Now, fortunately, I have received the instruction of your words,
and have thus reached this point;
why do you hesitate halfway through?"
Zǐxū said:
"I have heard that for a minister who provides counsel,
how could he be fit to dwell in a place of peril and ruin?
However, once worries are removed and matters are settled,
he will surely no longer be treated with intimacy by his lord."
Hélǘ said:
"Not so.
I have no one but you with whom to discuss everything fully;
how can you decline?
Our state is remote,
situated in the lands of the southeast,
rugged and damp,
and plagued by the hazards of rivers and seas.
The ruler has no defenses,
the people have nothing to rely on,
granaries and storehouses are not established,
and the fields are not cultivated.
What should be done about this?"
After a long pause, Zǐxū replied:
"I have heard that in the way of governing a state,
pacifying the lord and managing the people
are the highest priorities."
Hélǘ said:
"As for pacifying the lord and governing the people,
what is the method?"
Zǐxū said:
"Generally, for one who wishes to pacify the lord and govern the people, rise as a hegemon and become a king, and control the distant from the near,
he must first build city walls,
establish defenses,
fill the granaries,
and manage the armories.
This, then, is the method."
Hélǘ said:
"Excellent.
Now, in building city walls
and establishing storehouses,
one adapts to the terrain;
is there any reckoning of the cosmic qi
with which to intimidate neighboring states?"
Zǐxū said:
"There is."
Hélǘ said:
"I entrust the planning to you."
Zǐxū then had the earth examined and the water tasted;
imitating Heaven and modeling after Earth,
he built the great city.
It was forty-seven lǐ in circumference.
There were eight land gates
to represent the eight winds of Heaven.
There were eight water gates
to model after the eight passages of Earth.
He built the inner city,
ten lǐ in circumference,
with three hill gates.
The reason the eastern side was not opened
was a desire to cut off the light of Yuè.
The Chāng Gate was established
to represent the Gate of Heaven
and to let in the Chānghé wind.
The Shé Gate was established
to represent the Door of Earth.
Hélǘ wished to break Chǔ in the west;
Chǔ is in the northwest,
so the Chāng Gate was established to communicate with the qi of Heaven,
and consequently it was also named the Break Chǔ Gate.
He wished to annex Great Yuè in the east;
Yuè is in the southeast,
so the Shé Gate was established to control the enemy state.
Wú is at the sign of chén,
its position is that of the Dragon;
therefore, on the south gate of the inner city, inverted feathers were made into two whales
to represent the horns of the Dragon.
Yuè is in the land of sì,
its position is that of the Snake;
therefore, on the Great South Gate, there was a wooden snake
facing north with its head pointing inward,
to show that Yuè is subordinate to Wú.
The walls being completed
and the storehouses prepared,
Hélǘ then ordered Zǐxū, Qū Gàiyú, and Zhú Yōng to practice the arts of warfare and the skills of riding, archery, and chariot-driving.
They had not yet been put to use.
He requested Gān Jiàng to cast two famous swords.
Gān Jiàng
was a man of Wú
who apprenticed under the same master as Ōu Yězǐ;
both were skilled at making swords.
Previously, Yuè had come to present three swords;
Hélǘ obtained and treasured them,
and therefore he had the sword-smith make two more.
One was called Gān Jiàng,
and the second was called Mòyé.
Mòyé
was the wife of Gān Jiàng.
In making the swords,
Gān Jiàng collected the essence of iron from five mountains
and the essence of metal from the six directions.
He watched Heaven and observed Earth;
Yin and Yang shone together,
and a hundred deities looked on.
The qi of Heaven descended,
but the essence of the metal and iron would not melt and flow.
At this, Gān Jiàng did not know the reason.
Mòyé said:
"You are known to the King for your skill in making swords.
He ordered you to make swords,
yet after three months they are not finished.
Do you have any idea why?"
Gān Jiàng said:
"I do not understand the principle of it."
Mòyé said:
"The transformation of divine things
requires a person for completion.
Now, in your sword-making,
could it be that they will only be completed after obtaining a person?"
Gān Jiàng said:
"In the past, when my master was smelting,
the metals would not melt;
the husband and wife both entered the furnace,
and only then was the work completed.
Down to later generations,
when people go to the mountains to smelt,
they wear hempen mourning bands and straw garments
before they dare cast metal in the mountains.
Now, the fact that my sword-making does not transform,
is it like this?"
Mòyé said:
"The master knew to sacrifice his body to complete the work;
why should I find it difficult?"
Thereupon, Gān Jiàng's wife cut her hair and clipped her nails
and threw them into the furnace.
She ordered three hundred young women and men to blow the bellows and load the charcoal;
the metal and iron then melted
and the swords were finally completed.
The Yang sword was named Gān Jiàng,
and the Yin sword was named Mòyé.
The Yang sword had tortoise-shell patterns,
and the Yin sword had flowing patterns.
Gān Jiàng hid the Yang sword
and brought out the Yin sword to present it.
Hélǘ valued it greatly.
After obtaining the precious sword,
it happened that Jì Sūn, an envoy of Lǔ, came on a mission to Wú.
Hélǘ ordered the Grand Master of Swords to present Mòyé to him.
When Jì Sūn drew the sword, there was a chip in the edge as large as a millet grain;
he sighed and said:
"How beautiful!
This sword!
Even a master of a great state
could not surpass it!
The completion of this sword
signifies Wú's hegemony.
Since there is a chip,
then it signifies ruin.
Although I admire it,
how can I accept it?"
He did not accept it and left.
Hélǘ, having treasured Mòyé,
further ordered the making of golden hooks within the state,
issuing a command that said:
"Anyone who can make an excellent hook
will be rewarded with a hundred pieces of gold."
There were many hook-makers in Wú,
and there was one who, coveting the King's great reward,
killed his two sons
to smear the metal with their blood
and thus completed two hooks.
He presented them to Hélǘ
and went to the palace gate to seek the reward.
Wáng said:
"Those who make hooks are many,
yet you alone seek a reward.
How is yours different from the hooks of the other masters?"
The one who made the hooks said:
"When I was making these hooks,
I was so covetous that I killed my two sons,
and used their blood to consecrate the two hooks."
Wáng then lifted up the multitude of hooks to show him:
"Which ones are they?"
Wáng's hooks were very many,
their shapes and forms were similar,
and he did not know where they were.
Thereupon, the hook master faced the hooks and called out the names of his two sons:
"Wú Hóng, Hù Jī,
I am here,
but Wáng does not know of your spirits."
Before the sound had died from his mouth,
both hooks flew up together
and attached themselves to their father’s chest.
Wú Wáng was greatly astonished
and said:
"Alas!
Guǎrén has truly wronged you."
He then rewarded him with a hundred pieces of gold,
and subsequently wore them, never letting them leave his person.
In the sixth month,
wishing to deploy troops,
it happened that Bái Xǐ of Chǔ came to flee to him.
Wú Wáng asked Zǐxū:
"What kind of man is Bái Xǐ?"
Zǐxū said:
"Bái Xǐ
is the grandson of Bái Zhōulí of Chǔ.
Píng Wáng executed Zhōulí,
so Xǐ fled as a result,
and having heard that I, your servant, am in Wú, he has come."
Hélǘ said:
"What was Zhōulí's crime?"
Zǐxū said:
"Bái Zhōulí,
the Zuǒyǐn of Chǔ,
was styled Xì Wǎn,
and served Píng Wáng.
Píng Wáng favored him,
often talking with him all day long,
and eating together immediately after the morning court session.
Fèi Wújì observed this and envied him,
so he said to Píng Wáng:
'Wáng loves and favors Wǎn,
as the whole state knows.
Why not prepare wine
and go once to Wǎn's house,
to show the ministers the depth of your favor for Wǎn?'
Píng Wáng said:
'Very well.'
He then prepared wine at the residence of Xì Wǎn.
Wújì instructed Wǎn, saying:
'Píng Wáng is very resolute and fierce, and he is fond of weapons.
You must deliberately display weapons in the hall and the courtyard.'
Wǎn believed his words
and did so accordingly.
When Píng Wáng arrived, he was greatly alarmed and said:
'What is Wǎn's intention?'
Wújì said:
'There is almost certainly a concern of usurpation and assassination.
Wáng must leave quickly,
for the matter is unpredictable.'
Píng Wáng was greatly enraged
and subsequently killed Xì Wǎn.
When the feudal lords heard of this,
none did not sigh.
Xǐ heard that I, your servant, am in Wú,
and so he has come;
I request that you see him."
Hélǘ saw Bái Xǐ and asked:
"Guǎrén's state is remote and far away,
bordering the sea to the east.
I have heard that your predecessor was the object of the violent rage of Chǔ Jīng
and the slandering tongue of Fèi Wújì.
Since you have come from afar to my state,
how will you instruct Guǎrén here?"
Xǐ said:
"A displaced captive of the state of Chǔ,
my predecessor was innocent
but was subject to a violent execution.
I heard that Dàwáng took in Wǔ Zǐxū in his distress,
regardless of the thousand-mile distance.
Therefore, I have come to entrust my life to you;
I only ask that Dàwáng grant me a place to die."
Hélǘ was moved to pity for him,
made him a Dàfū,
and consulted with him on state affairs.
The Wú Dàfū Bèilí attended a banquet
and asked Zǐxū:
"What did you see that you trust Xǐ?"
Zǐxū said:
"My grievances are the same as Xǐ's.
Have you not heard the song from the river?
'Those with the same illness pity one another;
those with the same worries save one another.'
Birds that are startled into flight
follow each other to settle down.
The waters below the rapids
flow together again because of it.
The horses of the Hú stand facing the northern wind,
and the swallows of Yuè bask toward the sun.
Who does not love those who are close to them,
or feel sorrow for those they long for!"
Bèilí said:
"Your words are external;
is there some internal meaning to resolve the doubt?"
Zǐxū said:
"I see none."
Bèilí said:
"When I observe Xǐ’s character,
he has the look of a hawk and the stride of a tiger.
He has a nature of monopolizing merit and killing at will;
he is not one to be close to."
Zǐxū did not agree with his words
and served Wú Wáng alongside him.
In the second year,
the King of Wú, having previously killed Wáng Liáo,
was also worried about Qìng Jì residing in a neighboring state,
fearing he would unite the feudal lords to come and attack.
He asked Zǐxū, saying:
“In the past, the service of Zhuān Zhū to me was profound.
Now I hear that Prince Qìng Jì has plans among the feudal lords;
my food has no taste,
and I do not rest easy in my bed.
I entrust this matter to you.”
Zǐxū said:
“I am unfaithful and lacking in conduct,
yet I plotted against Wáng Liáo with Your Majesty in private rooms.
Now you wish to punish his son again;
I fear this may not be the will of August Heaven.”
Hélǘ said:
“In the past, King Wǔ punished Zhòu and later killed Wǔ Gēng,
and the people of Zhōu showed no sign of resentment.
Now, if we act according to this deliberation,
how is this different from the Son of Heaven!”
Zǐxū said:
“I serve my King
intending to complete the unification of Wú,
so what is there to fear?
The person I hold in high regard
is a man of small stature,
who is willing to join in the plot.”
The King of Wú said:
“The object of my worry
is an enemy with the strength of ten thousand men;
how could a man of small stature plot against him?”
Zǐxū said:
“When this man of small stature plots a matter,
he possesses the strength of ten thousand men.”
The King said:
“Who is he?
You should speak of him.”
Zǐxū said:
“His surname is Yào,
and his name is Lí.
I once saw him humiliate the brave warrior Jiāoqiū Sù.”
The King said:
“How did he humiliate him?”
Zǐxū said:
“Jiāoqiū Sù
was a man from the Eastern Sea.
On behalf of the King of Qí, he was an envoy to Wú.
While crossing the Huái Ford,
he wanted to water his horse at the ford.
The ford official said:
‘There is a spirit in the water;
upon seeing a horse it will come out
to harm the horse.
Sir, do not water it.’
Sù said:
‘Where a brave warrior stands,
what spirit would dare interfere?’
He then ordered his attendant to water the horse at the ford.
The water spirit indeed took the horse;
the horse was submerged.
Jiāoqiū Sù was greatly enraged,
bared his chest and gripped his sword,
and entered the water to seek a decisive battle with the spirit.
He emerged only after several days,
having lost one of his eyes.
He then proceeded to Wú
and attended a friend’s funeral.
Sù relied on the courage he showed in fighting the water;
at the funeral gathering, he was dismissive and arrogant toward the scholar-officials.
His words were insolent,
and he had an overbearing air.
Yào Lí was sitting opposite him.
The whole gathering could not endure his excessive display of power.
Then Yào Lí humbled Sù, saying:
‘I have heard that when a brave warrior fights,
he fights with the sun without moving the sundial shadow;
he who fights spirits and ghosts does not turn his heel;
he who fights men does not let his voice be heard.
He goes forth living and returns in death,
and does not accept humiliation.
Now, you fought a spirit in the water,
lost your horse and lost control,
and furthermore suffered the affliction of a lost eye.
With a mangled body yet the name of a brave man,
this is what a brave warrior considers shameful.
Instead of losing your life to the enemy immediately,
you cling to life,
yet you still show an arrogant face to me!’
Thereupon,
Jiāoqiū Sù was cornered by the reprimand;
resentment and anger broke out together.
At nightfall, he went to attack Yào Lí.
Thereupon,
Yào Lí left the gathering and returned home.
He instructed his wife, saying:
‘I humiliated the brave warrior Jiāoqiū Sù at a public funeral.
His residual resentment is deep and angry;
he will surely come at nightfall.
Be careful not to close my door.’
When night came,
Jiāoqiū Sù indeed went.
He saw the door was not closed.
He ascended to the hall;
it was not barred.
He entered the inner room;
it was not guarded.
Yào Lí lay there with loosened hair, showing no fear.
Sù then gripped his sword and grabbed Yào Lí, saying:
‘You have three faults deserving of death;
do you know them?’
Lí said:
‘I do not.’
Sù said:
‘You humiliated me before a great crowd;
that is the first death.
You returned and did not bar your door;
that is the second death.
You lay down without guarding yourself;
that is the third death.
Since you have these three faults of death,
do not think to hold a grudge.’
Yào Lí said:
‘I have no three faults of death,
but you have three shames of unworthiness;
do you know them?’
Sù said:
‘I do not.’
Yào Lí said:
‘I humiliated you before a crowd of a thousand men,
yet you did not dare to retaliate;
that is the first unworthiness.
You entered the door without announcing yourself;
you ascended the hall without a sound;
that is the second unworthiness.
You stood before me and drew your sword,
your hand gripping and pulling my head,
only then daring to speak big words;
that is the third unworthiness.
You have three unworthinesses yet try to intimidate me;
is that not contemptible?’
Thereupon,
Jiāoqiū Sù threw down his sword and sighed, saying:
‘As for my courage,
no man has dared to even glare at me,
yet Lí has placed himself above me.
This man is truly a brave warrior of the world.’
I have heard Yào Lí is like this;
I have truly heard of it.”
The King of Wú said:
“I wish to host a banquet and wait for him.”
Zǐxū then went to see Yào Lí and said:
“The King of Wú has heard of your high righteousness
and only wishes to meet you once.”
He then went with Zǐxū to see the King of Wú.
The King said:
“What kind of man are you?”
Yào Lí said:
“I am
a man from a thousand lǐ to the east of the capital.
I am small and lack strength;
facing the wind, I fall stiff;
with the wind at my back, I bow down.
Yet if Your Majesty has a command,
how could I dare not to exert all my effort?”
The King of Wú inwardly criticized Zǐxū for recommending this person.
For a long time,
he remained silent and said nothing.
Yào Lí then stepped forward and said:
“Does Your Majesty worry about Qìng Jì?
I can kill him.”
The King said:
“The courage of Qìng Jì
is known to the world.
His muscles and bones are resolute and strong,
such that ten thousand men cannot withstand him.
He runs to chase down fleeing beasts
and catches flying birds with his hands.
His bones leap and his flesh flies;
he can cover several hundred lǐ just by slapping his knees.
I once chased him at the river,
but a team of four horses galloping could not catch him.
When I shot at him,
he caught the arrows in the dark and they could not hit him.
Now your strength is not equal to his.”
Yào Lí said:
“If Your Majesty has the intent,
I can kill him.”
The King said:
“Qìng Jì is a man of clear wisdom;
though he is in dire straits among the feudal lords,
he does not place himself below the scholars of the feudal lords.”
Yào Lí said:
“I have heard that to enjoy the comforts of one’s wife and children
and not fulfill the duty of serving one’s ruler
is not loyalty.
To harbor love for one’s household
and not remove the source of the ruler’s worry
is not righteousness.
I shall feign a crime and flee in exile,”
"I wish for the King to execute my wife and children,
and cut off my right hand;
Qìng Jì will surely believe me then."
The King said:
"Agreed."
Yào Lí then feigned a crime and fled;
the King of Wú then seized his wife and children,
burned them, and discarded them in the marketplace.
Yào Lí then fled to the feudal lords and spread words of resentment,
so that his lack of guilt was known throughout the world.
He then went to Wèi
to seek an audience with Qìng Jì.
Upon seeing him, he said:
"Hé Lǘ is unprincipled,
as the Prince knows.
Now he has executed my wife and children
and burned them in the marketplace;
I have been punished without cause.
Regarding the affairs of the State of Wú,
I know the true situation.
I wish to rely on the Prince's bravery
so that Hé Lǘ may be captured.
Why not go east to Wú with me?"
Qìng Jì believed his scheme.
Three months later,
after selecting and training soldiers,
they then set out for Wú.
As they were about to cross the river,
in the middle of the current,
Yào Lí, whose strength was slight,
sat in the upwind position.
Taking advantage of the wind, he used a spear to hook Qìng Jì's cap
and stabbed Qìng Jì following the wind's force.
Qìng Jì turned and swatted him away;
three times he plunged Yào Lí's head into the water,
then placed him upon his knees:
"Haha!
You are indeed a brave warrior of the world,
to dare to use a weapon against me."
Those around him wished to kill him,
but Qìng Jì stopped them, saying:
"This is a brave warrior of the world.
How could we kill two of the world's brave warriors in a single day?"
He then cautioned his attendants, saying:
"Allow him to return to Wú
to signal his loyalty."
At this, Qìng Jì died.
Yào Lí crossed over and reached Jiānglíng,
but he stood in sorrow and would not proceed.
His followers said:
"Why do you not proceed, sir?"
Yào Lí said:
"Having my wife and children killed
to serve my lord
is not benevolent.
For the sake of a new lord, killing the son of a former lord
is not righteous.
To value his death
but not prize unrighteousness—
now if I were to covet life and abandon my integrity,
it would be unrighteous.
If a man stands in the world with three evils,
with what face can I look upon the scholars of the world?"
Having finished speaking,
he threw himself into the river.
Before he had expired,
his followers pulled him out.
Yào Lí said:
"How could I possibly not die?"
The followers said:
"Sir, do not die yet,
so as to await your noble rank and salary."
Yào Lí then cut off his own hands and feet,
fell upon his sword, and died.
In the third year,
the King of Wú wished to attack Chǔ,
but had not yet set out.
Wǔ Zǐxū and Bái Xǐ said to each other:
"We have trained soldiers for the King
and devised strategic plans
that are beneficial to the state,
yet the King persists in attacking Chǔ,
issues his orders,
but only pretends and has no real intention of raising the army;
what can be done?"
After a while,
the King of Wú asked Zǐxū and Bái Xǐ:
"I wish to dispatch the troops;
what do you two think?"
Zǐxū and Bái Xǐ replied:
"Your servants are ready to obey your commands."
The King of Wú privately calculated that both men harbored deep resentment against Chǔ
and feared they would go only to destroy and annihilate it.
He ascended a tower, whistled toward the south wind,
and after a while sighed;
among the many ministers, none understood the King's intent.
Zǐxū deeply understood the King's indecision
and thus recommended Sūn Zǐ to the King.
Sūn Zǐ,
whose name was Wǔ,
was a man of Wú.
He was skilled in military strategy,
but lived in seclusion,
so people of the time did not know of his abilities.
Zǐxū was clearly discerning and wise,
and knew that Sūn Zǐ could repel and eliminate enemies.
Thus one morning, he discussed military affairs with the King of Wú
and recommended Sūn Zǐ seven times.
The King of Wú said:
"Zǐxū makes the excuse of recommending a scholar
only because he wishes to advance his own interests."
Nevertheless, he summoned Sūn Zǐ and questioned him on military strategy.
Every time he presented a chapter,
the King could not stop praising him
and was greatly pleased in his heart.
He asked:
"Can military laws be tested on a small scale?"
Sūn Zǐ said:
"Yes!
They can be tested on the women of the inner palace."
The King said:
"Granted."
Sūn Zǐ said:
"I require two of your Majesty's favorite concubines
to serve as company commanders,
each leading one company."
He ordered three hundred women to don armor and helmets,
and stand with swords and shields;
he informed them of the military laws,
to advance and retreat according to the drums,
to turn left and right,
and ensured they knew the prohibitions.
Then he ordered:
"At the first drum, all stand at attention;
at the second drum, advance with weapons;
at the third drum, form the battle array."
At this, the palace women all covered their mouths and laughed.
Sūn Zǐ then personally took up the drumsticks and beat the drum,
repeating his orders three times and explaining them five times,
but they laughed as before.
Sūn Zǐ looked at the women laughing continuously without stopping;
Sūn Zǐ was greatly enraged,
his eyes suddenly widened,
his voice roared like a terrified tiger,
his hair bristled against his cap,
and the straps of his cap snapped at his neck.
He turned and said to the executioner:
"Bring the execution axe and block!"
Sūn Zǐ said:
"If the instructions are not clear
and the orders are not trusted,
it is the fault of the general.
Once the instructions have been clarified
and the orders repeated three times and explained five times,
if the soldiers still do not follow them,
it is the fault of the soldiers.
According to military law, what is the penalty?"
The executioner said:
"Beheading!"
Wǔ then ordered the two commanders to be beheaded,
who were the favorite concubines of the King of Wú.
The King of Wú had ascended the tower to watch,
and seeing that his two beloved concubines were about to be beheaded,
he hurriedly sent a messenger down with an order:
"I already know the general's skill in using troops.
Without these two concubines,
my food will have no flavor;
they should not be beheaded."
Sūn Zǐ said:
"Since I have already received the command to be general,
the general's laws apply in the army;
although the ruler has an order,
I do not accept it."
Sūn Zǐ again beat the drum for them,
and they advanced and retreated,
turning and circling according to the rules,
not daring even to blink;
the two companies were silent, and none dared to look around.
He then reported to the King of Wú:
"The troops are now orderly;
I wish for your Majesty to observe them.
You may use them however you desire;
even if ordered into water or fire,
they would have no difficulty,
and they can be used to stabilize the world."
The King of Wú was suddenly displeased
and said:
"I know you are good at using troops;
although I could become a hegemon,
I have no place to employ them.
General, dismiss the troops and return to your quarters;
I have no further desire for this."
Sūn Zǐ said:
"The King only likes the words but does not use the reality."
Zǐxū remonstrated, saying:
"I have heard that military affairs are a grave matter
and cannot be tested in vain.
Therefore, in military affairs,
if punishments and attacks are not carried out,
the way of the military will not be clear.
Now your Majesty sincerely seeks talented men
and wishes to raise an army to punish the violent Chǔ,
to become hegemon of the world and awe the feudal lords.
If not for Sūn Wǔ as general,
who could cross the Huái, pass over the Sì, and travel a thousand lǐ to fight?"
Thereupon the King of Wú was greatly pleased;
he sounded the drums to assemble the army
and gathered them to attack Chǔ.
Sūn Zǐ served as general,
captured Shū,
and killed the two fugitive generals of Wú, the princes Gàiyú and Zhúyōng.
They planned to enter Yǐng,
but Sūn Wǔ said:
"The people are weary and cannot yet be relied upon."
Chǔ heard that Wú had appointed Sūn Zǐ, Wǔ Zǐxū, and Bái Xǐ as generals;
the state of Chǔ suffered for it,
and the officials were all resentful,
all saying that Fèi Wújì's slanders had caused the deaths of Wǔ Shē and Bái Zhōulí,
and now Wú was constantly invading the borders like bandits,
causing the officials of Chǔ to have constant anxiety.
At this time,
Sīmǎ Chéng said to Zǐcháng:
"Grand Tutor Wǔ Shē and Left Counselor Bái Zhōulí—
the people of the state did not know their crimes,
yet you and the King plotted to execute them;
slanders have spread through the state,
and until today,
the talk of it has not ceased;
this is truly baffling.
I have heard that even a benevolent man would not kill someone to cover up slander,
yet now you have killed people and stirred up slander in the state;
is this not strange!
Fèi Wújì is the slandering mouth of Chǔ;
the people did not know his faults.
Now three worthy men have been killed without guilt,
creating a grudge with Wú.
Internally, it hurts the hearts of loyal ministers;
externally, we are mocked by neighboring states.
Moreover, the families of Qiè and Wǔ fled to Wú;
Wú now has Wǔ Yuán and Bái Xǐ,
who wield authority with sharp determination
and have a blood feud with Chǔ,
so the troops of our powerful enemy grow more alarming by the day.
If the state of Chǔ has trouble,
you will be in danger.
A wise man removes slanders to secure himself;
a fool listens to flattery to destroy himself.
Now you have listened to slander,
and the state is in danger."
Zǐcháng said:
"This is the fault of me, Wǎ;
how could I not deal with it?"
In the ninth month,
Zǐcháng and Zhāo Wáng together executed Fèi Wújì
and subsequently exterminated his clan;
then the slanders among the people ceased.
The King of Wú had a daughter named Téng Yù;
while planning to attack Chǔ,
he was eating steamed fish with his wife and daughter.
The King had first tasted half and then gave it to his daughter.
The daughter was enraged and said:
"The King eating the fish and giving me the rest is an insult to me;
I will not live long with such treatment."
She then committed suicide.
Hélǘ grieved for her
and buried her outside the Chāngmén Gate to the west of the capital.
He dug a pond and piled up earth,
used polished stones for the outer coffin,
and stacked timber for the inner chamber;
treasures such as golden cauldrons, jade cups, silver wine vessels, and pearl-embroidered garments
were all sent with his daughter.
He then had white cranes dance in the market of Wú
and ordered the multitude of people to follow and watch them,
Upon returning,
he caused young men and women to enter the tomb passage together with the cranes,
and then triggered the mechanism to seal them inside.
To kill the living to accompany the dead,
the people of the state condemned him.
The sword Zhàn lú loathed the unprincipled ways of Hé lǘ,
so it departed and left,
traveling through the water to reach Chǔ.
King Zhāo of Chǔ was lying down and woke up,
finding the Zhàn lú sword of the King of Wú on his bed.
King Zhāo did not know the reason for this,
so he summoned Fēng Hú Zǐ and asked,
“I woke from sleep and obtained a precious sword,
but I do not know its name.
What sword is this?”
Fēng Hú Zǐ said,
“This is called the Zhàn lú sword.”
King Zhāo said,
“On what basis do you say this?”
Fēng Hú Zǐ said,
“I have heard that the King of Wú obtained three precious swords presented by Yuè:
the first is called Yú cháng,
the second is called Pán yǐng,
and the third is called Zhàn lú.
The Yú cháng sword has already been used to kill King Liáo of Wú;
Pán yǐng was used to accompany his deceased daughter;
now Zhàn lú has entered Chǔ.”
King Zhāo said,
“As for the reason Zhàn lú left,
what was it?”
Fēng Hú Zǐ said,
“I have heard that King Yǔn Cháng of Yuè ordered Ōu Yě Zǐ to forge five swords
and showed them to Xuē Zhú.
Zhú replied:
‘The Yú cháng sword goes against principle and is not compliant;
it cannot be worn.
A minister may use it to kill his lord,
or a son may use it to kill his father.’
Thus Hé lǘ used it to kill King Liáo.
One was named Pán yǐng,
also called Háo cáo;
it is an inauspicious thing
that has no benefit to people;
thus it was used to accompany the dead.
One was named Zhàn lú,
the essence of the five metals
and the spirit of the Great Yang.
It harbors Qi and enshrines spirits;
when drawn, it is divine;
when worn, it possesses majesty,
and it can be used to repel assaults and ward off enemies.
However, if a lord has plots that go against principle,
the sword will immediately depart;
thus it leaves the unprincipled to go to those who possess the Dao.
Now the King of Wú is unprincipled:
he killed his lord and plots against Chǔ;
therefore Zhàn lú has entered Chǔ.”
King Zhāo said,
“What is its value?”
Fēng Hú Zǐ said,
“I have heard that when this sword was in Yuè,
there was a guest who offered a price for it:
thirty townships with markets, a thousand fine horses, and two cities of ten thousand households.
This was for that one sword.
Xuē Zhú replied:
‘Chì jǐn Mountain has already been stripped of its clouds;
Ruò yé Stream is deep and unfathomable;
the spirits of the ministers have ascended to heaven,
and Ōu Yě is dead.’
Though one emptied a city's wealth to weigh out gold,
or though pearls and jade filled a river,
one still could not obtain this treasure;
how much less are thirty townships with markets, a thousand fine horses, and two cities of ten thousand households
worth mentioning?”
King Zhāo was greatly pleased
and consequently took it as his treasure.
When Hé lǘ heard that Chǔ had obtained the Zhàn lú sword,
he flew into a rage because of this
and sent Sūn Wǔ, Wǔ Xū, and Bái Xǐ to attack Chǔ.
Zǐ Xū secretly ordered a proclamation to be made in Chǔ, saying:
“If Chǔ uses Zǐ Qī as a general,
I will capture and kill him;
if Zǐ Cháng commands the troops,
I will withdraw.”
Chǔ heard this
and consequently used Zǐ Cháng
and dismissed Zǐ Qī.
Wú captured the two towns of Liù and Qián.
In the fifth year,
the King of Wú, because Yuè did not follow him in attacking Chǔ,
attacked Yuè to the south.
King Yǔn Cháng of Yuè said,
“Wú does not honor the previous alliance;
they abandon a state that pays tribute and gifts
and destroy its kinship ties.”
Hé lǘ did not consider his words to be right.
He then attacked
and crushed Zuì lǐ.
In the sixth year,
King Zhāo of Chǔ sent Gōngzǐ Náng Wǎ to attack Wú,
to avenge the campaigns of Qián and Liù.
Wú sent Wǔ Xū and Sūn Wǔ to strike them,
surrounding them at Yù Zhāng.
The King of Wú said,
“I wish to take advantage of the crisis to enter the capital of Chǔ and crush Yǐng;
if we cannot enter Yǐng,
what merit will you two have achieved?”
Thereupon, they surrounded the Chǔ army at Yù Zhāng
and soundly defeated them.
They then surrounded Cháo
and captured it.
Capturing Chǔ Gōngzǐ Fán, they returned,
taking him as a hostage.
In the ninth year,
the King of Wú said to Zǐxū and Sūn Wǔ:
"In the beginning, you said that Yǐng could not be entered.
Now, how has it actually turned out?"
The two generals said:
"In war,
to borrow a victory to establish one's prestige
is not the way of constant victory."
The King of Wú said:
"What do you mean?"
The two generals said:
"The raising of troops by Chǔ
makes them a powerful enemy under Heaven.
Now that your subjects have contended with them,
we survived in a situation where ten would perish for one that lived;
that the King entered Yǐng
was due to Heaven.
Your subjects did not dare to be certain of it."
The King of Wú said:
"I wish to strike Chǔ again;
how can I achieve success?"
Wǔ Xū and Sūn Wǔ said:
"Náng Wǎ
is greedy and has committed many transgressions against the feudal lords,
and Táng and Cài resent him.
If the King must launch a campaign,
once you have Táng and Cài, what cause for worry is there?"
The two generals said:
"Formerly, Marquis Zhāo of Cài went to the court of Chǔ.
He had two beautiful furs and two fine jade pendants,
and he offered one of each to King Zhāo.
The King wore them when he attended court,
and Marquis Zhāo himself wore one set as well.
Zǐcháng wanted them,
but Marquis Zhāo would not give them.
Zǐcháng detained him for three years and would not let him return to his state.
Duke Chéng of Táng went to the court of Chǔ.
He had two dappled horses.
Zǐcháng wanted them,
but the Duke would not give them,
and he also stopped him for three years.
Táng Chéng conspired with others,
requesting the horses from Duke Chéng's attendants
to ransom Duke Chéng.
They gave the attendants wine to drink,
made them drunk,
stole the horses and presented them to Zǐcháng,
and Zǐcháng then sent Duke Chéng back to his state.
The various ministers criticized him, saying:
'Because of one horse,
the ruler was self-imprisoned for three years.
We wish to reward the merit of stealing the horse.'
At this,
Duke Chéng constantly thought of repaying Chǔ;
the ruler and ministers never stopped talking about it.
The people of Cài heard of this
and insisted on offering the furs and pendants to Zǐcháng,
and the Marquis of Cài was able to return.
He went to Jìn to report the situation,
offering Zǐyuán and the Crown Prince as hostages
to request an attack on Chǔ.
Therefore it is said
that by gaining Táng and Cài, Chǔ can be attacked."
Thereupon the King of Wú sent an envoy to say to Táng and Cài:
"Chǔ acts without the Way,
cruelly killing the loyal and good,
encroaching upon and consuming the feudal lords,
and distressing and humiliating the two rulers.
I wish to raise troops to attack Chǔ
and hope the two rulers will join the plan."
The Marquis of Táng sent his son Qián as a hostage to Wú,
and the three states joined in a plan to attack Chǔ.
They stationed their troops at Huáinùi
and, from Yùzhāng, faced Chǔ across the Hànshuǐ to form their ranks.
Zǐcháng then crossed the Hàn and formed ranks,
stretching from Mount Xiǎobié to Mount Dàbié.
Three times they were disadvantaged,
and knowing they could not advance,
they wished to flee.
Shǐ Huáng said:
"Now Zǐcháng has for no reason joined with the King to kill three loyal ministers.
The calamity from Heaven is descending,
brought about by the King."
Zǐcháng did not respond.
In the tenth month,
two Chǔ divisions formed ranks at Bǎijǔ.
Hélǘ's younger brother Fúgài rose at dawn and requested of Hélǘ:
"Zǐcháng is not benevolent;
he is greedy and shows little kindness.
None among his subordinates have the will to die for him.
If we pursue them, we will surely break them."
Hélǘ did not grant permission.
Fúgài said:
"What is called 'a minister carrying out his will without waiting for orders'
refers to this."
He then used his division of five thousand men to attack Zǐcháng,
defeating them soundly.
Zǐcháng fled to Zhèng,
and the Chǔ army fell into great chaos.
The Wú army took advantage of this
and then broke the Chǔ masses.
The people of Chǔ had not yet crossed the Hàn
and it happened that the Chǔ people were eating;
Wú rushed upon them and defeated them.
After five battles at Yōngzhì,
they reached Yǐng directly.
The King was pursued by the Wú invaders.
If he went out he was certainly going to perish.
He fled with his younger sister Jìmǐ to the area between the Hé and Suī rivers.
The Chǔ Grand Master Yǐn Gù departed with the King in the same boat.
The Wú army then entered Yǐng
and sought King Zhāo.
The King waded across the Suī and crossed the Jiāng,
entering Yúnzhōng.
While staying overnight,
a group of bandits attacked them.
They struck the King's head with a halberd.
Grand Master Yǐn Gù shielded the King,
receiving the blow with his back,
which hit his shoulder.
The King was afraid
and fled to Yún.
Grand Master Zhòng Jiàn carried Jìmǐ on his back to follow.
Xīn, the Duke of Yún, found King Zhāo.
He was greatly delighted
and wished to restore him.
His younger brother Huái said angrily:
"King Zhāo is our enemy."
He wished to kill him
and said to his elder brother Xīn:
"In the past, King Píng killed our father.
If I kill his son,
is that not also acceptable?"
Xīn said:
"When a ruler punishes his minister,
who dares to hold a grudge?
To take advantage of a person's calamity
