is not benevolent.
To destroy a clan and abolish its sacrifices
is not filial.
To act without a good reputation
is not wise."
Huái's anger was not dispelled.
Xīn secretly fled with the King and his youngest brother Cháo to Suí.
The Wú soldiers pursued them
and said to the Ruler of Suí:
"The descendants of Zhōu along the Hànshuǐ
were destroyed by Chǔ.
This is Heaven's retribution for their calamity,
inflicting punishment upon Chǔ.
Why does the Ruler treasure him?
What crime did the House of Zhōu commit that you hide their enemy?
If you can hand over King Zhāo,
that would be a great favor."
The Ruler of Suí performed divination regarding King Zhāo and the King of Wú.
It was inauspicious.
He then declined the King of Wú, saying:
"Now Suí is remote and small,
and closely situated to Chǔ.
Chǔ actually preserved us.
We have an alliance that has not changed to this day.
If there is trouble now and we abandon them,
if things become peaceful,
how could Chǔ then submit?"
The Wú army respected his words
and then withdrew.
At this time,
although Grand Master Zǐqī had fled together with King Zhāo,
he secretly made a deal with the Wú army,
intending to hand over King Zhāo.
The King heard of it
and was able to escape.
He then cut out Zǐqī's heart to make a blood oath with the Ruler of Suí before departing.
The King of Wú entered Yǐng
and stayed there.
Because Wǔ Xū could not find King Zhāo,
he then dug up King Píng's tomb,
took out his corpse,
and whipped it three hundred times.
With his left foot he stepped on the belly,
and with his right hand he gouged out the eyes.
He scolded it, saying:
"Who made you use a slandering and flattering mouth
to kill my father and elder brother?
Is this not an injustice!"
He then ordered Hélǘ to take King Zhāo's wife as a wife,
and Wǔ Xū, Sūn Wǔ, and Bái Xǐ also took the wives of Zǐcháng and Sīmǎ Chéng as wives
to humiliate the ruler and ministers of Chǔ.
Then they led the army to attack Zhèng.
Duke Dìng of Zhèng had previously killed Crown Prince Jiàn and had distressed and pressured Zǐxū.
Because of this, Duke Dìng of Zhèng was greatly afraid
and then issued an order within the state, saying:
"Whoever is able to turn back the Wú army,
I will share the state with him and rule together."
The son of a fisherman answered the call, saying:
"I am able to turn them back.
I do not need a single weapon or a peck of grain.
I only need an oar to go singing along the road,
and they will turn back."
The Gōng then rowed with the son of the fisherman.
The army of Zǐxū was about to arrive;
in the middle of the road, the son tapped his oar and sang, saying:
"Man among the reeds!"
He did this twice.
Zǐxū heard it
and was startled and greatly surprised.
He said:
"Who is this?"
He spoke with him:
"Who are you?"
He replied:
"I am the son of the fisherman.
My country's lord is terrified
and has issued an order in the state:
anyone who can turn back the army of Wú
will be given half the state to rule.
I remembered my predecessor and you met on the road,
and now I beg of you the state of Zhèng."
Zǐxū sighed and said:
"How tragic!
I received the kindness of your predecessor
and thus reached this position;
the vast heavens above,
how could I dare forget?"
Thereupon,
he released the state of Zhèng,
returned the army to occupy Chǔ,
and sought the location of Zhāo Wáng more urgently every day.
Shēn Bāoxū had fled into the mountains;
when he heard of this,
he sent someone to say to Zǐxū:
"Your revenge,
is it not excessive!
You
were once a subject of Píng Wáng
and personally served him facing north;
now you have gone so far as the insult of desecrating his corpse—
is this not the extreme of unprincipled behavior?"
Zǐxū said:
"Give my apologies to Shēn Bāoxū and say:
'The sun is setting and the road is long,
so I act in reverse and go against the natural order of the way.'"
Shēn Bāoxū knew he could not be persuaded,
so he went to Qín
to seek help for Chǔ.
By day he galloped and by night he hurried,
his heels and soles were cracked,
and he tore his clothes to wrap his knees.
He stood leaning like a crane and wept in the court of Qín;
for seven days and seven nights, his voice did not cease.
Qín Āi Gōng was habitually given to indulgence
and did not care for state affairs.
After Shēn Bāoxū finished weeping, he sang, saying:
"Wú acts without principle,
like a giant boar and a long serpent,
to devour the superior states.
They wish to possess all under heaven,
and their campaign began with Chǔ.
My humble lord has fled to the marshes
and sent me to report the emergency."
After seven days of this,
Qín Āi Gōng was greatly amazed:
"Chǔ has a worthy minister like this,
yet Wú still wishes to destroy it.
If I do not have a minister like this,
my own destruction will be imminent."
For him, he composed the poem of Wú Yī, which said:
"Who says we have no clothes?
I shall share my robe with you.
The king raises the army;
I share the same enemy with you."
Bāoxū said:
"I have heard that perverse virtue is never satisfied.
If the king does not worry about the troubles on the borders of a neighboring state,
while Wú is not yet settled,
the king should take a share of it.
If Chǔ is eventually destroyed,
what benefit is there for Qín?
It would also be the land of a fallen lord.
I wish the king would preserve it with divine spirit,
and we will serve the king for generations."
Qín Bó sent a refusal,
saying:
"I have heard your request.
You should go to the guest house;
I will consider it and let you know."
Bāoxū said:
"My humble lord is now in the wilds
and has not found a place to hide;
how could I dare seek comfort?"
He stood in the court again,
leaning against the wall and weeping,
his voice not ceasing day or night,
and no water entered his mouth.
Qín Bó shed tears for him
and immediately sent out the army to accompany him.
In the tenth year,
the Qín army had not yet set out.
Yuè Wáng Yǔncháng resented that Hélǘ had defeated him at Zuìlǐ,
and he raised troops to attack Wú.
While Wú was in Chǔ,
the Yuè bandits launched a surprise attack upon it.
In the sixth month,
Shēn Bāoxū arrived with the Qín army.
Qín sent Gōngzǐ Zǐpú and Gōngzǐ Zǐhǔ to lead five hundred chariots
to rescue Chǔ and strike Wú.
The two Gōngzǐ said,
"We do not yet know the tactics of Wú."
They had the Chǔ army go forward to engage Wú in battle,
while they themselves joined them from Jì,
greatly defeating Fúgài.
In the seventh month,
Sīmǎ Zǐchéng of Chǔ and Gōngzǐ Zǐpú of Qín held their positions against the Wú Wáng,
while secretly using a diversionary force to attack Táng Guó,
destroying it.
Zǐxū remained in Chǔ for a long time seeking Zhāo Wáng,
and would not leave.
Fúgài's army was defeated and retreated.
In the ninth month,
he returned in secret
and established himself as Wú Wáng.
When Hélǘ heard of this,
he then abandoned the Chǔ army,
wanting to kill Fúgài.
Fúgài fled to Chǔ,
and Zhāo Wáng enfeoffed Fúgài at Tángxī.
Hélǘ then returned.
Zǐxū, Sūn Wǔ, and Bái Xǐ remained
and defeated the Chǔ army at Huáishì.
The Qín army again defeated the Wú army,
and Zǐqī of Chǔ intended to set fire to the Wú army.
Zǐxī said,
"The fathers and brothers of our state have fought in person and their bones are exposed in the wilderness;
if we do not collect them
but instead burn them,
can that be acceptable?"
Zǐqī said,
"The state is ruined and the people are lost;
where survival or demise is at stake,
why sacrifice the living to cherish the dead?
If the dead have consciousness,
they will surely rise with the smoke to assist us.
If they have no consciousness,
why pity the bones among the grass
and allow the Wú Guó to perish?"
They then set fire and fought,
and the Wú army was greatly defeated.
Zǐxū and the others said to one another,
"Though Chǔ has defeated our remaining troops,
they have not yet caused us any real loss."
Sūn Wǔ said,
"With the weapons of Wú, I have broken Chǔ in the west,
pursued Zhāo Wáng and desecrated the tomb of Jīng Píng Wáng,
cutting and mutilating his corpse;
this is already enough."
Zǐxū said,
"Since the time of the Bàwáng,
no minister has ever taken revenge in such a manner.
Let us depart!"
After the Wú army left,
Zhāo Wáng returned to his state.
Yuèshī Hùzǐ criticized Jīng Wáng for believing in slanders and flattery,
killing Wǔ Shē and Bái Zhōulí,
which caused incessant invasions at the borders,
even leading to the excavation of Píng Wáng's tomb and the mutilation of his corpse,
and the wicked joy that insulted the Chǔ ruler and ministers;
he also grieved for Zhāo Wáng's distress and entrapment,
which nearly made him a great laughingstock to the world,
yet he felt ashamed.
He then took up his qín and composed the *Qióngjié zhī Qǔ* for Chǔ,
to express the ruler's narrow escapes and the eventual relief of his distress.
The lyrics said:
"Oh Wáng,
Oh Wáng,
how contrary and fierce!
Ignoring the ancestral temple and listening to slanderous evils.
Employing Wújì who killed so many,
exterminating the Bái Shì until they were nearly gone.
The two sons fled east to Wú and Yuè,
the Wú Wáng was grieved and assisted their distress.
Shedding tears, he raised troops to attack the west,
Wǔ Xū, Bái Xǐ, and Sūn Wǔ were decisive.
In three battles they broke Yǐng and the Wáng fled,
leaving troops and letting cavalry loose to capture the Jīng gates.
The skeletal remains of Chǔ and Jīng were excavated,
the whip's insult to the decayed corpse is a shame hard to wash away.
Nearly endangering the ancestral temples and the state being destroyed,
what crime did Yán Wáng commit that the state was nearly ended?
The high officials are sorrowful and the people are pained,
though the Wú army has left, the fear does not cease.
May the Wáng change his ways and nurture loyalty and integrity,
and not allow slanderous mouths to defile and insult."
Zhāo Wáng shed tears,
deeply understanding the sentiment of the qín song,
and Hùzǐ never played it again.
When Zǐxū and the others passed by the Lài Shuǐ in Lìyáng,
he let out a long sigh and said,
"I once hungered here
and begged food from a woman;
the woman fed me,
then threw herself into the water and died."
He wished to reward her with a hundred gold pieces but did not know her home,
so he threw the gold into the water and left.
A short while later,
an old woman came walking and crying.
Someone asked,
"Why do you cry so sadly?"
The woman said,
"I had a daughter
who stayed home until thirty and did not marry;
last year she was beating silk here
and met a gentleman in desperate straits and fed him,
then fearing the matter would leak,
she threw herself into the Lài Shuǐ.
Now I hear Wǔ Jūn has come,
yet she has not received her reward,
and I grieve that she died in vain;
therefore I am sad."
The person said,
"Zǐxū wanted to reward her with a hundred gold pieces,
but not knowing her home,
he threw the gold into the water and left."
The woman then took the gold and went home.
Zǐxū returned to Wú.
Wú Wáng heard the three generals were about to arrive
and prepared fish as kuài.
On the day they were to arrive,
the time passed and they did not come,
so the fish turned foul.
A moment later,
Zǐxū arrived,
Hélǘ brought out the kuài to eat,
and did not notice it was foul.
The Wáng had it prepared again,
and its taste was as before.
The Wú people making kuài
started from Hélǘ's creation.
After the generals returned from Chǔ,
they renamed the Chāng Mén as the Pòchǔ Mén.
They again planned to attack Qí Guó.
Qí Zǐ sent his daughter as a hostage to Wú,
and the Wú Wáng therefore betrothed the Qí girl for Tàizǐ Bō.
The girl was young and longed for Qí,
crying day and night,
and consequently fell ill.
Hélǘ then built the North Gate,
naming it the Wàngqí Mén,
and ordered the girl to go and walk upon it.
The girl's longing did not cease,
her illness became more severe every day,
and finally she passed away.
The girl said,
"If the dead have consciousness,
you must bury me on the peak of Yú Shān,
to gaze toward the Qí Guó."
Hélǘ grieved for her,
and just as she said,
he buried her on the peak of Yú Shān.
At that time,
the Tàizǐ also fell ill and died.
Hélǘ planned to choose among the Gōngzǐ one who could be established,
but had no fixed plan.
Tàizǐ Bō's son Fūchāi daily and nightly said to Wǔ Xū,
"The Wáng wants to establish a Tàizǐ;
if not me, then who should be established?
This plan lies with you, my lord."
Wǔ Zǐxū said,
"The Tàizǐ has not yet been decided;
when I go in, it will be settled."
A while later, Hélǘ summoned Zǐxū to plan the establishment of the Tàizǐ.
Zǐxū said,
"I have heard that sacrifices are abandoned when there is no heir
and flourish when there is a successor.
Now that the Tàizǐ has passed away,
having lost his attendants early,
if the Wáng now wishes to establish a Tàizǐ,
none is more suitable than Bō Qín’s son Fūchāi."
Hélǘ said,
"Fūchāi is foolish and lacks benevolence;
I fear he cannot uphold the succession of the Wú Guó."
Zǐxū said,
"Fūchāi is trustworthy and loves the people;
he is upright in maintaining integrity
and sincere in ritual and righteousness.
That a son succeeds his father
is a clear text of the classics."
Hélǘ said,
"I shall follow you."
He established Fūchāi as the Tàizǐ.
He ordered the Tàizǐ to station troops to guard Chǔ and remain there.
He himself built palaces,
establishing a Shètái in Ānlǐ,
the Huá Chí in Píngchāng,
and the Nánchéng Gōng in Chánglè.
Hélǘ went in and out for leisure and sleep,
In autumn and winter he governed within the city,
and in spring and summer he governed outside the city.
He managed the Gūsū Terrace,
ate at Shàn Shān in the morning,
and roamed the Sū Terrace during the day.
He practiced archery at Ōu Bēi
and galloped at Yóu Tái.
He found joy at Shí Chéng
and coursed his hounds at Cháng Zhōu.
This was when Hélǘ was at the height of his hegemony.
At this time, Tàizǐ Dìng was established;
consequently, they attacked Chǔ,
defeating their army and capturing Fān.
Chǔ feared the Wú troops would return,
so they abandoned Yǐng
and moved to Wěiruò.
During this time,
Wú utilized the strategies of Zǐxū, Bái Xǐ, and Sūn Wǔ
to crush the powerful Chǔ in the west,
overawe Qí and Jìn in the north,
and attack Yúyuè in the south.
In the eleventh year,
Fūchā went north to attack Qí.
Qí sent the Grand Master of the Gāo clan to plead with the Wú army, saying:
“Qí is an isolated and meager state;
its granaries and storehouses are empty,
and its people are scattered.
Qí regards Wú as a powerful support,
yet now, before we have even gone to report an emergency,
Wú has seen fit to attack us.
We request to have our people prostrate themselves in the suburbs;
we do not dare to offer words of warfare.
We only hope that Wú will take pity on Qí and not be indiscriminate.”
The Wú army then returned.
In the twelfth year,
Fūchā again went north to attack Qí.
The King of Yuè heard of this
and led his followers to pay court to Wú,
offering precious treasures and generous gifts to Tàizǎi Pǐ.
Pǐ joyfully accepted the bribes from Yuè
and grew extremely fond of and trusting toward Yuè,
speaking for them to the King of Wú day and night.
The King trusted and followed Pǐ’s plans.
Wǔ Xū was greatly alarmed
and said:
“This is to abandon us.”
He then went to remonstrate, saying:
“Now, Yuè
is a disease in the heart and vitals.
If you do not first eliminate this sickness
but instead trust in hollow words and deceptions while coveting Qí—
defeating Qí
is like acquiring a field of solid rock,
where no seedlings can be raised.
I wish the King would let go of Qí and prioritize Yuè.
Otherwise,
your regrets will come too late.”
The King of Wú would not listen
and sent Zǐxū as an envoy to Qí
to announce the date of the battle meeting.
Zǐxū said to his son:
“I have repeatedly remonstrated with the King,
but the King does not employ my advice.
Now I see the downfall of Wú.
If you and I perish together,
our deaths will be for nothing.”
He then entrusted his son to the Bào clan of Qí and returned.
Since Tàizǎi Pǐ already had a rift with Zǐxū,
he took this opportunity to slander him, saying:
“Zǐxū acts with stubbornness and force in his remonstrance.
I hope the King will be slightly more firm with him.”
The King said:
“I am aware of it.”
Before the army was raised,
it happened that Lǔ sent Zǐgòng on a diplomatic mission to Wú.
In the thirteenth year,
the Qí Dàfū, Chén Chénghéng, wished to assassinate Jiǎn Gōng.
Secretly, he dreaded Gāo, Guó, Bǎo, and Yàn;
therefore, he beforehand raised troops to attack Lǔ.
The Lǔ Jūn was worried about this.
Kǒngzǐ was distressed by this
and summoned his disciples, saying to them:
"When there are Zhūhóu who attack one another,
I, Qiū, always feel ashamed of it.
As for Lǔ,
it is the land of my parents,
and my ancestral graves are there.
Now that Qí is about to attack it,
do none of you intend to step forward once?"
Zǐlù asked to go out,
but Kǒngzǐ stopped him.
Zǐzhāng and Zǐshí requested to go,
but Kǒngzǐ did not grant permission.
Zǐgòng asked to go out,
and Kǒngzǐ sent him.
Zǐgòng went north to Qí
and saw Chénghéng.
He then said to him:
"As for Lǔ,
it is a state difficult to attack,
yet you, Sir, attack it;
this is an error."
Chénghéng said:
"Why is Lǔ difficult to attack?"
Zǐgòng said:
"Its city walls are thin and low,
its moats are narrow and shallow,
its ruler is foolish and lacks benevolence,
its high officials are deceitful and useless,
and its soldiers and people detest the affairs of armor and weapons;
this state cannot be fought against.
You would be better off attacking Wú.
As for Wú,
its walls are thick and high,
its moats are wide and deep,
its armor is strong and its soldiers are elite,
its equipment is abundant and its crossbows are powerful,
and moreover, it has brilliant Dàfū guarding it;
this is easy to attack."
Chénghéng showed anger in his expression
and said:
"What you consider difficult,
others consider easy;
what you consider easy,
others consider difficult.
Yet you use this to teach me, Héng;
why is that?"
Zǐgòng said:
"I have heard that if a lord is enfeoffed three times and three times it is not accomplished,
it is because the high officials have something they do not obey.
Now you wish to crush Lǔ to expand Qí,
and destroy Lǔ to elevate yourself,
yet your merit would not be involved therein.
This would, above, make the heart of the ruler arrogant,
and below, make the various officials licentious;
to seek to accomplish a great task in this way
is difficult.
Furthermore, when those above are arrogant, they become transgressive;
when officials are arrogant, they become contentious.
This would mean that, above, you would be in a state of alarm regarding the ruler
and, below, you would be in conflict with the high officials.
In such a case,
your standing in Qí
would be more precarious than a pile of eggs.
Therefore, I say it is better to attack Wú.
Moreover, the Wú Wáng is fierce and resolute;
he can carry out his orders.
The common people are practiced in battle and defense,
and the generals are clear about the laws and prohibitions.
That Qí will be captured upon meeting them
is certain.
Now, if you exhaust the resources within your four borders
and lead out the high officials to surround them,
the people will die abroad,
and the power of the high officials will be emptied at home.
In this way, above you will have no officials who are powerful enemies,
and below you will have no commoners to oppose you.
The one who will control Qí as a solitary ruler
will be you."
Chénghéng said:
"Excellent.
Although this is so,
my troops are already at the walls of Lǔ.
If I leave and go to Wú,
the high officials will have doubts about me.
What can be done about this?"
Zǐgòng said:
"You should halt your troops and not attack.
Please allow me to go south for you to see the Wú Wáng,
and request that he save Lǔ and attack Qí.
You can then use your troops to meet him."
Chénghéng gave his consent.
Zǐgòng went south to see the Wú Wáng
and said to the Wú Wáng:
"I have heard that
a true king does not allow a lineage to be extinguished,
and a hegemon has no powerful enemies.
A weight of a thousand jūn can be moved by adding a zhū or a liǎng.
Now, for Qí, a state of ten thousand chariots, to take for itself Lǔ, a state of a thousand chariots,
and thus compete for strength with Wú—
I privately fear for you.
Furthermore, saving Lǔ
will bring a glorious reputation;
attacking Qí
will bring great profit.
It is righteous to preserve the perishing Lǔ,
and in reality, it harms the violent Qí and overawes the powerful Jìn;
then you, Wáng, need not have doubts."
The Wú Wáng said:
"Excellent.
Although this is so,
I have fought with Yuè before
and cornered them at Huìjī.
They entered into servitude to Wú,
and I did not immediately execute them.
After three years, I allowed them to return.
The Yuè Jūn is a worthy lord,
toiling his body and exerting his effort,
continuing into the night what began in the day.
Internally, he refines his governance,
and externally, he serves the Zhūhóu.
He will certainly have the intention to take revenge on me.
Wait for me to attack Yuè, and then I will listen to you."
Zǐgòng said:
"That is not possible.
The strength of Yuè is not greater than that of Lǔ,
and the strength of Wú is not greater than that of Qí.
If you, Great Lord, attack Yuè and do not listen to me,
Qí will have already taken Lǔ for itself.
Moreover, to fear the small Yuè while loathing the strong Qí
is not brave.
To see small profit while forgetting a great harm
is not wise.
I have heard that a benevolent person does not restrict themselves from expanding their virtue,
a wise person does not discard the opportunity to achieve their merit,
and a true king does not extinguish a lineage to establish his righteousness.
Since you fear Yuè so much,
I request to go east to see the Yuè Wáng
and make him send forth his army to follow your subordinate officials."
The Wú Wáng was greatly pleased.
Zǐgòng went east to see the Yuè Wáng.
When the Yuè Wáng heard of this,
he cleared the road and met him in the suburbs.
He personally drove the chariot to the guest house and asked:
"This is a remote and narrow state of barbarian people.
Why have you, Dàfū, come from such a distance, as if you did not consider it a disgrace
to arrive here?"
Zǐgòng said:
"I have come because of your situation."
Gōujiàn, the Yuè Wáng, bowed twice and prostrated,
saying:
"I have heard that
misfortune and fortune are neighbors.
Now that you, Dàfū, have come to console me,
it is my fortune.
How could I dare not ask for your explanation?"
Zǐgòng said:
"I have just seen the Wú Wáng
and spoke to him about saving Lǔ and attacking Qí.
His heart is set on it,
but his will fears Yuè.
Furthermore, to have no intention of taking revenge on someone while making them suspect it
is clumsy.
To have the intention of taking revenge on someone while making them aware of it
is dangerous.
To have one's plans heard before they are executed
is perilous.
These three
are the great taboos in undertaking any action."
The Yuè Wáng bowed twice
and said:
"I lost my predecessors when I was young,
and internally I did not measure my own strength,
so I fought with the people of Wú.
My army was defeated and I was humiliated,
leaving shame upon my ancestors.
I fled and went into exile,
living above on Huìjī
and below guarding the seashore,
where only fish and turtles were seen.
Now you, Dàfū, have deigned to console me and seen me personally,
and moreover have uttered jade-like words to teach me.
I rely on the blessing of Heaven.
How could I dare not accept your teaching?"
Zǐgòng said:
"I have heard that
an enlightened ruler employs people without missing their abilities,
and an upright scholar promotes the worthy even if he is not accepted by the world.
Therefore, when facing wealth and dividing profit, he employs the benevolent;
when traversing trouble and facing difficulty, he employs the brave;
when using wisdom to plan for the state, he employs the worthy;
when rectifying the world and stabilizing the Zhūhóu, he employs the sage.
If one's troops are strong yet one cannot exercise their authority,
and one's position is superior yet one cannot implement their governance and orders below..."
"Is Your Majesty almost ready?"
"It is difficult!"
"I have privately selected one with whom success can be achieved and who can reach the rank of a true King;
is it not perhaps Your Majesty?
Now the King of Wú has the ambition to attack Qí and Jìn.
Your Majesty should not begrudge precious vessels to please his heart,
and do not dislike using humble words to fulfill the rites;
if he attacks Qí,
Qí will certainly fight.
If he does not win,
it will be Your Majesty’s blessing;
if he fights and wins,
he will certainly lead his troops against Jìn.
His knights and elite soldiers will be worn out in Qí,
and his heavy treasures, chariots, and banners will be exhausted in Jìn;
then Your Majesty can control what remains of him."
The King of Yuè bowed twice
and said:
"In the past,
the King of Wú divided his many people to ravage my state,
killed and defeated my people,
shamed my subjects,
leveled my ancestral temple,
making the state a wasteland of thorns
and me like a fish or turtle.
My resentment toward Wú
is deeper than my marrow;
yet my service to Wú
is like a son fearing his father
or a younger brother respecting his elder brother.
These are my words even unto death.
Now that you, the Great Officer, have bestowed your counsel,
how could I dare to have doubts?
Please continue speaking.
I have not sat on comfortable mats,
my mouth has not tasted rich flavors,
my eyes have not looked upon beauty,
and my ears have not listened to refined music
for three years now.
With scorched lips and dry tongue,
I toil my body and labor my strength;
above I serve the ministers,
and below I nurture the subjects.
I wish for one battle with Wú on the open plains of the world,
to exert myself with my own body and arms.
Even if the soldiers of Wú and Yuè should die one after another, their livers and brains smeared on the ground,
that is my wish.
I have thought of this for three years,
but it could not be attained.
Now, internally I weigh my state and find it insufficient to harm Wú,
and externally I serve the feudal lords but cannot succeed.
I am willing to empty the state, abandon my ministers, change my appearance, change my name, and hold a broom and dustpan to serve them by tending their cattle and horses.
Even though I know my waist and neck might be severed,
my hands and feet separated,
and my four limbs scattered
to be the laughingstock of the villages,
my intent would still be fulfilled.
Now that you, the Great Officer, have bestowed your counsel,
it is to preserve a dying state and revive the dead.
I rely on the blessings of my ancestors;
how could I dare not await your command?"
Zǐ Gòng said:
"As for the King of Wú's character,
he is greedy for fame and merit but does not understand profit and harm."
The King of Yuè solemnly stood up from his seat.
Zǐ Gòng said:
"I observe that the King of Wú has fought many wars;
his soldiers are not shown kindness,
his ministers are divided within,
and slanderers are becoming more numerous.
As for Zǐ Xū's character,
he is sincere and upright within,
clear-sighted externally and knows the times;
he would not hide the ruler's faults to save his own life,
but spoke correctly to be loyal to the ruler
and acted straightforwardly for the sake of the state;
yet he was put to death and his advice was not heard.
As for Tài Zǎi Pǐ's character,
he is clever yet foolish,
strong yet weak;
he uses clever talk and sharp words to secure his own position
and is good at deceit to serve his ruler.
He knows what is in front of him but not what follows
and follows the ruler's faults to satisfy his private interests.
He is a sycophant who ruins the state and harms the ruler."
The King of Yuè was greatly pleased.
Zǐ Gòng departed.
The King of Yuè sent him a hundred yì of gold, one precious sword, and two fine horses,
but Zǐ Gòng did not accept them.
He arrived in Wú
and said to the King of Wú:
"I have conveyed the words of a low official to the King of Yuè,
and the King of Yuè was greatly terrified,
saying:
'In the past, I was unfortunate
and lost my predecessors while young;
internally I did not measure my own strength
and committed an offense against Wú.
My army was defeated and I was humiliated;
I fled as a fugitive
and perched upon Huì Jī.
The state became a wasteland
and I was like a fish or turtle.
Relying on the Great King's benevolence,
I was allowed to offer sacrifice vessels
and maintain ancestral rites;
even in death I would not dare forget it,
how could I dare to plot anything?'
His spirit is very fearful
and he will send an envoy to apologize to the King."
Zǐ Gòng stayed for five days,
and the envoy from Yuè indeed arrived
and said:
"The envoy Zhòng of Gōu Jiàn, the laboring servant of the Eastern Sea,
dares to perform the duties of a low official
and has heard a little from your attendants:
'In the past, I was unfortunate
and lost my predecessors while young;
internally I did not measure my own strength
and committed an offense against the Superior State.
My army was defeated and I was humiliated;
I fled as a fugitive
and perched upon Huì Jī.
Relying on the King's benevolence, I was allowed to perform ancestral rites,
and even in death I will not forget.
Now I have heard that the Great King will raise a grand righteous cause
to punish the strong and save the weak,
to trouble the tyrannical Qí and comfort the Zhōu House;
therefore, I have sent a lowly servant to offer vessels stored by former kings:
twenty suits of armor, the Spear of Qū Lú, and the Sword of Bù Guāng,
to congratulate your military officers.
If you will pursue this grand righteous cause,
my humble district, though small,
requests to muster three thousand soldiers from within its borders to follow your low officials.
I personally request to wear armor and hold weapons
to face the arrows and stones in the front;
thus ruler and subjects may die without regret.'"
The King of Wú was greatly pleased,
and then summoned Zǐ Gòng, saying:
"The envoy from Yuè has indeed come,
requesting to send out three thousand soldiers,
and their ruler will also follow
to attack Qí with me.
Is this acceptable?"
Zǐ Gòng said:
"It is not.
To empty another man's state,
to take all of his people,
and also make their ruler follow
is not benevolent.
Your Majesty should accept his gifts
and permit his troops
but decline their ruler;
that would be proper."
The King of Wú agreed.
Zǐ Gòng left and went to Jìn,
and saw Dìng Gōng, saying:
"I have heard:
if plans are not predetermined,
one cannot respond to sudden emergencies;
if troops are not prepared in advance,
one cannot defeat the enemy.
Now Wú and Qí are about to fight;
if they fight and Wú does not win,
Yuè will certainly cause trouble.
If they fight and win,
he will certainly lead his troops against Jìn.
What will Your Majesty do about it?"
Dìng Gōng said:
"How should I prepare for it?"
Zǐ Gòng said:
"Maintain your weapons and set ambushes to wait for them."
The Lord of Jìn agreed.
Zǐ Gòng returned to Lǔ.
The King of Wú indeed raised the troops of nine commanderies
to fight with Qí.
The road went out of Xū Mén,
and they passed by the Platform of Gū Xū.
Suddenly, during the day, he took a nap on the Platform of Gū Xū and had a dream.
When he woke up,
his heart was tranquil yet unsettled.
He then ordered Tài Zǎi Pǐ
and said:
"I had a dream while sleeping during the day,
and upon waking, I felt tranquil yet unsettled.
Please divine it;
might there be something to worry about?
I dreamed I entered the Zhāng Míng Palace;
I saw two cauldrons,
steaming without being heated;
two black dogs were howling to the south and howling to the north;
two hoes were planted in my palace walls;
flowing water was surging,
overflowing my palace halls;
in the rear chambers, drums shook and there was the rattling sound of blacksmiths;
in the front garden, a horizontal rope grew into a parasol tree.
You, divine it for me."
Tài Zǎi Pǐ said:
"How wonderful!
Your Majesty's raising of the army to attack Qí!"
Your servant has heard that the word zhāng
refers to virtue sounding resplendent.
Míng
means that the fame of your victory over the enemy is bright and clear.
The two cauldrons steaming without being cooked over a fire
signify that the Great King’s sagely virtue and vital energy are more than sufficient.
The two black dogs howling to the south and to the north
mean that the barbarians of the four directions have already submitted
and the feudal lords are coming to pay court.
The two plows standing against the palace walls
mean that the farmers will successfully cultivate the fields.
The rushing water overflowing the palace hall
means that neighboring countries will offer tribute and wealth will be more than sufficient.
The sounds of boxes being moved and blacksmiths working in the rear chambers
mean that the palace ladies are joyful and the lutes and zithers are in harmony.
The paulownia trees growing across the front garden
represent the sound of the drums of the Yuè Fǔ."
The Wú Wáng was greatly pleased,
yet his mind was not at rest.
He summoned Wángsūn Luò and asked,
"I suddenly had a dream during the day;
explain it for me."
Wángsūn Luò said,
"Your servant is superficial and shallow in the Way;
I cannot grasp the vast and great.
Regarding the King's dream,
your servant cannot interpret it.
One who might have knowledge of it
is Gōngsūn Shèng, the younger brother of Chángchéng Gōng, the pavilion head of the Dōng Yè Mén.
Shèng was fond of traveling when young
and fond of learning when grown;
he has seen and observed much
and knows the nature and circumstances of ghosts and gods.
I hope the King will ask him."
The King then sent Wángsūn Luò to invite Gōngsūn Shèng,
saying,
"The Wú Wáng was lying down during the day at the Gūxū zhī Tái
when he suddenly had a dream.
He woke up feeling unsettled
and wants you to interpret it.
Hurry to the Gūxū zhī Tái."
Gōngsūn Shèng fell to the ground and wept.
After a while, he rose.
His wife from the side said to Shèng,
"Why is your nature so lowly?
You rarely see the sovereign,
and now that you are suddenly summoned in haste,
your tears and weeping are like rain."
Gōngsūn Shèng looked up to heaven and sighed,
"How tragic!
This is not something you can understand.
Today is the Rénwǔ day,
and the time is in the south.
My fate belongs to Heaven,
and I cannot escape.
My falling to the ground and weeping
was not merely for my own sorrow,
but truly out of grief for the Wú Wáng."
His wife said,
"You reached the sovereign through the Way;
if there is a Way to follow,
you should use it above to admonish the King
and below to discipline yourself.
Now, hearing a sudden summons,
you are filled with worry, confusion, and disorder;
this is not befitting a worthy man."
Gōngsūn Shèng said,
"How foolish!
These are the words of a woman.
I have received the Way for ten years,
hiding myself to avoid harm,
wishing to live out my natural lifespan.
Unexpectedly, I am suddenly summoned in haste;
I will be cast away in mid-life,
and therefore I am sad to be parted from you."
He then departed
and went to the Gūxū Tái.
The Wú Wáng said,
"I am about to go north to campaign against Qí and Lǔ.
My path led out of the Xū Mén
and past the Gūxū zhī Tái,
where I suddenly had a dream during the day.
Interpret it for me,
and tell me if it is auspicious or ominous."
Gōngsūn Shèng said,
"If your servant does not speak,
my life and reputation will be preserved;
if I speak,
I will surely die in a hundred pieces before the King.
However, a loyal official does not care for his own body."
He then looked up to heaven and sighed,
"Your servant has heard that those who love boats will surely drown,
and those who love war will surely perish.
Your servant loves to speak directly
and does not care for his life.
I hope the King will consider this.
Your servant has heard that zhāng
means that in battle you will not be victorious and will flee in panic.
Míng
means leaving the light and entering the darkness.
Entering the gate and seeing cauldrons steaming without being cooked over a fire
means the Great King will not have food cooked by fire.
The two black dogs howling to the south and the north
—black is Yin,
and north is hiding.
The two plows standing against the palace walls
mean that the Yuè army will enter the state of Wú,
destroy the ancestral temple,
and dig up the altars of land and grain.
Rushing water overflowing the palace hall
means the palace will be empty.
The boxes shaking and drumming sounds in the rear chambers
mean sitting and sighing in grief.
The paulownia trees growing across the front garden
—the heart of the paulownia is hollow;
they will not be used for utensils,
but only for the blind attendants
to be buried together with the dead.
I hope the Great King will halt the troops and cultivate virtue;
do not campaign against Qí,
and then this can be dispelled.
Send the subordinates Tàizǎi Pǐ and Wángsūn Luò to remove their caps and sashes,
bare their torsos and go barefoot,
and kowtow in apology to Gōujiàn.
Then the state can be preserved in peace,
and you yourself can avoid death."
When the Wú Wáng heard this,
he became pale with rage
and said,
"I was born of Heaven
and am employed by the spirits!"
He looked to the strongman Shí Pān to kill him with an iron hammer.
Shèng then lifted his head toward heaven and said,
"Alas!
Does Heaven know my grievance?
Being loyal and yet receiving punishment,
dying though innocent.
If you bury me for being upright,
I would rather become a pillar of sound;
cast me to the deep mountains,
and in future generations, I will follow as an echo."
Thereupon, the Wú Wáng ordered his followers to carry him to Zhēng Qiū,
"Let the jackals and wolves eat your flesh,
and the wildfires burn your bones.
When the east wind frequently arrives
and scatters your remains,
with your flesh and bones rotted away,
how can you become an echo?"
Tàizǎi Pǐ hurried forward and said,
"I congratulate the Great King;
the calamity has already been extinguished.
We should therefore raise our cups;
the troops can set out."
The Wú Wáng then appointed Tàizǎi Pǐ as the Right Division Marshal
and Wángsūn Luò as the Left Division Marshal,
and followed the army from Yuè to campaign against Qí.
When Wǔ Zǐxū heard of this,
he admonished him, saying,
"Your servant has heard that to raise an army of one hundred thousand
and lead the troops a thousand li,
the expenses of the people
and the expenditures of the state
amount to thousands of pieces of gold daily.
If you do not care for the deaths of the soldiers and people
but struggle for a single day's victory,
your servant believes this is the height of endangering the state and losing one's life.
Furthermore, you live beside an enemy
yet do not know the danger,
and instead seek enmity abroad,
hoping for luck in another country.
This is like trying to cure a skin rash
while ignoring a disease of the heart and belly;
once it breaks out, you will die.
A skin rash,
a disease of the skin,
is not worth worrying about.
Now Qí is declining a thousand li away,
beyond the borders of Chǔ and Zhào.
If Qí is a disease,
it is only a rash.
Yuè being a disease,
it is in the heart and belly.
If it does not break out, it causes harm;
if it moves, there is death.
I hope the Great King will pacify Yuè and then plan for Qí.
Your servant's words are decisive;
how could I dare not be fully loyal?
Your servant is old this year,
my ears and eyes are not sharp,
and with a mad and confused mind,
I can no longer benefit the state.
I have privately observed the eighth chapter of the Jīn Kuì,
and it is truly distressing."
The Wú Wáng asked,
"What do you mean?"
Wǔ Zǐxū said,
"At dawn on the Xīnhài day of the seventh month of this year,
the Great King began this matter.
Xīn
is the position of the year."
Hài
is the branch that precedes Yīn.
Combined with the Rénzǐ year, it matches the predecessor;
it is advantageous for military action.
Military matters will be decided successfully,
yet virtue resides within.
When the Dipper matches and strikes Chǒu,
and Chǒu
is the root of Xīn.
Dàjí becomes Báihǔ and approaches Xīn,
while Gōngcáo is where Tàicháng approaches Hài.
Dàjí obtaining Xīn constitutes the Jiǔchǒu,
and it is doubled when combined with Báihǔ.
If someone initiates an undertaking under these conditions,
although there may be small victories at first,
there will surely be a great defeat afterward;
Heaven and Earth will bring calamity,
and misfortune will not be long in coming!"
The King of Wú did not listen,
and subsequently, in the ninth month, he sent Tàizǎi Pǐ to attack Qí.
When the army reached the northern suburbs,
the King of Wú said to Pǐ:
"Go forth!
Do not forget those with merit,
and do not pardon those with guilt.
Love the people and nurture the soldiers,
treating them like newborn infants.
Plan with the wise,
and befriend the benevolent."
Tàizǎi Pǐ received the command
and then departed.
The King of Wú summoned the Dàfū Bèlǐ
and asked:
"You were always of one heart and one will with Zǐxū,
sharing thoughts and plans together.
Now that I have raised an army to attack Qí,
why is Zǐxū the only one speaking against it?"
Bèlǐ said:
"Zǐxū wishes to show his full sincerity to the former king;
he calls himself an old madman
whose ears and eyes are not sharp,
who does not understand the ways of the present world,
and who is of no benefit to the state of Wú."
The King then attacked Qí.
Qí fought with Wú at Àilíng,
and the army of Qí suffered a crushing defeat.
After the King of Wú had won,
he sent the Xíngrén Chéng to establish good relations with Qí,
saying:
"The King of Wú heard that Qí had concerns about being submerged
and led his army here to observe.
Since Qí raised an army in the reeds,
Wú did not know how to pacify them;
he set up battle arrays as a precaution
and unexpectedly damaged the Qí army somewhat.
He wishes to conclude a peace treaty and depart."
The King of Qí said:
"I reside here on the northern border
and have no plans to go beyond the boundaries.
Now Wú has crossed the Jiāng and Huái,
traveling over a thousand lǐ to reach our territory
and slaughter our masses.
Relying on the mercy and preservation of Shàngdì,
the state has not yet fallen to ruin.
Since the King now condescends to offer a peace treaty,
how could I dare not obey the command?"
Wú and Qí then made a covenant and departed.
When the King of Wú returned,
he reproached Zǐxū, saying:
"Our former king practiced virtue and was so bright and sagely that he reached Shàngdì.
Bequeathing achievements and exerting effort,
he formed a powerful enmity with Chǔ for your sake.
Now, the former king was like a farmer cutting down the weeds in all directions
to establish a name among the Jīngmán;
this was also due to the Dàfū's efforts.
Now, the Dàfū is senile and restless;
you create changes and stir up trickery,
expressing resentment and malice.
When you come out, you blame my soldiers and masses,
and you disrupt my laws and regulations,
wishing to use omens and portents to frustrate and defeat my army.
Relying on the sincerity sent by Heaven,
the Qí army has submitted.
How could I dare claim the credit for myself?
It is the legacy of virtue from the former king
and the blessings of the divine spirits.
As for you, what effort have you contributed to Wú?"
Wǔ Zǐxū rolled up his sleeves in great anger,
released his sword, and replied:
"In the past, when our former king
had a minister who did not attend court,
it was because he could pursue doubtful plans and avoid evil
so as not to fall into great disaster.
Now Your Majesty casts aside the elders;
the troubles you fear are not external worries.
These are the plans of a lonely youth,
not the affairs of a hegemon king.
When Heaven has not yet abandoned someone,
they will surely rush toward small joys
and approach their great sorrow.
If Your Majesty realizes this and awakens,
the state of Wú will exist for generations.
If you do not realize it and awaken,
the life of the state of Wú will be cut short.
I, Yuán, cannot bear to feign illness and withdraw,
only to see Your Majesty being captured.
I truly prefer to die first;
hang my eyes upon the gate
so I may observe the funeral of the state of Wú."
The King of Wú did not listen.
Sitting in the palace hall,
he alone saw four people in the courtyard leaning back-to-back.
The King found it strange and looked at them.
The ministers asked:
"What does the King see?"
The King said:
"I see four people leaning back-to-back.
I heard someone speak, and then they fled in four directions."
Zǐxū said:
"According to the King's words,
you are about to lose the masses."
The King of Wú said angrily:
"Your words are inauspicious!"
Zǐxū said:
"Not only are they inauspicious,
but Your Majesty's state is also lost."
Five days later,
the King of Wú was again sitting in the palace hall
when he saw two people facing each other;
the person facing north killed the person facing south.
The King asked the ministers:
"Do you see them?"
They said:
"We see nothing."
Zǐxū said:
"What did the King see?"
The King said:
"Where I saw four people the other day,
today I saw two people facing each other again,
and the person facing north killed the person facing south."
Zǐxū said:
"I have heard that four people fleeing
is rebellion.
The north-facing killing the south-facing
is a minister killing the ruler."
The King did not respond.
The King of Wú set out wine on the Wéntái;
all the ministers were present.
Tàizǎi Pǐ held the administration,
the King of Yuè sat in attendance,
and Zǐxū was also there.
The King said:
"I have heard this:
A ruler does not despise a minister with merit;
a father does not hate a son with strength.
Now Tàizǎi Pǐ has merit for me,
so I shall grant him a noble rank and the highest reward.
The King of Yuè is compassionate, benevolent, loyal, and trustworthy;
he serves me with filial piety.
I shall further increase the size of his state
to repay his merit in assisting the campaign.
What do the Dàfū think?"
The ministers congratulated him, saying:
"The Great King personally practices the highest virtue
and nurtures scholars with an open mind.
All the ministers advance together;
when they see difficulty, they compete to die for it.
Your name and title are illustrious,
and your majesty shakes the Four Seas.
Those with merit receive rewards,
and lost states are restored.
The achievements of a hegemon and the affairs of a king
are all bestowed upon the ministers."
Thereupon,
Zǐxū crouched on the ground, weeping, and said:
"Alas,
how sorrowful!
To encounter this silence;
loyal ministers cover their mouths,
while slanderers are at your side.
Governance is ruined and the Way is destroyed;
flattery and fawning are without limit.
Wicked talk and false words
turn the crooked into straight.
Embracing slander to attack the loyal,
this will destroy the state of Wú.
Once the ancestral temple is leveled
and the altars of soil and grain receive no offerings,
the city walls will become ruins,
and brambles and thorns will grow in the palace halls."
The King of Wú was greatly enraged and said:
"Old minister, you are full of trickery
and are a bane to Wú.
You wish to monopolize power and arrogate authority,
to single-handedly overthrow the state of Wú.
Because of the former king,
I have not had the heart to apply the law.
Now, withdraw and reflect on yourself;
do not obstruct the plans of Wú."
Zǐxū said:
"Now your servant is neither loyal nor trustworthy,
and can no longer serve as a minister to the former King.
I do not dare to cherish my own life,
but I fear for the downfall of the state of Wú.
In the past, Jié killed Guān Lóngféng,
and Zhòu killed Prince Bǐgān.
Now your Great Majesty executes your servant,
thus joining the ranks of Jié and Zhòu.
May your Great Majesty exert yourself;
your servant now takes his leave."
Zǐxū returned home
and spoke to Bèilí, saying:
"I shouldered my bow and fitted my arrows at the borders of Zhèng and Chǔ,
crossed the Jiāng and the Huái rivers,
and brought myself to this place.
The former King listened to and followed my plans,
and we crushed Chǔ to avenge the humiliation we suffered.
I wished to repay the former King's kindness, yet it has come to this.
It is not that I pity myself,
but disaster is about to reach you as well."
Bèilí said:
"If your remonstrances are not heard,
what benefit is there in suicide?
Why not go into exile?"
Zǐxū said:
"Where can an exiled minister go?"
When the King of Wú heard of Zǐxū's resentment,
he sent a man to bestow upon him the Zhǔlòu sword.
Zǐxū received the sword,
went barefoot and hitched up his robes,
and descended from the hall into the middle of the courtyard.
Looking up to the heavens and crying out in grievance,
he said:
"In the beginning, I served your father as a loyal minister to establish Wú,
devised strategies to crush Chǔ,
subjugated the powerful Yuè in the south,
and spread our prestige among the feudal lords,
achieving the merits of a hegemon king.
Now you do not use my words,
but instead bestow this sword upon me.
I die today,
but the palace of Wú will become a ruin,
creeping weeds will grow in the courtyards,
and the people of Yuè will dig up your altars of state.
How could you forget me?
In the past, the former King did not wish to establish you as heir,
but I contended for it at the risk of my life,
and in the end, your wish was fulfilled;
for this, the other princes bore much resentment against me.
I have only performed merits for Wú,
yet now you forget my kindness in stabilizing the state
and instead bestow death upon me;
is this not preposterous!"
When the King of Wú heard this,
he was greatly enraged and said:
"You are neither loyal nor trustworthy.
When you served as my envoy to Qí,
you entrusted your son to the Bào clan of Qí;
you had a heart that turned outward from me."
He urgently ordered him to commit suicide,
saying, "I will not let you see anything."
Zǐxū grasped the sword,
looked up to the heavens and sighed, saying:
"After I die,
future generations will surely regard me as loyal.
Above, I shall match the eras of Xià and Yīn,
and I shall be able to be friends with Guān Lóngféng and Bǐgān."
He then fell upon the sword and died.
The King of Wú then took Zǐxū's body,
placed it in a chīyí leathern bag,
and threw it into the river,
saying:
"Xū,
after you have died once,
how can you have any awareness?"
He then cut off his head,
placed it atop a high tower,
and said to it:
"The sun and moon will scorch your flesh,
the swirling winds will blow against your eyes,
the blazing light will burn your bones,
the fish and turtles will eat your flesh,
and your bones will turn to shapeless ash;
what will there be to see?"
He then discarded the torso
and threw it into the river.
Zǐxū then followed the current and raised the waves,
coming and going with the tide,
surging and battering the banks until they collapsed.
Thereupon, the King of Wú said to Bèilí:
"You once discussed my shortcomings with Zǐxū."
He then shaved Bèilí's head and punished him.
When Wángsūn Luò heard of this,
he did not attend court.
The King summoned him and asked:
"Why do you find fault with me and not attend court?"
Luò said:
"Your servant is simply afraid!"
The King said:
"Do you consider my killing of Zǐxū to be a grave matter?"
Luò said:
"Your Great Majesty's temper is high,
while Zǐxū's position was below you,
so the King executed him.
How is my life any different from Zǐxū's?
It is because of this that I am afraid."
The King said:
"It was not that I listened to Zǎi Pǐ to kill Zǐxū,
but that Xū was plotting against me."
Luò said:
"I have heard that for one who is a ruler of men,
there must be ministers who dare to remonstrate;
for those in high positions,
there must be associates who dare to speak out.
As for Zǐxū,
he was an old minister of the former King.
If he were not loyal and trustworthy,
he could not have been a minister to the former King."
The King of Wú felt a pang of sorrow in his heart
and regretted killing Zǐxū, saying:
"Could it be that Zǎi Pǐ slandered Zǐxū?"
and he wished to kill him.
Luò said:
"You must not.
If the King kills Pǐ,
this would make for two Zǐxūs."
Consequently, he did not execute him.
In the fourteenth year,
after Fūchāi had killed Zǐxū,
for successive years the harvests were poor,
and the people harbored much resentment.
The King of Wú again attacked Qí,
digging a canal between Shāng and Lǔ,
connecting north to Qì
and west to Jì.
He wished to join Lǔ and Jìn to launch an attack at Huángchí.
Fearing his ministers would remonstrate again,
he issued an order to the capital saying:
“I shall attack Qí;
anyone who dares to remonstrate shall die.”
Tàizǐ Yǒu knew that Zǐxū was loyal but ignored, and that Tàizǎi Pǐ was sycophantic and monopolized power;
he wanted to speak frankly
but feared incurring blame,
so he used a parable to provoke the King.
At dawn, holding pellets and a slingshot,
he came from the rear garden,
his clothes soaked and his shoes wet.
The King found it strange and asked him:
“Why are your clothes soaked and shoes wet,
and your body in such a state?”
Tàizǐ Yǒu said:
“Just now, while strolling in the rear garden,
I heard the sound of autumn cicadas
and went to observe them.
The autumn cicada climbs a tall tree,
drinks the pure dew,
sways with the wind,
and chirps mournfully,
thinking itself secure.
It does not know that a praying mantis is leaping over branches and climbing twigs,
dragging its waist and raising its claws,
crouching its body.
The mantis focuses its heart and advances,
its intent on the prize.
It does not know that yellow birds fill the green woods,
hovering in the shade of the branches,
inching forward,
wanting to peck at the mantis.
The yellow bird only knows the flavor of the mantis,
but does not know that I am holding a slingshot and aiming,
about to let fly a pellet to strike its back.
Just now, I was single-mindedly intent on the yellow bird,
not noticing the deep pit beside me, and suddenly falling into it,
plunging into a deep well.
That is why my body is soaked and my shoes are wet;
I have almost become a laughingstock for Your Majesty.”
The King said:
“The stupidity of the world
is no greater than this.
Only coveting the profit ahead,
without seeing the disaster behind.”
The Prince said:
“The stupidity of the world
has instances even worse.
Lǔ inherits the legacy of Zhōu Gōng
and has the teachings of Kǒngzǐ;
they maintain benevolence and embrace virtue,
having no designs on neighboring states,
yet Qí raised troops to attack them,
not caring for the lives of the people,
only for what they can gain.
Now Qí has merely raised troops to attack Lǔ,
unaware that Wú has mobilized all the soldiers within its borders
and exhausted the wealth of its treasuries,
exposing its army across a thousand lǐ to attack them.
Wú only knows to cross borders and campaign against a country that is not its own,
unaware that the King of Yuè will select suicide squads
to emerge from the mouths of the Sānjiāng,
enter into the midst of the Wǔhú,
slaughter our state of Wú,
and destroy our Wú palaces.
The danger of the world
is no greater than this.”
The King of Wú did not listen to the Prince’s remonstrance
and proceeded to attack Qí in the north.
The King of Yuè heard that the King of Wú was attacking Qí
and sent Fàn Lǐ and Xiè Yōng to lead troops to station at the sea and open the river,
to cut off the route of Wú.
They defeated Tàizǐ Yǒu at Gūxióngyí,
and through the river and the Huái, they turned back to raid Wú,
thereupon entering the state of Wú,
burning the Gūxū Tower,
and seizing their large ships.
Wú defeated the army of Qí at Àilíng,
then returned with the army to face Jìn,
and disputed precedence with Dìng Gōng but had not yet come to an agreement.
Urgent reports from the border arrived,
reporting the chaos caused by Yuè.
King Fūchāi of Wú was greatly afraid
and gathered the feudal lords to deliberate, saying:
“Our road is far,
and we have no meeting point ahead;
what is the best course?”
Wángsūn Luò said:
“It is better to advance;
then you will hold power over the feudal lords
to achieve your aim.
I ask the King to assemble the soldiers
to make the orders clear,
encourage them with high rank,
shame them for non-compliance,
and order each to fight to the death.”
At dusk, Fūchāi issued orders to fodder the horses and feed the soldiers;
at midnight, he ordered them to take up weapons and don armor,
bridle the horses and hold gags,
extinguish the cooking fires,
and advance in darkness.
The Wú army all had patterned rhinoceros hide armor, long shields, and Biǎnzhū swords,
marching in square formation.
The army of the central division all had white skirts, white banners, white armor, and white-feathered arrows,
looking like flowering reeds from afar.
The King himself held a battle-axe,
standing in formation under his flag.
The left army all had red skirts, red banners, cinnabar armor, and vermilion-feathered arrows,
looking like fire from afar.
The right army all had black skirts, black carriages, black armor, and black-feathered arrows,
looking like ink from afar.
There were thirty-six thousand armored men,
and all were in place by cockcrow.
Once the formation was set,
they were one lǐ from the Jìn army.
It was not yet dawn
when the King took up the drumsticks and personally sounded the gongs and drums;
the three armies shouted in unison
to rouse the troops,
and the sound shook the heavens and moved the earth.
The army of Jìn was greatly alarmed
and did not come out,
but instead stayed behind their strong fortifications.
They sent Tónghè to the army,
who said:
“The border soldiers of the two armies are on good terms;
there was no appointment for today.
Now your great state has skipped proper sequence and arrived at the military fortifications of our humble town;
I venture to ask the reason.”
The King of Wú personally replied:
“The Son of Heaven has issued a command;
the House of Zhōu is humble and diminished,
and the tributes of the feudal lords
no longer enter the royal treasury,
so that God and the spirits cannot be informed.
There was nothing to inspire awe in those of the Jī surname,
so they sent an envoy to inform me,
with caps and canopies filling the road.
Initially, Zhōu relied on Jìn
and thus neglected the barbarians.
But now that Jìn has rebelled like this,
I have come in prostration to you,
as I am unwilling to be ranked as a younger brother
merely for the sake of struggling for strength.
I have advanced and dare not leave;
if you do not grant me precedence,
I will be laughed at by the feudal lords.
Whether I serve you will be decided today,
and whether I cannot serve you will also be decided today.
I venture to trouble the messenger to travel back and forth;
I personally await your command outside the fortifications.”
As Tónghè was about to return,
the King of Wú stepped on his left foot to seal the matter with Tónghè.
Upon his report,
Tónghè sat in rank with the feudal lords and grandees before Dìng Gōng of Jìn.
After conveying the message,
he told Zhào Yāng:
“I observed the King of Wú’s expression;
he seems to have a great anxiety.
At least a favorite concubine or legitimate son has died,
or else the state of Wú is in trouble;
at most the people of Yuè have entered Wú
and he cannot return.
His mind is filled with bitter sorrow,
and whether to advance or retreat is a difficult matter for him;
we must not do battle with him.
My lord should grant him precedence as previously arranged;
do not endanger the state by struggling over rank.
However, do not simply grant it;
you must make him demonstrate his sincerity.”
Zhào Yāng agreed
and went to see Dìng Gōng, saying:
“Among the Jī surname in Zhōu,
Wú is the elder branch and may take precedence
to fulfill the protocols of the state.”
Dìng Gōng agreed
and ordered Tónghè to report back.
Thereupon,
the King of Wú felt ashamed by the righteousness of Jìn
and withdrew the screen to meet.
The lords and ministers of both states were present together;
the King of Wú was addressed as Duke first,
and the Lord of Jìn followed,
and all the ministers completed the covenant.
After Wú had taken precedence over Jìn and was returning,
before they had crossed beyond Huángchí,
Yuè heard that the King of Wú had stayed away for a long time and had not returned;
so they mobilized all their soldiers and were about to cross Zhāngshān,
cross the Sānjiāng,
wishing to attack them.
Wú also feared the harm caused by Qí and Sòng,
so he ordered Wáng Sūn Luò to report his achievements to Zhōu,
saying:
"In the past, Chǔ did not provide its tributes,
so as to distance itself from the brotherly states.
My former ruler Hélǘ could not endure their wickedness;
girding his sword and brandishing his spear,
he pursued Chǔ Zhāo Wáng in the Zhōngyuán.
Heaven took note of his loyalty,
and the Chǔ army suffered a crushing defeat.
Now Qí is no more virtuous than Chǔ,
and it also does not respect the orders of the King,
distancing itself from the brotherly states.
Fūchāi could not endure their wickedness;
wearing armor and girding a sword,
he went directly to Àilíng.
Heaven bestowed blessings upon Wú,
and the Qí army turned back their blades and retreated.
How could Fūchāi dare to boast of his own achievements?
This was the assistance and protection of the virtue of Wén and Wǔ.
When it was time to return to Wú,
the harvests of the year were not ripe;
therefore, following the Jiāng and going up the Huái, he dug deep water channels,
coming out between Shāng and Lǔ,
and returned to report to the attendants of the Tiānzǐ."
The King of Zhōu replied:
"Has the Elder Uncle sent you here?
The One Man of the covenant states shall rely on him;
I truly commend it.
If the Elder Uncle can assist me, the One Man,
then we shall both receive eternal blessings.
What worry would the house of Zhōu have?"
He then bestowed bows, crossbows, and royal gifts
to enhance his titles and posthumous names.
The King of Wú returned from Huángchí
to rest the people and disband the troops.
In the twentieth year, the King of Yuè raised an army to attack Wú,
and Wú fought with Yuè at Zuìlǐ.
The Wú army was greatly defeated;
the troops scattered,
and the dead were beyond counting.
Yuè pursued and crushed Wú.
The King of Wú was in dire straits;
he sent Wáng Sūn Luò to kowtow and request peace,
just as Yuè had once come to him.
The King of Yuè replied:
"In the past, Heaven gave Yuè to Wú,
but Wú did not accept it.
Now Heaven gives Wú to Yuè;
how can I go against it?
I request to offer the land east of Gōuyǒng [for you to live],
so that I and you may be two rulers!"
The King of Wú said:
"When I was in Zhōu,
I performed the ritual of sharing a meal with the former kings.
If the King of Yuè does not forget the righteousness of the Zhōu house
and allows me to be a dependency,
that would also be my wish.
The envoy requests a peace settlement based on the righteousness between states;
I hope the Great King will consider it."
Dàfū Zhòng said:
"Wú has been unprincipled;
now that we have fortunately captured them,
I wish for the King to decide their fate."
The King of Yuè said:
"I shall destroy your altars of earth and grain and level your ancestral temples."
The King of Wú remained silent.
He requested peace seven times,
but the King of Yuè would not listen.
In the twenty-third year,
in the tenth month,
the Yuè Wáng again attacked Wú.
The state of Wú was in distress and did not fight;
the soldiers dispersed,
the city gates were not guarded,
and Wú was eventually slaughtered.
The Wú Wáng led his ministers and fled,
galloping by day and running by night.
For three days and three nights,
they journeyed until they reached Qín Yúháng Shān.
His heart was filled with sorrow and worry,
his eyes stared blankly,
his steps were frantic,
his stomach was empty and his mouth hungry.
Finding raw rice, he ate it,
and he lay prostrate on the ground to drink water.
He looked at his attendants and asked:
"What is the name of this?"
They replied:
"This is raw rice."
The Wú Wáng said:
"This is what Gōngsūn Shèng spoke of: not having cooked food and fleeing in panic."
Wángsūn Luò said:
"After eating your fill, let us depart;
ahead is Xū Shān,
and within the western slope, we can hide and rest."
The King went,
and after a short while,
they found raw melons that were already ripe.
The Wú Wáng picked and ate them.
He said to his attendants:
"Why do melons grow in winter,
and why do the people near the road not eat them?"
The attendants said:
"These are things grown from excrement;
people do not eat them."
The Wú Wáng asked:
"What do you mean by grown from excrement?"
The attendants said:
"During the height of summer,
people eat raw melons
and relieve themselves by the roadside;
the seeds sprout again,
but the autumn frost makes them unpalatable,
so they are not eaten."
The Wú Wáng sighed and said:
"This is what Zǐxū called 'the morning eater'."
He said to Tàizǎi Pǐ:
"I executed Gōngsūn Shèng
and threw him on the peak of Xū Shān.
Because I fear the reproach and shame of the world,
my feet cannot advance,
and my heart cannot go forward."
Tàizǎi Pǐ said:
"Death and life,
failure and success—
should one avoid them?"
The King said:
"Indeed.
Does he have no consciousness?
You, try calling him from the front;
if Shèng is there,
he should respond immediately."
The Wú Wáng stopped at Qín Yúháng Shān
and called out:
"Gōngsūn Shèng!"
Three times he called,
and Shèng responded from within the mountain, saying:
"Gōngsūn Shèng!"
Three calls and three responses.
The Wú Wáng looked up to heaven and cried:
"How can I return?
I have encountered Shèng throughout the generations."
In a moment,
the Yuè troops arrived
and surrounded Wú on three sides.
Fàn Lǐ was in the middle column;
with his left hand he held a drum,
and with his right hand he held the drumstick and beat it.
The Wú Wáng wrote on his arrows and shot them into the armies of Zhòng and Lǐ;
the message said:
"I have heard that once the cunning rabbit is dead,
the good dog is cooked.
If the enemy state is destroyed,
the strategists must perish.
Now Wú is ailing;
what do you, Great Officers, have to worry about?"
Dàfū Zhòng and Xiàngguó Lǐ attacked urgently.
Dàfū Zhòng wrote on an arrow and shot it back,
saying:
"High Heaven is vast and blue,
as if both existing and not.
The humble servant Zhòng of the Yuè ruler Gōujiàn dares to say:
Formerly, Heaven granted Yuè to Wú,
but Wú refused to accept it;
this was a reversal of Heaven's will.
Gōujiàn respected Heaven and achieved merit;
having returned to his state,
now High Heaven rewards Yuè's merit.
Respectfully we receive it,
and we dare not forget.
Moreover, Wú has six great transgressions
that led to its ruin.
Does the King know them?
There was the loyal minister Wǔ Zǐxū, who gave loyal admonitions and met his death;
that is the first great transgression.
Gōngsūn Shèng spoke directly but had no reward;
that is the second great transgression.
Tàizǎi Pǐ is foolish and uses flattering words,
is frivolous and slanders,
and speaks recklessly as he pleases;
you listened and employed him;
that is the third great transgression.
Qí and Jìn did not act in rebellion,
nor did they have the faults of arrogance or excess,
yet Wú attacked these two states,
humiliated their rulers and ministers,
and destroyed their altars;
that is the fourth great transgression.
Furthermore, Wú and Yuè share the same language and the same music,
above they align with the same stars,
and below they share one principle,
yet Wú invaded and attacked;
that is the fifth great transgression.
Long ago, Yuè personally killed the former King of Wú;
no crime is greater than that.
Yet you were fortunate enough to attack us,
but you did not follow Heaven's command and abandoned your enmity,
which later became a great disaster;
that is the sixth great transgression.
The Yuè Wáng carefully follows what is carved by Blue Heaven;
how could he dare not obey?"
Dàfū Zhòng said to the Yuè ruler:
"In mid-winter the qi is settled,
and Heaven is about to execute.
If one does not carry out Heaven's execution,
one will instead receive its calamity."
The Yuè Wáng bowed respectfully
and said:
"Indeed.
Now regarding the Wú Wáng,
what shall we do?"
Dàfū Zhòng said:
"Your Majesty should wear the garments of the five victories,
gird the Bùguāng sword,
hold the Qūlú spear,
and with glaring eyes and loud words, seize him."
The Yuè Wáng said:
"Indeed."
Then, following Dàfū Zhòng's advice, he said to the Wú Wáng:
"I have indeed received the command today."
After some time passed,
the Wú Wáng did not commit suicide.
The Yuè Wáng again sent word to him, saying:
"How can the King endure such humiliation and deep shame!
In this world, there is no king who lives for ten thousand years;
death and life are the same.
Now you still have some remaining honor;
why must you force my army to use their blades on the King?"
The Wú Wáng still would not commit suicide.
Gōujiàn said to Zhòng and Lǐ:
"Why do you two not execute him?"
Zhòng and Lǐ said:
"We
hold the positions of ministers
and dare not carry out an execution on a sovereign.
We wish for our Lord to be swift in giving the order;
Heaven's execution must be carried out
and cannot be long delayed."
The Yuè Wáng again glared with angry eyes and said:
"Death
is what people loathe.
One who is loathed
should have no crime against Heaven
and not fail his fellow men.
Now you bear the guilt of six transgressions,
yet you do not know shame or humiliation and seek to live;
is that not base?"
The Wú Wáng then sighed heavily,
looked all around him,
and said:
"Agreed!"
He then drew his sword and fell upon it, dying.
The Yuè Wáng said to Tàizǎi Pǐ:
"As a minister,
you were disloyal and untrustworthy,
destroying the state and ruining your king."
He then executed Pǐ along with his wife and children.
When the Wú Wáng was about to fall on his sword,
he looked at his attendants and said:
"In life I have been ashamed,
and in death I am disgraced.
If the dead have consciousness,
I will be ashamed before the former kings in the underworld,
and I cannot bear to see the loyal ministers Wǔ Zǐxū and Gōngsūn Shèng.
If they have no consciousness,
I have failed my life.
In death, you must link silk cords to cover my eyes,"
Fearing that they will not suffice to cover me,
I wish to have three more layers of embroidered silk
to cover my eyes.
In life I was not enlightened,
so in death do not let him see my form.
What can I do!"
The Yuè Wáng then buried the Wú Wáng with ritual propriety
at Bēiyóu on Qínyúháng Shān.
The Yuè Wáng commanded the soldiers who had contributed to the success of our army
to each provide a basket of earth to bury him.
Zǎi Pǐ was also buried beside Bēiyóu.
Among the former rulers of Yuè was Wúyú,
who was the last of the enfeoffments by Xià Yǔ.
Yǔ's father was Gǔn,
a descendant of Dì Zhuānxū.
Gǔn took a wife from the daughter of the Yǒushēn clan,
named Nǚxī.
Though she had reached maturity, she had not yet borne offspring.
While playing at Dǐshān,
she found a Job’s tear seed and swallowed it.
Feeling as if she were moved by a person,
she consequently became pregnant
and gave birth to Gāomì through her side.
The family lived among the Xīqiāng,
in a place called Shíniǔ.
Shíniǔ is located in the western rivers of Shǔ.
During the time of Dì Yáo,
they encountered surging floodwaters;
the world was submerged,
the Jiǔzhōu were blocked,
and the Sìdú were obstructed.
The Emperor then worried that Zhōngguó was not at peace
and grieved for the common people who suffered calamity.
He then commanded the Sìyuè,
who then recommended the worthy and good
to be tasked with controlling the waters.
From Zhōngguó to Tiáofāng,
no one recommended anyone,
and the Emperor had no one to appoint.
The Sìyuè then raised Gǔn and recommended him to Yáo.
The Emperor said:
“Gǔn goes against commands and ruins his kin;
he will not do.”
The Sìyuè said:
“Comparing him to the other ministers, there is none like Gǔn.”
Yáo employed him to control the waters;
he received the command for nine years,
but his work was not successful.
The Emperor angrily said:
“I knew he was incapable.”
He then sought another
and found Shùn.
He made him act as regent for the administration of the Tiānzǐ
and go on tours of inspection.
Observing that Gǔn’s water control had shown no progress,
he then executed Gǔn at Yǔshān.
Gǔn threw himself into the water
and transformed into a huángnái,
thus becoming the god of Yǔyuān.
Shùn and the Sìyuè recommended Gǔn’s son, Gāomì.
The Sìyuè said to Yǔ:
“Because the water control was unsuccessful under Shùn,
we raise you to continue your father's merit.”
Yǔ said:
“Yes!
I, your servant, dare to exhaustively achieve results to unify with the will of Heaven;
I rely only on my assignment!”
Yǔ was pained that his father’s work was not successful;
he followed the Jiāng and went up the Hé,
crossing the Zhēn and Huái completely.
He toiled his body and exhausted his thoughts
in this way for seven years.
Hearing music, he did not listen;
passing his own door, he did not enter;
his cap snagging, he did not look back;
his sandal left behind, he did not step back for it.
Before his work could be completed,
he was lost in sorrowful deep thought.
He then examined the *Huángdì Zhōngjīnglì*,
which was recorded by the sages,
and it said:
“In the southeast of the Jiǔshān,
the pillar of heaven is called Wǎnwei.
The Chìdì is at the palace gate;
at the peak of its crags, it is supported by patterned jade
and covered by a massive rock.
Its book is of golden tablets,
with characters of green jade,
bound with white silver,
all with their patterns carved.”
Yǔ then toured east and climbed Héngyuè;
he sacrificed a white horse with its blood,
but unfortunately did not find what he sought.
Yǔ then climbed the mountain
and looked up at the sky and whistled.
Consequently, in a dream, he saw a man in red embroidered robes
who called himself the messenger of Xuányí Cāngshuǐ.
“I heard the Emperor sent Wénmìng here,
so I have come to attend to him.
It is not yet the right time,
but I shall inform you of the date.
Do not make playful chants;
therefore rely on the songs of Fùfǔshān.”
Looking east, he said to Yǔ:
“If you wish to obtain my mountain god’s book,
fast below the rocky peak of Huángdì.
On the Gēngzǐ day of the third month,
climb the mountain and open the rock;
the book of golden tablets will be there.”
Yǔ withdrew and fasted again.
On the Gēngzǐ day of the third month,
he climbed Wǎnweishān,
opened the book of golden tablets,
and by examining the golden tablets and jade characters,
he understood the principles of managing the waters.
He returned again to the peaks
and rode the four vehicles to travel the rivers,
starting at Huòshān
and circling around to gather at the Wǔyuè.
The *Shī* says:
“In truth, that Nánshān,
only Yǔ cultivated it.”
He then toured the Sìdú
and consulted with Yì and Kuí.
Traveling to famous mountains and great marshes,

he summoned their gods and asked them about the veins and principles of mountains and rivers, the presence of gold and jade, the types of birds, beasts, and insects, as well as the customs of the people in the eight directions, and the distance in lǐ of the lands of unique and distant countries.
He ordered Yì to draft and record these.
Therefore it was named the *Shānhǎijīng*.
Yǔ was thirty and not yet married.
Traveling to Túshān,
he feared the lateness of the time
and that he would lose his proper measure;
he then spoke:
“If I am to marry,
there must be a sign.”
Thereupon a nine-tailed white fox came to Yǔ.
Yǔ said:
“White
is the color of my garments.
The nine tails
are the proof of a king.”
The song of Túshān says:
“The white fox wanders slowly,
its nine tails are thick and lush.
My family has a good relative,
who comes as a guest to be king.
Establishing a house and home,
my prosperity is built by him.”
“The intersection of Heaven and man is here;
then my actions are clear!”
Yǔ consequently married from Túshān,
calling her Nǚjiāo,
and spent only the days Xīn, Rén, Guǐ, and Jiǎ with her.
Yǔ had been traveling for ten months
when Nǚjiāo gave birth to a son, Qǐ.
Since his birth, Qǐ did not see his father,
and wailed and wept day and night.
Yǔ traveled on,
ordering Tàizhāng to pace the east and west,
and Shùhài to measure the north and south,
reaching the breadth of the Bājí
and determining the numbers of Heaven and Earth.
Yǔ crossed to the south of the Jiāng to examine the principles of the water,
and a yellow dragon carried the boat on its back.
The people in the boat were terrified,
but Yǔ chuckled and laughed, saying:
“I received my command from Heaven,
exhausting my strength to labor for the myriad people.
Life
is nature;
death
is fate;
what can you do to me?”
His expression did not change,
and he said to the boatmen:
“This is how Heaven serves me.”
The dragon dragged its tail, left the boat, and departed.
Traveling south to reach Cāngwú,
he saw a bound person,
and Yǔ patted his back and wept.
Yì said:
“This person committed a crime
and it is only right that he be thus;
why weep for him?”
Yǔ said:
“When the world follows the Way,
the people do not suffer guilt.
When the world lacks the Way,
crimes reach even good people.
I have heard that if one man does not plow,
someone will suffer hunger;
if one woman does not tend silkworms,
someone will suffer cold.
I govern the water and land for the Emperor,
harmonizing the people to live in peace,
allowing them to find their place.
Now, for him to suffer the law like this,
is proof that my virtue is thin and I cannot transform the people.
Therefore, I weep out of sorrow.”
Thereupon,
he traveled all around the world,
reaching the end of tracks in the east,
extending to Jīshí in the west,
crossing Chìàn in the south,
passing Hángǔ in the north,
circling Kūnlún,
inspecting the Liùhù,
mapping the veins of the earth,
and naming the metals and stones.
He drained the Liúshā in the western corner,
He redirected the Ruòshuǐ at Běihàn.
Qīngquán and Chìyuān were divided to enter caverns,
connecting to the Jiāng and flowing east to Jiéshí.
He dredged the Nine Rivers at Qiányuān,
opened the Five Waters in the northeast,
cut through Lóngmén,
and opened Yīquè.
He leveled and surveyed the soil
and observed the land to divide it into provinces.
Various regions each stepped forward
to offer their tributes;
the people left the rugged highlands
and returned to the Zhōngguó.
Yáo said:
“Indeed!
By this, Jì is made secure.”
Thus he bestowed upon Yǔ the name Bóyǔ,
his office was called Sīkōng,
and he was granted the surname Sì.
He led the regional lords to inspect the twelve divisions.
When Yáo passed away,
Yǔ observed three years of mourning,
as if mourning his own father and mother,
wailing by day and weeping by night
until his breath could hardly sustain his voice.
Yáo abdicated the throne to Shùn,
and Shùn recommended Dà Yǔ,
changing his office to Sītú
to assist internally in the position of Yú
and act externally as the leader of the Nine Lords.
When Shùn passed away,
he abdicated and commanded Yǔ to take the throne.
Yǔ observed mourning for three years;
his body became gaunt and withered,
and his face and eyes turned dark and black.
He ceded the throne to Shāngjūn
and withdrew to live south of Yángshān and north of Yīn’ā.
The myriad people did not follow Shāngjūn
but followed to wherever Yǔ was.
They were like startled birds taking to the sky
or frightened fish entering a deep pool;
they sang by day and hummed by night,
climbing high places to cry out,
saying:
“Yǔ has abandoned us,
whom shall we support!”
When Yǔ’s three years of mourning were finished,
out of pity for the people and having no other choice,
he ascended to the position of the Son of Heaven.
After three years he examined merits,
and after five years his governance was settled.
He traveled throughout the world
and returned to Dàyuè,
climbing Máoshān to receive the lords of the four quarters,
while the various ministers looked on.
Among the feudal lords of the central states,
Fángfēng arrived late;
he was executed to show the public,
demonstrating that the whole world belonged to Yǔ.
Then he held a grand assembly to deliberate on the ways of governing the state,
