internally praising the merit of carefulness at Fǔshān,
and externally displaying sagely virtue to respond to the heart of Heaven.
He then renamed Máoshān as Huìjīzhīshān.
Thus he handed down the state's governance,
allowing the myriad people to rest and flourish,
and the state's name was called Xiàhòu.
He enfeoffed those with merit
and gave titles to those with virtue;
no evil was too small to go unpunished,
and no merit was too slight to go unrewarded.
The whole world looked up with expectation,
like a child longing for its mother
or a son returning to his father,
yet he remained in Yuè.
Fearing that his ministers would not follow,
he spoke, saying:
“I have heard that those who eat the fruit
do not damage its branches;
those who drink the water
do not muddy its stream.
I obtained the scrolls of Fùfǔ
and was able to eliminate the disasters of the world,
allowing the people to return to their neighborhoods;
such virtue is manifest—
how could such things be forgotten?”
Then he accepted suggestions and listened to remonstrances,
setting the people at ease and managing their dwellings;
he cleared the mountains and felled timber to build towns,
designed seals,
and used crossbeams to make gates.
He adjusted the weights and balances,
standardized the dry measures,
and created wells to show the people,
establishing them as laws and regulations.
Fènghuáng perched in the trees,
Luánniǎo nested nearby,
Qílín walked in the courtyard,
and all sorts of birds gathered in the marshes.
Having reached old age,
he sighed and said:
“My years are late and I am in the twilight of my life,
my lifespan is nearly finished;
this is the end.”
He commanded his ministers, saying:
“After my hundred generations,
bury me on Huìjīzhīshān,
with a reed outer coffin and a paulownia inner coffin.
Dig the pit seven feet deep,
but let it not reach the springs below;
let the mound be three feet high,
and bury me with three levels of earthen steps.”
Later he said:
“Do not change the field boundaries; those who live there find joy in them,
but those who implement changes find them bitter.”
After Yǔ passed away,
all the auspicious omens departed together.
Heaven appreciated Yǔ’s virtue and rewarded his merit,
causing the hundred birds to return and till the people's fields,
with a difference between the great and small,
moving in order,
one group flourishing while another declined,
coming and going with regularity.
When Yǔ passed away,
he passed the throne to Yì.
Yì observed mourning for three years,
and whenever he thought of Yǔ, he never failed to speak of him.
When the mourning was finished,
Yì withdrew in favor of Yǔ’s son, Qǐ, to the south of Jīshān.
The feudal lords left Yì and paid court to Qǐ,
saying:
“Our lord
is the son of Emperor Yǔ.”
Qǐ then ascended to the position of the Son of Heaven
and ruled the state in Xià.
He followed the excellence of the Yǔgòng,
surveyed all the lands of the Jiǔzhōu
to plant the five grains,
which continued for successive years without end.
Qǐ sent messengers to sacrifice to Yǔ in Yuè during the spring and autumn seasons,
establishing an ancestral temple atop Nánshān.
Six generations after Yǔ came Emperor Shàokāng;
Shàokāng feared that the sacrifices to Yǔ would be cut off,
so he enfeoffed his concubine's son in Yuè,
giving him the name Wúyú.
When Yú first received the fief,
the people lived in the mountains;
although they had the benefit of the bird-tilled fields,
the taxes and tributes barely covered the expenses of the ancestral temple sacrifices.
Thus they continued to follow the hills and dry lands to farm,
or pursued birds and deer to provide food.
Wúyú was simple and plain;
he did not set up decorations for his palaces
and lived among the people,
offering sacrifices at Yǔ’s tomb in Huìjī in spring and autumn.
Wúyú’s lineage passed down for over ten generations;
the last ruler was weak and inferior
and could not maintain his position,
so he joined the commoners as a registered citizen.
The sacrifices to Yǔ were cut off.
After ten and some years,
there was a person who could speak from birth,
and his words sounded like “niǎoqínhū.”
Chattering and warbling,
he pointed to heaven and faced Yǔ’s tomb, saying:
“I am a descendant of Lord Wúyú.
I am about to restore the sacrifices of the former lords,
restoring the sacrifices at the tomb of our Yǔ,
to pray for blessings from Heaven for the people
and to communicate with the ways of ghosts and gods.”
The people were joyful
and all helped to perform the sacrifices to Yǔ,
offering tributes during the four seasons.
Consequently, they together enfeoffed and established him
to succeed as the heir of the Lords of Yuè
and restore the sacrifices of the Xià King.
He settled the auspicious omen of the bird-tilled fields
to request life for the people.
From then on, there was gradually the righteousness of lord and minister,
and he was named Wúrén.
Rén fathered Wúyì;
Wúyì focused his heart on guarding the state
and did not lose the mandate of Heaven.
When Wúyì died,
the successor was Fūtán.
Fūtán fathered Yǔncháng;
Yǔncháng was established,
and during the times of the Kings of Wú: Shòumèng, Zhūfán, and Hélǘ,
the rise of Yuè to hegemony began with Yǔncháng.
In the fifth year of King Gōu Jiàn of Yuè,
in the fifth month,
he entered into servitude in Wú together with the Grandees Zhòng and Fàn Lǐ.
The various ministers all saw them off at the edge of the Zhèjiāng River.
Facing the water, they performed the ancestral sacrifice for travel,
and the army arrayed at Gùlíng.
The Grandee Wén Zhòng stepped forward to offer a prayer,
and his words were:
"May August Heaven provide protection and aid;
what was formerly submerged shall later be raised high.
Calamity is the root of virtue,
and worry is the hall of blessings.
Those who intimidate others shall perish;
those who submit shall flourish.
Though the King is being led away,
there shall be no disaster thereafter.
The separation of lord and minister in life
moves the August Sovereign above.
The multitudes of heaven feel sorrow,
and none are not moved to grief.
Your servant requests to present dried meat
and offer three cups of wine."
The King of Yuè looked up to heaven and sighed deeply,
raising his cup with tears falling,
silent and saying nothing.
Zhòng again stepped forward to pray, saying:
"May the Great King enjoy virtuous longevity,
without bound or limit.
May Heaven and Earth receive the spirit,
and the divine deities provide support.
Our King treats them with depth,
and auspicious protection is at his side.
Virtue dissolves a hundred calamities,
and benefit receives its blessing.
Leave that court of Wú,
and return to the state of Yuè.
Now that the cups of wine have been raised,
we request to cry 'Ten Thousand Years'."
The King of Yuè said:
"I inherited the remaining virtue of the former kings
to guard the state at the border.
Fortunately, I received the counsel of the various grandees
and thus preserved the ancestral mounds of the former kings.
Now I encounter disgrace and shame,
becoming a laughingstock for the world.
Is this the fault of me alone,
or the responsibility of the various grandees?
I do not know where the blame lies;
I wish for you gentlemen to discuss its meaning."
The Grandee Fú Tóng said:
"How base these words are!
Long ago, Tāng was imprisoned at Xiàtái,
and Yī Yǐn did not leave his side.
King Wén was imprisoned in the Stone Chamber,
and Tàigōng did not abandon his state.
Prosperity and decline rest with Heaven;
survival and ruin depend on man.
Tāng changed his demeanor to flatter Jié,
and King Wén submitted to find favor with Zhòu.
Xià and Yīn relied on force to mistreat the two sages,
while the two lords humbled themselves to attain the Way of Heaven.
Therefore, King Tāng did not grieve because of his destitution,
and King Wén of Zhōu did not consider his distress an illness."
The King of Yuè said:
"Long ago, Yáo employed Shùn and Yǔ and the world was governed.
Although there was the harm of the great flood,
it did not become a disaster for the people.
Strange portents did not reach the common folk,
so how much less should they reach a ruler of men?"
The Grandee Kǔ Chéng said:
"It is not as the King says.
Heaven has its cycles of destiny,
and virtue has its depth or shallowness.
Huángdì did not yield,
while Yáo transmitted the throne of the Son of Heaven.
Among the Three Kings,
ministers assassinated their lords.
Among the Five Hegemons,
sons assassinated their fathers.
Virtue has its breadth or narrowness,
and qì has its highs and lows.
The present world is like a marketplace for men,
where goods are set out to practice deceit,
and schemes are held to wait for the enemy.
If one is unfortunately trapped in hardship,
one simply seeks to overcome it.
If the Great King does not observe this
but instead harbors joy and anger..."
The King of Yuè said:
"One who employs others does not disgrace his person;
one who acts on his own endangers his state.
All the grandees previously planned for matters before they occurred,
toppling the enemy and crushing the foe,
and while sitting, beckoned the blessings of Mount Tài.
Now I am in such destitution,
yet you say that Tāng and Wén were distressed but later surely became hegemons.
How do these words not violate ritual propriety?
A gentleman disputes every inch of time but casts away pearls and jade.
Now I hoped to be free from the worries of military campaigns,
yet I have instead been captured and held in the hands of the enemy.
My person is a servant and slave;
my wife is a servant and concubine.
Going but not returning,
dying as a guest in an enemy state.
If my soul has consciousness,
I will be ashamed before the former kings.
If it has no consciousness,
my body and bones will be abandoned.
Why do the words of the grandees
not align with my intentions?"
Then the Grandees Zhòng and Fàn Lǐ said:
"We have heard the ancients say:
'If one's dwelling is not secluded,
one's will will not be broad;
if one's form is not distressed,
one's thoughts will not be far-reaching.'
Sage kings and worthy masters
all encountered the difficulties of destitution and hardship
and suffered unpardonable disgrace.
Their persons were confined but their names became honored;
their bodies were insulted but their reputations became glorious.
They occupied low positions but did not consider them evil;
they dwelt in danger but did not consider it trivial.
The Five Emperors had profound virtue and no regrets regarding hardships,
yet they still had the worry of floods.
The Three Kings endured the disgrace of violent hardship
and did not escape the difficulties of the Three Peaks.
They shed tears and suffered injustice;
they walked and wept as slaves.
They elaborated the Yì and created the hexagrams,
and the Way of Heaven protected them.
When the time exceeded the expected period,
obstruction ended and prosperity began.
The feudal lords joined together to save the King's mandate.
Signs were seen in the red-maned horse and the black fox.
Assisting ministers bound their hair in service,
mountains were split and shackles broken.
Returning to their states to cultivate virtue,
they finally punished their enemies.
Their reputation rose within the seas
as easily as turning over the back of a hand.
The whole world revered them,
and their achievements lasted for ten thousand generations.
Though the Great King is humbled and in hardship,
your servants will truly exhaust their schemes.
A sword that can cut through bone has no advantage in carving or paring;
a spear that can pierce iron has no convenience in splitting a hair.
A gentleman who establishes strategies does not have talk of sudden success.
Now your servants follow the celestial patterns
and examine the earthly records.
The two qì sprout together,
but survival and ruin reside in different places.
When they flourish, we are disgraced;
when we become hegemons, they perish.
The two states contend for the Way,
and it is not yet known which will succeed.
The King's danger
is a matter of the calculation of Heaven's Way;
why must you grieve for yourself?
Good fortune
is the gate of misfortune;
blessing
is the root of calamity.
Now, though the Great King is in a time of danger and hardship,
who knows if it is not the omen of future success?"
The Grandee Jì Ní said:
"Now the King makes his state at Huìjī
and is destitute upon entering Wú.
His words are sorrowful and his phrases are bitter,
and the various ministers weep for him.
Although there is a heart of resentment and stubbornness,
there is none who is not moved.
But why does the King use deceptive words and clamorous talk
to deceive one another?
Your servant truly does not accept this."
The King of Yuè said:
"I am about to leave and enter Wú,
and will entrust the state to the various grandees.
I wish for each of you to state your views,
and I shall entrust the state to them."
The Grandee Gāo Rú said:
"I have heard that the Grandee Zhòng is loyal and good at planning;
the people are close to his wisdom,
and the officers are happy to be of use.
If you now entrust the state to this one man,
its path will surely be maintained.
Why follow your heart and oppose the mandates of the various ministers?"
The Grandee Yè Yōng said:
"The Grandee Wén Zhòng
is the pillar and beam of the state
and the claws and teeth of the ruler.
A thoroughbred horse cannot be matched in a race,
and the sun and moon cannot shine together.
If the King entrusts the state to Zhòng,
then the ten thousand guidelines and thousand principles will all be upheld."
The King of Yuè said:
"The state
is the state of the former kings.
I am weak in strength and inferior in power,"
I have been unable to protect the *Shè Jì*,
or to uphold the ancestral temples.
I have heard that when a father dies, the son succeeds him;
when a ruler perishes, his ministers remain close to him.
Now, I am leaving these matters to the various *Dà fū*,
as I go to serve as an official guest in *Wú*.
Entrusting the state and handing over the people
to you gentlemen
is my own doing,
but it is also your worry.
Ruler and minister share the same path;
father and son share the same spirit;
this is the natural essence of Heaven.
How can those who remain show loyalty while those who depart are deemed unfaithful?
Why do you *Dà fū* discuss matters with such inconsistency,
causing me (*gū*) to feel uncertain in my heart?
To govern the state and employ the worthy, to evaluate merit and achieve success,
is the mandate of the ruler.
To follow instructions and obey principles,
and to not fail in one's station,
is the duty of the minister.
I look to you *Dà fū* for your respective abilities,
while I simply say that I dedicate myself to service.
Alas!
How tragic!"
*Jì Ní* said:
"What the King has expressed
is indeed the correct principle.
In the past, when *Tāng* entered *Xià*,
he entrusted the state to *Wén Sì*.
When *Xī Bó* went to *Yīn*,
he entrusted the state to one elder.
Now, while our hearts are delayed in *Xià*,
our will is set upon returning.
A wife going to the market instructs her heir in sweeping and cleaning;
a ruler going into exile commands his ministers to defend and protect.
You ask of these matters,
and we ministers advise according to our abilities.
Now the King wishes for the aspirations of the officers,
that each may present their true feelings,
to highlight those who are capable,
and deliberate on what is appropriate."
The *Yuè Wáng* said:
"The *Dà fū*'s argument is correct.
I am about to depart;
I wish to hear of your intentions."
*Dà fū Zhòng* said:
"To manage the labors within the borders,
and to prepare for farming and warfare without;
ensuring no land is left waste,
and the people remain loyal and attached—
this is my duty."
*Dà fū Fàn Lǐ* said:
"To assist a ruler in peril,
and to preserve a state that is perishing;
to not be ashamed of the hardships of humiliation,
and to calmly endure a place of disgrace;
to go and surely return, and to take revenge alongside the King—
this is my duty."
*Dà fū Kǔ Chéng* said:
"To issue the King's commands
and make manifest the King's virtue;
to share in distress when in poverty,
and to share in hegemony when advancing;
to organize the complex and manage the chaotic,
making the people understand their roles—
this is my duty."
*Dà fū Yè Yōng* said:
"To follow orders and accept missions,
forming alliances with the feudal lords;
to convey commands and transmit intentions,
managing gifts and exchanges;
to resolve worries and avert calamities,
ensuring there is no doubt;
when departing, not forgetting the mission;
when returning, being free from blame—
this is my duty."
*Dà fū Hào Jìn* said:
"To be of one mind and united will,
matching the superiors;
below, not disobeying orders,
acting according to the King's command;
to cultivate virtue and practice righteousness,
to maintain trust and cherish old knowledge;
to decide doubts when facing wrongs,
and to remonstrate if the King errs;
to have a straightforward heart without yielding,
listing faults and maintaining fairness;
not showing favoritism to relatives,
nor being selfish toward outsiders;
to offer oneself to the ruler,
remaining consistent from beginning to end—
this is my duty."
*Dà fū Zhū Jī Yǐng* said:
"To gaze at the enemy and set the formation,
with flying arrows and raised weapons;
stepping on bellies and wading through corpses,
while blood flows abundantly;
eager to advance and never retreating
when two armies confront each other;
to break the enemy and attack the masses,
with power that overawes a hundred nations—
this is my duty."
*Dà fū Gāo Rú* said:
"To cultivate virtue and perform kindness,
comforting and soothing the people;
to personally face worries and toil,
attending to every action in person;
mourning the dead and caring for the sick,
saving the lives of the people;
accumulating old stores and gathering new harvests,
eating without luxury;
making the state wealthy and the people prosperous,
nurturing strength for the King—
this is my duty."
*Dà fū Jì Ní* said:
"To watch the heavens and observe the earth,
recording the calendar and the *Yīn* and *Yáng*;
to observe changes and compare disasters,
distinguishing between omens and auspicious signs;
when the sun and moon change color,
and the five essences move out of order;
knowing fortune when blessings appear,
and knowing misfortune when portents arise—
this is my duty."
The *Yuè Wáng* said:
"Although I (*gū*) am entering the northern state
to be a wretched captive of *Wú*,
with you *Dà fū* cherishing virtue and possessing skills,
each maintaining your respective duties
to protect the *Shè Jì*,
what cause have I to worry?"
Thus they parted at the *Zhè Jiāng* River.
The ministers wept,
all filled with sorrow.
The *Yuè Wáng* looked up to the sky and sighed, saying:
"Death
is what men fear.
But for me to hear of death,
there is no trepidation within my heart."
Then he boarded the ship and departed directly,
never looking back.
The *Yuè Wáng* Lady leaned against the ship and wept.
Looking at the crows and magpies pecking at shrimp on the riverbank,
flying away and returning again,
she sang while weeping:
"I look up at the flying birds, the crows and kites,
soaring through the dark void, calling as they flutter.
They gather on the islets, free and at ease,
pecking at shrimp and raising their wings toward the clouds.
They go and come as they please.
I am without guilt yet I must endure this land;
what crime have I committed to be condemned by Heaven?
Sailing alone toward the west,
who knows in what year I shall return!
My heart is anxious as if being cut;
my tears flow down in two streams."
She further chanted in sorrow:
"Those flying birds, the kites and crows,
have wheeled and soared, coming together and relaxing.
Their hearts are set only on white shrimp;
why do they dwell and feed in the rivers and lakes?
They hover and soar again, wandering and flying;
departing and returning—alas!
I began serving my lord by leaving my home;
let my life end in the lord's capital.
What fortune to have met him at last,
yet now I leave my state to go to *Wú*.
The wife shall wear coarse hemp and be a maidservant;
the husband shall cast aside his crown and be a slave.
The years ahead are distant and hard to reach;
the injustice and grief are bitter, my heart is pained.
My bowels are knotted a thousand times, held within my breast;
alas, in such sorrow I forget to eat.
I wish my body were like a bird,
soaring high on strong wings.
Leaving my state, my heart wavers;
who can know my feelings of indignation and grief!"
The *Yuè Wáng* heard the Lady's resentful song,
and was moved with inward grief;
he then said:
"What have I (*gū*) to worry?
My six quill-feathers are fully prepared!"
Thereupon he entered *Wú*.
Seeing *Fū Chāi*,
he kowtowed, bowed twice, and declared himself a servant,
saying:
"Your humble servant from the Eastern Sea, *Gōu Jiàn*,
is ashamed before *Huáng Tiān* above
and has failed *Hòu Tǔ* below.
Not measuring my own strength,
I brought disgrace upon the King's soldiers
and committed crimes at the border.
The Great King has pardoned my profound guilt
and deigned to make me a laboring servant,
allowing me to hold the winnowing fan and broom.
Truly receiving such great kindness,
and being able to preserve my life for a moment longer,
I cannot overcome my upward gratitude and downward shame.
Your servant *Gōu Jiàn* kowtows and bows his head."
Wú Wáng Fūchāi said:
"I have been lenient toward you;
do you not remember the enmity of the former king?"
Yuè Wáng said:
"If I, your servant, am to die, then I shall die;
I only hope Dàwáng will pardon me."
Wǔ Xū was by his side,
his eyes like flaring fire,
his voice like thunder,
he stepped forward and said:
"When a flying bird is high above the blue clouds,
one still wishes to release a silk-tethered arrow to shoot it down.
How much more so when it is lying near the Huá chí
or perched upon the halls of the courtyard?
Now Yuè Wáng has been banished among the southern mountains,
wandering in a place where he cannot survive.
Fortunately, he has come to cross our territory
and entered our gates.
This is like a chef's prepared meal;
how can it be let slip away?"
Wú Wáng said:
"I have heard that executing those who have surrendered and killing those who are submissive
brings disaster upon three generations.
It is not that I love Yuè and thus do not kill him;
I fear the punishment of Huángtiān,
who instructs me to pardon him."
Tàizǎi Pǐ remonstrated, saying:
"Zixū is clear about temporary schemes
but does not understand the way to bring peace to the state.
I hope Dàwáng will persist in what you hold to
and not be constrained by the mouths of the common crowd."
Fūchāi then did not execute Yuè Wáng,
but ordered him to drive carriages and tend horses,
keeping him secretly within the palace.
After three months,
Wú Wáng summoned Yuè Wáng to an audience.
Yuè Wáng prostrated himself in front,
while Fàn Lǐ stood behind him.
Wú Wáng said to Fàn Lǐ:
"I have heard that a virtuous woman does not marry into a broken and ruined house,
and the benevolent and worthy do not serve as officials in a destroyed and extinguished state.
Now Yuè Wáng is without the Way,
his state is about to perish,
its Shèjì have collapsed,
he himself faces death and his lineage will be cut off,
becoming a laughingstock to the world.
Yet you and your master have both become slaves
and come to submit to Wú;
is this not contemptible?
I wish to pardon your crimes.
Can you change your heart and renew yourself,
abandoning Yuè to return to Wú?"
Fàn Lǐ replied:
"I have heard that an official of a fallen state does not dare to speak of governance,
and a general of a defeated army does not dare to speak of courage.
I was neither loyal nor trustworthy in Yuè.
Now Yuè Wáng did not follow Dàwáng’s commands
and used troops to hold out against Dàwáng
until he incurred guilt.
Master and servant have both surrendered.
We have received Dàwáng’s great grace,
and master and servant are able to protect each other.
I wish to be permitted to enter and prepare for sweeping and cleaning,
and to go out to serve as an attendant;
this is my wish."
At this time, Yuè Wáng lay prostrate on the ground weeping,
thinking to himself that he had finally lost Fàn Lǐ.
Wú Wáng knew that Fàn Lǐ could not be obtained as a servant
and said to him:
"Since you will not shift your will,
I shall again place you in the Shíshì."
Fàn Lǐ said:
"I request to follow your command."
Wú Wáng rose and entered the palace,
and Yuè Wáng and Fàn Lǐ hurried into the Shíshì.
Yuè Wáng wore a loincloth
and a woodcutter's headgear.
His wife wore a skirt without hems
and a jacket with the left opening.
The husband chopped fodder and tended the horses;
the wife provided water, removed dung, and swept.
For three years they showed no resentment or anger,
and their faces bore no look of regret.
Wú Wáng climbed a distant tower
and saw Yuè Wáng, his wife, and Fàn Lǐ sitting beside horse manure;
the etiquette of ruler and subject was maintained,
and the decorum of husband and wife was complete.
Wáng turned and said to Tàizǎi Pǐ:
"That Yuè Wáng
is a man of singular integrity.
Fàn Lǐ
is a gentleman of singular character.
Although in a place of extreme distress,
they do not lose the etiquette of ruler and subject.
I am moved to pity for them."
Tàizǎi Pǐ said:
"I hope Dàwáng, with the heart of a sage,
will take pity on these destitute and solitary men."
Wú Wáng said:
"For your sake, I shall pardon them."
Three months later,
he chose a lucky day with the intent to pardon them.
He summoned Tàizǎi Pǐ to consult, saying:
"Yuè and Wú
share the same land and contiguous borders.
Gōujiàn was ignorant and dim,
personally wishing to act as an enemy.
I, succeeding the spirits of Huángtiān
and the inherited virtue of former kings,
punished the Yuè bandits
and imprisoned them in the Shíshì.
My heart cannot bear to see it
and I wish to pardon them.
What do you think?"
Tàizǎi Pǐ said:
"I have heard that no virtue goes unrequited.
Dàwáng bestows benevolent grace upon Yuè;
how would Yuè dare not to repay it?
I hope Dàwáng will complete your intention."
When Yuè Wáng heard this,
he summoned Fàn Lǐ and told him:
"I have heard word from outside
and my heart is personally joyful,
yet I also fear it will not be completed."
Fàn Lǐ said:
"Dàwáng, be at peace.
The matter will have a purpose.
In the first door of Yùmén,
on the Wùyín day of the twelfth month this year,
the time was at sunrise.
Wù
is the day of imprisonment.
Yín
is the hour of the Yīnhòu.
It matches the later meeting of the Gēngchén year.
To hear joy on a Wùyín day
and not be punished for one's crimes
is the nature of the day.
The time was added to Mǎo, which harms Wù.
Gōngcáo became Téngshé and overlooked Wù.
Planning for profitable matters lies with Qīnglóng.
Qīnglóng is present,
winning at first.
But it overlooks Yǒu,
which is the Qì of death.
And it overcomes Yín.
This is the time overcoming the day,
and the application further assists this.
Regarding the matter being sought,
there is worry from top to bottom.
Is this not the Net of Heaven spread in four directions,
where all things are entirely harmed?
Why should Dàwáng rejoice?"
Indeed, Zixū remonstrated with Wú Wáng, saying:
"In the past, Jié imprisoned Tāng but did not execute him;
Zhòu imprisoned Wén Wáng but did not kill him.
Tiāndào turns back,
and calamity turns into fortune.
Thus Xià was executed by Tāng,
and Yīn was destroyed by Zhōu.
Now Dàwáng has already imprisoned the Yuè ruler but has not carried out the execution.
I say Dàwáng is deeply deluded.
Might there not be the disaster of Xià and Yīn?"
Wú Wáng then summoned Yuè Wáng,
but did not see him for a long time.
Fàn Lǐ and Wén Zhòng were worried and performed divination, saying:
"Wú Wáng will be captured."
After a while,
Tàizǎi Pǐ came out,
saw Dàfū Zhòng and Fàn Lǐ, and said that Yuè Wáng was again detained in the Shíshì.
Wǔ Zixū again remonstrated with Wú Wáng, saying:
"I have heard that when a king attacks an enemy state,
if he conquers it, he should add execution to it.
Thus, afterward there is no worry of retaliation,
and he avoids disaster for his descendants.
Now Yuè Wáng has already entered the Shíshì;
you should plan against him early,
or he will surely become a disaster for Wú."
Tàizǎi Pǐ said:
"In the past, Qí Huán carved off land where he had reached to bestow it upon the Yān Gōng,
and the ruler of Qí obtained a beautiful reputation.
Sòng Xiāng crossed the river and then fought;
the Chūnqiū praised his righteousness.
When success is established, the name is praised;
even if the army is defeated, virtue remains.
If Dàwáng truly pardons Yuè Wáng,
then your achievements will top the Wǔ Bà,
and your name will surpass those of ancient times."
Wú Wáng said:
"Wait until my illness is cured,
then for the Tàizǎi’s sake, I shall pardon him."
One month later,
Yuè Wáng came out of the Shíshì,
and summoned Fàn Lǐ, saying:
"Wú Wáng is ill
and has not recovered for three months.
I have heard of the way of a subject:
when the ruler is ill, the subject worries.
Moreover, Wú Wáng has treated me
with very deep grace."
Regarding the failure of the illness to heal,
only you, sir, can divine it."
Fàn Lǐ said:
"That the Wú Wáng will not die
is clear.
By the day of jǐsì,
he shall recover.
May the Dàwáng take note of this."
The Yuè Wáng said:
"The reason I have reached such straits yet did not die
is due solely to your strategies, sir.
If I were to hesitate again,
how could that be my intention?
Whether it is feasible or not,
please plan it, sir."
Fàn Lǐ said:
"I have privately observed that the Wú Wáng is truly not a normal person;
he often speaks of the righteousness of Chéng Tāng but does not practice it.
I wish for the Dàwáng to request to inquire after his illness;
when granted an audience,
then request his stool and taste it,
observe its color and appearance,
and then you should bow in congratulation.
State that he will not die,
and set the date of his recovery.
Once your words are proven true,
what then will the Dàwáng have to worry about?"
The next day, the Yuè Wáng said to Tàizǎi Pǐ:
"This captive servant wishes to see the King once to inquire after his illness."
Tàizǎi Pǐ immediately went in to speak to the Wú Wáng,
and the King summoned him for an audience.
It happened that the Wú Wáng was relieving himself;
Tàizǎi Pǐ was carrying the urine and excrement out,
and encountered him in the doorway.
The Yuè Wáng then bowed
and requested to taste the Dàwáng's waste
to determine the fortune of his health.
He then took the waste and excrement with his hand and tasted it.
He then entered and said:
"Your lowly captive servant Gōujiàn congratulates the Dàwáng;
the King's illness will improve by the day of jǐsì,
and by the rénshēn day of the third month, the illness will be cured."
The Wú Wáng said:
"How do you know this?"
The Yuè Wáng said:
"I once served a master and heard regarding stool that
those whose taste aligns with the grains but opposes the seasonal qì will die,
while those that align with the seasonal qì will live.
Just now,
I privately tasted the Dàwáng's stool;
its foul taste was bitter, pungent, and sour.
This taste
corresponds to the qì of spring and summer.
Based on this, I know it."
The Wú Wáng was greatly pleased
and said:
"He is a benevolent man."
He then pardoned the Yuè Wáng, allowing him to leave his stone chamber
and go to his palace quarters,
where he performed his duties of herding as before.
After the Yuè Wáng tasted the foul stool,
he suffered from bad breath.
Fàn Lǐ then ordered the attendants to all eat cén grass
to mask the odor.
Afterwards,
the Wú Wáng's illness was cured on the day the Yuè Wáng had predicted.
In his heart, he was mindful of his loyalty.
After returning to administrative affairs,
he held a grand drinking feast at Wéntái.
The Wú Wáng issued an order saying:
"Today, prepare a north-facing seat for the Yuè Wáng,
and the ministers shall serve him with the rituals due to a guest."
Wǔ Zǐxū hurried out,
went to his quarters,
and did not take his seat.
When the wine had flowed freely,
Tàizǎi Pǐ said:
"How strange!
Among those seated today,
each has their own words.
The unrighteous flee,
while the righteous remain.
I have heard:
similar sounds harmonize with each other,
and similar hearts seek each other out.
Now, the State Minister is a man of rigid bravery;
perhaps he is inwardly ashamed of the presence of supreme benevolence,
and so does not take his seat;
is that not so?"
The Wú Wáng said:
"Indeed."
Thereupon, Fàn Lǐ and the Yuè Wáng both rose
to offer a toast for the Wú Wáng's longevity.
Their words were:
"The lowly servant Gōujiàn, following the minor official Fàn Lǐ,
offers this goblet for a thousand years of longevity.
Our words are:
The August One is above,
his brilliance shines down upon the four seasons,
with a united heart observing the compassionate and benevolent.
The Dàwáng personally bestows great grace,
establishing righteousness and practicing benevolence.
The nine virtues fill the four borders,
and his majesty subdues the ministers.
Oh, how wonderful!
May his virtue be passed on without limit,
moving the sun above,
with auspicious omens descending in abundance.
May the Dàwáng's life be extended for ten thousand years,
long preserving the state of Wú.
All within the four seas submit,
and the feudal lords come as guests to serve.
Now that the wine goblet has been raised,
may you forever receive ten thousand blessings."
Thereupon, the Wú Wáng was greatly pleased.
The next day,
Wǔ Zǐxū entered to remonstrate, saying:
"What did the Dàwáng see yesterday?
I have heard that one may harbor the heart of a tiger or wolf within,
while maintaining beautiful words without,
merely using external appearances to preserve their life.
A jackal cannot be called honest,
and a wolf cannot be befriended.
Now the Dàwáng enjoys listening to momentary words
but does not consider the troubles of ten thousand years.
You cast aside loyal and straightforward speech
and listen to the words of slanderous men.
You do not eliminate an enemy of blood-soaked vengeance,
nor do you end a resentment that harbors poison.
This is like letting hair fall onto a charcoal stove and expecting it to be charred,
or throwing an egg under a weight of a thousand jūn and expecting it to remain whole—
is this not perilous?
I have heard that when Jié climbed high, he knew he was in danger,
yet he did not know how to secure himself;
when facing a sharp blade, one knows one will die,
yet one does not know how to preserve oneself.
The confused should know to return;
the path of the lost is not far.
I hope the Dàwáng will examine this."
The Wú Wáng said:
"I was ill for three months,
yet I did not hear a single word from the Xiàngguó;
this shows the Xiàngguó's lack of compassion.
Furthermore, you did not provide what my mouth desired,
and your heart did not miss me;
this shows the Xiàngguó's lack of benevolence.
Now, if a minister is neither benevolent nor compassionate,
how can one know if he is loyal or faithful?
The Yuè Wáng was confused and lost,
abandoned the duty of guarding his borders,
and personally led his subjects
to submit to me;
this is his righteousness.
He personally served as a captive,
and his wife personally served as a concubine,
without resenting me.
When I was ill,
he personally tasted my urine;
this is his compassion.
He emptied his storehouses
and exhausted his treasures and silks,
not dwelling on past grievances;
this is his loyalty and faithfulness.
These three qualities being established,
he uses them to support me.
If I were to listen to the Xiàngguó and execute him,
that would be my lack of wisdom,
merely to satisfy the Xiàngguó's private whims!
Would that not betray August Heaven?"
Zǐxū said:
"Why are the Dàwáng's words so reversed?
When a tiger lowers its posture,
it is about to strike.
When a wildcat lowers its body,
it is seeking what it will seize.
A pheasant is caught in a net because it is dazzled by movement;
a fish dies from the bait because it finds it pleasing.
Furthermore, when the Dàwáng first took over the government,
you occupied the ninth position of the Jade Gate;
if you were cautious of failure in affairs,
there would be no blame.
This year, on the jiǎxū day of the third month,
the time was at the crowing of the cock.
Jiǎxū
is the meeting of the year's positions.
Qīnglóng is in Yǒu,
virtue is in Earth,
and punishment is in Metal;
this day harms its own virtue.
It is known that a father will have a disobedient son,
and a ruler will have a minister with rebellious intentions.
The Dàwáng considers the Yuè Wáng's submission to Wú as righteousness,
considers his drinking urine and eating waste as compassion,
and considers his emptying the storehouses as benevolence.
Yet these are the actions of one who has no love for others,
and thus he cannot be befriended.
He listens with his face and observes with his appearance
only to preserve his life.
Now that the Yuè Wáng has entered into service to Wú,
his schemes are deep indeed."
Emptying his treasuries,
and showing no sign of resentment,
this is deceiving our King.
Down below, drinking the King’s urine,
is, up above, devouring the King’s heart.
Down below, tasting the King’s excrement,
is, up above, devouring the King’s liver.
How extreme!
The Yuèwáng’s honoring of Wú
means that Wú will be captured by him.
May the Great King pay heed and examine this;
your servant dares not flee death and thereby fail the former King.
Once the state is reduced to ruins
and the ancestral temples are overgrown with thorns,
can such regret be remedied?"
The Wúwáng said:
"Xiàngguó, set it aside.
Do not speak of it again;
I cannot bear to hear it any longer."
Thereupon,
he finally pardoned the Yuèwáng to return to his state,
seeing him off outside the Shémén.
The various ministers performed the roadside sacrifice.
The Wúwáng said:
"I pardon you
and let you return to your state.
You must remember this from beginning to end;
King, you must exert yourself."
The Yuèwáng kowtowed and said:
"Now that the Great King has pitied your servant's isolation and destitution,
allowing me to return to my state alive and whole,
along with the likes of Zhǒng and Lǐ,
I wish to die beneath your carriage wheels.
By the azure Heavens above,
your servant dares not be unfaithful."
The Wúwáng said:
"Alas!
I have heard that a gentleman does not go back on his word;
it has already been carried out.
King, exert yourself."
The Yuèwáng bowed twice and knelt prostrate.
The Wúwáng then led the Yuèwáng to mount the carriage;
Fàn Lǐ took the reins,
and they departed.
Arriving at the Sānjīn,
he looked up to the sky and sighed:
"Alas!
In my time of hardship and distress,
who could have thought I would live to cross this ford again?"
He said to Fàn Lǐ:
"Today is the Jiǎchén day of the third month,
and the sun has begun to decline.
I have received the mandate of Heaven
to return to my homeland;
will there be no future troubles?"
Fàn Lǐ said:
"Great King, do not doubt;
look straight ahead and proceed on your way.
Yuè shall have good fortune,
and Wú shall have sorrow."
Arriving at the Zhèjiāng River,
he saw that the mountains and rivers of Great Yuè were beautiful once more,
and heaven and earth were clear again.
The King and his Lady sighed:
"I had already lost all hope
and bidden eternal farewell to the myriad people.
Who could have expected to return once more
and see my homeland again?"
Having finished speaking, he covered his face,
his tears streaming down.
At this time, the myriad people were all joyful,
and the various ministers all offered their congratulations.
Yuè Wáng Gōujiàn served Wú,
until his return to Yuè,
in the seventh year of Gōujiàn.
The common people bowed to him on the road,
saying:
"The King alone has suffered no more hardship.
Now the King receives the blessing of Heaven
and returns to the state of Yuè;
the traces of the Hegemon and King take their rise from here."
The King said:
"I was not prudent with the teachings of Heaven
and had no virtue toward the people.
Now I cause the ten thousand surnames to toil by gathering at the crossroads;
what virtue or transformation shall I use to repay the people of the state?"
Looking back, he spoke to Fàn Lǐ, saying:
"Today is the twelfth month, on the Jǐsì day,
and the time is approaching Yúzhōng.
I wish to use this moment to arrive at the capital;
how is that?"
Fàn Lǐ said:
"Let the Great King stay for a moment
while your servant divines the day."
Thereupon Fàn Lǐ stepped forward and said:
"How extraordinary!
The Great King’s choice of the day.
The King should hasten quickly,
with carriages galloping and men running."
Yuè Wáng whipped his horse and flew in his carriage,
and thus returned to the palace.
Wú enfeoffed a hundred lǐ of land to Yuè,
reaching east to Tàndù,
stopping west at Zhōuzōng,
going south to Yúshān,
and bordering north on the sea.
Yuè Wáng said to Fàn Lǐ:
"I have suffered disgrace for successive years;
the situation was enough to die for.
But having obtained the Minister's strategy,
I have returned once more to the southern lands.
Now I wish to settle the state and establish a city,
but the people are insufficient,
and the work cannot be raised.
What should be done about this?"
Fàn Lǐ replied:
"Táng and Yú divined the land,
Xià and Yīn enfeoffed states,
Gǔgōng planned the city,
and the Zhōu capital of Luò overawed ten thousand lǐ,
its virtue reaching the eight poles.
Was it merely that they wished to break strong enemies and seize neighboring states?"
Yuè Wáng said:
"I could not uphold the systems of former rulers
or cultivate virtue to defend myself;
my lost multitudes took refuge on the mountain of Huìjī,
pleading for life and begging for mercy.
I suffered humiliation and bore shame,
imprisoned in the Wú palace.
Fortunately, I have returned to my state,
followed by a fief of a hundred lǐ.
I intend to honor the will of the former rulers
by returning to the heights of Huìjī,
and it is appropriate to relinquish the land of Wú."
Fàn Lǐ said:
"In the past, Gōng Liú left Tái and his virtue was manifested in the Xià;
Dǎnfù yielded his land and his fame arose at Qí.
Now the Great King wishes to build a capital for the state
and annex the borders of enemy states;
if you do not reside in a capital of level and easy terrain
or occupy a place accessible from all four directions,
how will you establish the achievements of a Hegemon and King?"
Yuè Wáng said:
"My plans are not yet determined.
To build the inner and outer city walls
and distribute the neighborhoods and gates,
I wish to entrust these matters to the Minister."
Thereupon Fàn Lǐ observed the heavenly patterns,
modeled the design after the Zǐgōng,
and constructed the small city.
Its perimeter was one thousand one hundred and twenty-one paces,
with one circular side and three square sides.
To the northwest, he erected the Lóngfēi Yìzhī Lóu
to symbolize the Heavenly Gate.
To the southeast, he placed a hidden stone drainage hole
to symbolize the Earthly Door.
The gates of the mounds reached out in four directions
to symbolize the eight winds.
The outer city wall was built but was incomplete in the northwest
to show service to Wú,
not daring to block the way.
Internally it was for the purpose of taking Wú,
hence it was incomplete in the northwest,
but Wú did not know this.
Facing north, he called himself a vassal,
entrusting his life to the state of Wú.
Left and right were switched,
not in their proper positions,
clearly showing the status of a subordinate.
Once the city was completed,
a strange mountain spontaneously appeared;
it was the mountain from the sea of Dōngwǔ in Lángyá.
It arrived on its own in one night,
so it was named Guàishān.
Fàn Lǐ said:
"My construction of the city
corresponds to Heaven.
The image of Kūnlún resides within it."
Yuè Wáng said:
"I have heard that Kūnlún Shān is the pillar of the earth,
above it supports the August Heaven,
its breath exhales through the universe,
below it resides on Hòutǔ,
receiving bounty without limit.
It nurtures sages and gives birth to spirits,
providing for the gathering of emperors.
Thus the emperors reside on its sunny heights,
and the Three Kings dwell in its central land.
As for my state,
it is on the remote edge of the world,
riding on the southeast corner;
the Big Dipper is far to the extreme north.
It is not a city of dung and earth,
but how can it compare in majesty and prosperity to that of a King?"
Fàn Lǐ said:
"The King only sees the outside
and has not seen the inside.
I have modeled the city upon the Heavenly Gate
and harmonized its breath with Hòutǔ.
The image of the peaks is already set,
and Kūnlún has thus emerged;
this is the hegemony of Yuè."
Yuè Wáng said:
"If it is as the Minister says,
it is my destiny."
Fàn Lǐ said:
"Heaven and Earth gave it a cry
to manifest its reality;
its name is Dōngwǔ.
Build a Yóutái upon it.
To the southeast make the Sīmǎmén,
and erect a multi-storied tower crowning the mountain peak
to serve as a Língtái."
He built a Língōng at Huáiyáng,
the Zhòngsùtái at Gāopíng,
the Jiàtái at Chéngqiū,
established a park at Lèyě,
the Yàntái at Shíshì,
and the Zhāitái at Jìshān.
When Gōujiàn went out on excursions,
he would rest and eat in the Bīngchú.
Yuè Wáng then summoned Minister Fàn Lǐ, Dàfū Zhǒng, and Dàfū Yǐng,
asking:
"I wish to ascend the Míngtáng today to oversee the state's governance,
to exclusively dispense grace and issue commands
to comfort the common people.
On which day would it be possible?
I rely on you three sages to maintain the principles."
Fàn Lǐ said:
"Today
is a Bǐngwǔ day.
Bǐng
is the Yángjiāng;
this day is auspicious.
Moreover, by following this good time,
your humble servant believes you can have a beginning and an end
and attain the center of all under Heaven."
Dàfū Zhǒng said:
"The front carriage has overturned,
the rear carriage must take warning.
I hope the King examines this deeply."
Fàn Lǐ said:
"The Master only sees one side and not the other.
Our King now returns to govern on a Bǐngwǔ day,
solving the problem at its root;
this is the first suitability.
Metal controls the beginning,
and Fire saves the end;
this is the second suitability.
The sorrow of accumulated Metal
turns and reaches Water;
this is the third suitability.
Between ruler and minister there is a distinction,
without losing the proper principle;
this is the fourth suitability.
When the King and his Minister rise together,
all under Heaven shall be established;
this is the fifth suitability.
Your servant wishes for you to quickly ascend the Míngtáng to oversee governance."
Yuè Wáng established his governance on that day;
he was cautious and careful.
When going out he dared not be extravagant;
when staying in he dared not be profligate.
Yuè Wáng thought of taking revenge against Wú;
it was not a matter of a single day.
He toiled his body and exhausted his mind,
night followed by day.
If his eyes were closing in sleep, he would stimulate them with smartweed;
if his feet were cold, he would soak them in water.
In winter he often held ice,
and in summer he grasped fire.
His heart was full of sorrow and his will was steeled by hardship.
He hung a gall bladder by his door,
and whenever he went in or out, he would taste it.
Its taste never left his mouth.
In the middle of the night, he would weep in secret,
and after weeping, he would whistle and sing.
The Yuè Wáng said:
“The Wú Wáng enjoys wearing garments that are light and fine.
I wish to harvest arrowroot
and have female workers weave fine cloth to present to him,
in order to win the heart of the Wú Wáng.
What do you think of this?”
The ministers said:
“Excellent.”
Thus, the men and women of the state were sent into the mountains to harvest arrowroot
to make cloth of yellow silk,
wishing to present it.
Before an envoy could be dispatched,
the Wú Wáng heard that the Yuè Wáng was wholeheartedly maintaining himself,
eating no foods of complex flavors,
wearing no clothes of multiple colors,
and although he had the pleasure of the Wǔtái towers,
he never once ascended them for recreation.
“I wish to take this opportunity to bestow a letter upon him
and increase his fief.”
To the east it reached Gōuyǒng,
to the west it reached Zuìlǐ,
to the south it reached Gūmò,
and to the north it reached Píngyuán,
spanning over eight hundred lǐ in length and breadth.
The Yuè Wáng then ordered Dàfū Zhòng to seek out one hundred thousand pieces of arrowroot cloth, nine dǎng of sweet honey, seven decorated boxes, five pairs of fox skins, and ten sōu of Jìn bamboo
to reciprocate the gift of the fief.
The Wú Wáng received them
and said:
“The remote and barbarian land of Yuè has no treasures.
Now they have brought forth their tributary goods to reciprocate the ritual.
This shows that Yuè is careful and mindful of my merit,
and has not forgotten the efficacy of Wú.
Now, Yuè originally was a state of a thousand lǐ.
Although I have enfeoffed it,
I have not yet restored its entire territory.”
When Wǔ Zǐxū heard of this,
he retired to his lodging and lay down,
saying to his attendants:
“Our lord has lost the prisoner of the Shíshì
and released him into the Nánlín.
Now he merely takes the wilderness of tigers and leopards and gives it away as the grass of the wild outskirts.
In my heart,
how could this not be a loss?”
Having received the presentation of arrowroot cloth,
the Wú Wáng again increased the fief of Yuè,
bestowing feather decorations, stools and canes, and the garments of a feudal lord.
The state of Yuè was greatly pleased.
The women who harvested the arrowroot, pained by the bitterness of the Yuè Wáng’s intent,
then composed the "Poem of Bitterness,"
saying:
“The arrowroot vines do not connect, growing in clusters.
My lord’s heart is bitter, and his fate has changed.
Tasting the gall is not bitter, it is sweet as malt sugar,
causing me to harvest arrowroot to make silk.
The female workers weave it, not daring to be late.
Finer than gauze, light as falling mist,
it is called pure fine linen, and shall be presented.
The Yuè Wáng is pleased, for his crimes are removed;
the Wú Wáng is joyful, sending letters swiftly.
Increasing the fief and adding land, bestowing rare feathers,
stools, canes, mats, and cushions, the rituals of a feudal lord.
The ministers bow and dance, the heavenly countenance relaxes.
How could my King's worries not be shifted!”
Thereupon,
the Yuè Wáng internally cultivated his virtue
and externally spread his Way.
The ruler did not make a name of teaching,
the ministers did not make a name of plotting,
the people did not make a name of being employed,
and the officials did not make a name of their duties.
Throughout the state, all was vast and tranquil,
as if there were no government decrees.
The Yuè Wáng internally filled the treasuries
and cleared the fields.
The people became wealthy and the state grew strong;
the masses were at peace and the Way was prosperous.
The Yuè Wáng then followed the eight ministers and his four friends as teachers,
frequently asking about governance.
Dàfū Zhòng said:
“It is simply loving the people.”
The Yuè Wáng said:
“How is that done?”
Dàfū Zhòng said:
“Profit them and do not harm them;
bring them to success and do not bring them to failure;
give them life and do not kill them;
give to them and do not seize from them.”
The Yuè Wáng said:
“I wish to hear more.”
Dàfū Zhòng said:
“Do not seize what the people like,
and then they are profited.
Do not let the people lose their seasonal timing,
and then they are brought to success.
Reduce punishments and eliminate penalties,
and then they are given life.
Lighten their taxes and levies,
and then they are given to.
Do not have many pleasure towers or outings,
and then they are made joyful.
Be quiet and not harsh,
and then they are made happy.
If the people lose what they like,
then they are harmed.
If the farmers lose their seasonal timing,
then they are brought to failure.
If there are crimes and no pardons,
then they are killed.
If taxes are heavy and levies are thick,
then they are seized from.
If many pleasure towers and outings are made to weary the people,
then they are made to suffer.
If the people's strength is labored and disturbed,
then they are made angry.
I have heard that those who are good at governing a state
treat the people as parents love their children,
or as an elder brother loves his younger brother.
Hearing of their hunger or cold, they grieve for them;
seeing their labor and suffering, they feel sorrow for them.”
The Yuè Wáng then relaxed punishments, lightened penalties,
and reduced his taxes and levies.
Consequently,
the people became prosperous and wealthy,
and all possessed the courage of armored soldiers.
In the ninth year,
in the first month,
the Yuè Wáng summoned the Five Dàfū and told them:
“In the past,
the state of Yuè fled and abandoned its ancestral temple.
I myself became a wretched prisoner,
ashamed to be heard of by the world,
and disgraced before the feudal lords.
Now, I think of Wú
just as a cripple does not forget how to run,
or a blind man does not forget how to see.
I do not yet know the strategy or plan;
I only ask you, Dàfū, to instruct me.”
Fú Tóng said:
“In the past, the news of our fallen state and wandering people
was heard and known by all under heaven.
Now, if you wish to have a plan,
you should not reveal your words beforehand.
I have heard that when a bird of prey moves,
it first crouches down.
When a fierce beast is about to strike,
it must flatten its fur and crouch low.
When a raptor is about to pounce,
it must fly low and tuck its wings.
When a sage is about to move,
he must use humble words and harmonize the masses.
In the plans of a sage,
one cannot see their form
and one cannot know their true nature.
He approaches the matter and then attacks;
therefore, in front, there are no troops to intercept him,
and in back, there is no worry of ambush or pursuit.
Now, if Your Majesty approaches the enemy to destroy Wú,
you should use humble words
and let nothing leak out.
I have heard that the Wú Wáng’s troops are stronger than those of Qí and Jìn,
but he has deep resentment with Chǔ.
Your Majesty should be close to Qí,
deeply bonded with Jìn,
secretly allied with Chǔ,
and serve Wú generously.
The ambition of Wú is fierce, arrogant, and self-important;
he will surely treat the feudal lords lightly and oppress neighboring states.
When the three states decide to assert their power,
they will return to being enemy states,
and will surely compete and struggle for dominance.
Yuè will then take advantage of their exhaustion,
and attacking them at that point,
we can be victorious.
Even the troops of the Five Emperors
could not surpass this.”
Fàn Lǐ said:
“I have heard that in planning for a state and destroying an enemy,
one moves by observing the signs.
At the meeting of Mèngjīn,
the feudal lords said it was possible,
but Wǔ Wáng declined.
Currently, Wú and Chǔ have formed a feud,
and their resentment is unresolved.
Although Qí is not close,
it acts as their savior externally.
Although Jìn is not attached,
it still follows their righteousness.
When internal ministers plan and their strategies resolve the enmity,
and neighboring states communicate without cutting off their aid,
this is precisely when Wú rises as a hegemon
and is honored above the feudal lords.
I have heard that those who are steep and high will crumble,
and those whose leaves are lush will be broken.
When the sun is at its zenith, it begins to move,”
The moon wanes once it is full.
The four seasons do not flourish at the same time,
and the five elements do not run together.
Yīn and Yáng alternate their lead,
and the Qì has periods of flourishing and decline.
Therefore, water that overflows the dikes
does not exceed its capacity for long;
a fire that singes and dries
cannot sustain its intensity.
When water is still, it lacks the fury of churning waves;
when fire is extinguished, it lacks the heat that singes hair.
Now Wú relies on the prestige of the Zhūhóu
to issue commands to Tiānxià,
unaware that its virtue is meager and its grace is shallow,
its Dào is narrow and the resentment against it is broad,
its power is precariously suspended and its wisdom is fading,
its strength is exhausted and its prestige is broken,
its weapons are blunted and its army is retreating,
and its soldiers are scattering as the multitude disperses.
I request that we halt the troops and organize the army,
wait for their collapse and defeat,
and then follow and attack them.
Without staining the blades with blood
and without the soldiers even turning their heels,
the ruler and ministers of Wú will be captured.
I wish for Dàwáng to remain silent,
not show any movement,
and observe their stillness."
Dàfū Kǔ Chéng said:
"Now, water can float plants and trees,
but it can also sink them.
The earth can give birth to all things,
but it can also kill them.
The rivers and seas can place themselves below the mountain valleys,
and thus make the valleys pay court to them.
A sage can follow the multitude,
but also command them.
Now Wú inherits the military system of Hé Lǘ and the laws and teachings of Zǐ Xū;
its administration is balanced and not yet diminished,
and it has won battles without suffering defeat.
As for Dàfū Pǐ,
he is a mad and sycophantic person;
though he is clever in strategy,
he treats court affairs lightly.
Zǐ Xū devoted his strength to war and conquest,
but died because of his remonstrance.
As these two men exercise power,
there will surely be ruin and defeat.
I wish for the Wáng to humble his heart and hide himself,
show no plans or strategies,
and then Wú can be destroyed."
Dàfū Hào said:
"Now the ruler of Wú is arrogant and his ministers are extravagant;
the people are well-fed and the army is brave;
abroad there are enemies invading the borders,
and within there is the shock of contending ministers;
they can be attacked."
Dàfū Gōu Rú said:
"Heaven has four seasons,
and man has five victories.
Formerly, Tāng and Wǔ took advantage of the four seasons to overcome Xià and Yīn;
Huán and Mù relied on the convenience of the five victories to stand among the Liùguó.
These are those who won by seizing their opportunity."
The Wáng said:
"We do not yet have the advantage of the four seasons nor the convenience of the five victories;
I wish for each of you to return to your duties."
In the second month of the tenth year of King Gòujiàn of Yuè,
the King of Yuè contemplated deeply and thought far ahead.
Having been invaded and humiliated by Wú,
he received Heaven’s blessings
and regained the state of Yuè.
His ministers offered instruction,
and each devised a strategy.
Their words were in accord and their intentions were the same;
Gòujiàn respectfully followed them,
and his state had become wealthy.
In the five years since returning to Yuè,
he had not yet heard of any companions willing to die for the cause.
Some said that the ministers loved their own lives
and cherished their own bodies.
He then ascended the Jiàn Tái
to observe whether his ministers felt concern or not.
Chancellor Fàn Lǐ, Minister Zhòng, Jù Rú, and their peers sat in a dignified line;
though they harbored worries,
it did not show on their faces.
The King of Yuè then rang the bells and issued urgent summons to call his ministers,
and made an alliance with them, saying:
“I have suffered insult and received shame.
Above, I am ashamed before the Zhōu King;
below, I am embarrassed before Jìn and Chǔ.
Fortunately, I received the strategies of you ministers
and was able to return to the state to cultivate governance,
enriching the people and nurturing the soldiers.
Yet in five years, I have not heard of a soldier willing to die or a minister who would avenge my grievance.
How then can we achieve success?”
Among the ministers, all were silent and none responded.
The King of Yuè looked up to the sky and sighed, saying:
“I have heard that when the ruler worries, the ministers are humiliated;
when the ruler is humiliated, the ministers die.
Now I personally suffered the disaster of being a slave and captive,
and endured the shame of imprisonment and defeat.
Being unable to support myself,
I must rely on the worthy and appoint the benevolent,
and only then can I punish Wú.
I have heavily burdened you ministers;
why is it that you are so easy to see but so difficult to employ?”
At this,
Jì Nǐ, who was young and held a low-ranking office,
was seated in the back row.
He raised his hand and hurried forward,
stepping onto the mats and advancing to say:
“How erroneous are Your Majesty’s words!
It is not that the ministers are easy to see but difficult to employ;
it is that Your Majesty is unable to employ them.”
The King of Yuè said:
“What do you mean?”
Jì Nǐ said:
“Official positions, wealth, and gold rewards
are things the ruler values lightly.
Wielding blades, treading on swords, sacrificing one’s life, and throwing oneself into death
are things the soldier values heavily.
Now Your Majesty offers the wealth you value lightly
and demands from the soldiers what they value heavily.
How dangerous this is!”
At this, the King of Yuè was silent and displeased,
his face showing a look of shame.
He immediately dismissed the ministers,
called Jì Nǐ forward, and asked:
“How can I win the hearts of the soldiers?”
Jì Nǐ replied:
“For a ruler of men to honor benevolence and righteousness
is the gate to governance.
The soldiers and the people
are the roots of the ruler.
To open the gate and strengthen the roots,
nothing is better than rectifying one’s own character.
The way to rectify one’s character
is to be cautious with those who are close to you.
Those who are close to you
are the reason why a ruler prospers or declines.
I hope Your Majesty will wisely select those close to you,
and simply obtain the worthy.
In the past, Tài Gōng waited for the nine sounds before he was satisfied;
he was but a starving man of Pán Xī,
yet the Earl of the West appointed him and became King.
Guǎn Zhòng
was a fugitive prisoner from Lǔ
with a reputation for greed and divisiveness,
but Huán of Qí obtained him and became Hegemon.
Therefore the tradition says:
‘He who loses scholars perishes;
he who gains scholars prospers.’
I hope Your Majesty will be careful about those close to you;
why worry that the ministers cannot be employed?”
The King of Yuè said:
“I employ the worthy and appoint the capable,
each with their specific duties.
I have waited with an open mind and high expectations,
hoping to hear plans for vengeance.
Now they all hide their voices and conceal their forms;
I hear not their words.
Where does the fault lie?”
Jì Nǐ said:
“In selecting the worthy and verifying facts,
each has a certain grade.
Send them far away on difficult tasks
to test their sincerity.
Inform them of secrets internally
to know their trustworthiness.
Discuss matters with them
to observe their wisdom.
Serve them wine to drink
to see if they become disorderly.
Direct them on missions
to examine their capability.
Observe their expressions
to distinguish their attitudes.
Once these five methods are established,
the scholars will reveal their true character,
and the people will exhaust their wisdom.
Knowing their wisdom and truth,
then why would ruler and minister worry?”
The King of Yuè said:
“I use strategists to verify the facts,
and the people exhaust their wisdom,
yet the scholars have not fully come forward with words to benefit me.”
Jì Nǐ said:
“Fàn Lǐ is enlightened and knows internal affairs;
Wén Zhòng is far-sighted and sees external affairs.
I hope Your Majesty will invite Minister Zhòng to deliberate deeply with you;
then the techniques of a Hegemon King will be found.”
The King of Yuè then invited Minister Zhòng and asked:
“In the past, I received your words
and escaped from a land of extreme hardship.
Now I wish to pursue a bold plan
to avenge my long-standing enemy;
what should I do to succeed?”
Minister Zhòng said:
“I have heard that high-flying birds die from delicious food,
and fish in deep springs die from fragrant bait.
Now if you wish to attack Wú,
you must first seek out what they love
and satisfy what they desire;
only then can you obtain the reality.”
The King of Yuè said:
“As for what people love,
even if it is their desire,
how can these be used to determine and control their death?”
Minister Zhòng said:
“For one who wishes to settle a grudge, take revenge, defeat Wú, and destroy the enemy,
there are nine techniques;
may Your Majesty examine them.”
The King of Yuè said:
“I have been humiliated and harbor worry;
internally I am ashamed before the court officials,
externally I am embarrassed before the feudal lords.
My mind is confused
and my spirit is empty;
even if there are nine techniques,
how can I know them?”
Minister Zhòng said:
“As for these nine techniques,
Tāng and Wén used them to become Kings;
Huán and Mù used them to become Hegemons.
Attacking cities and taking towns with them
is easier than shedding one’s shoes.
I hope Your Majesty will look upon them.”
Zhòng said:
“First: Honor Heaven and serve the ghosts
to seek their blessings.
Second: Use heavy wealth and currency to gift their ruler,
and many bribes to please their ministers.
Third: Buy grain and fodder at high prices to empty their state,
and profit from what they want to exhaust their people.
Fourth: Send beautiful women to confuse his heart
and disrupt his plans.
Fifth: Send skilled craftsmen and fine materials
to cause them to build palaces
and exhaust their wealth.
Sixth: Send flattering ministers
to make them easy to attack.
Seventh: Embolden his outspoken ministers
to cause them to commit suicide.
Eighth: May the King’s state become wealthy
and prepare sharp weapons.
Ninth: Sharpen armor and weapons to exploit their decline.
Regarding these nine techniques,
the King should keep his mouth closed and not spread them;
guard them with spirit,
and taking the world will not be difficult,
much less taking Wú.”
The King of Yuè said:
“Excellent!”
He then carried out the first technique,
setting up the eastern suburbs to sacrifice to the Yáng,
naming it Dōng Huáng Gōng;
setting up the western suburbs to sacrifice to the Yīn,
naming it Xī Wáng Mǔ;
sacrificing to the mountains at Huì Jī,
and making offerings to the waters and marshes at Jiāng Zhōu.
After serving the ghosts and gods for one year,
the state suffered no disasters.
The King of Yuè said:
“How excellent
is the minister’s technique!”
"I wish to discuss the rest."
Zhòng said:
"The King of Wú loves to build palaces and halls,
employing labor without ceasing.
Your Majesty should select divine timber from famous mountains
to offer and present to him."
The King of Yuè then sent more than three thousand woodworkers
into the mountains to fell timber.
For one year,
the expedition met with no success.
The laborers thought of returning home;
they all harbored resentment in their hearts
and sang the "Chant of the Wood-Guests."
One night,
Heaven produced a pair of divine trees,
twenty spans in girth
and fifty fathoms in length.
The sun-facing side was figured catalpa,
and the shade-facing side was *piánnán*.
Skilled craftsmen applied their tools,
fashioning them with compasses and plumb lines,
carving and turning them until round,
cutting, shaving, and polishing them.
They were colored with vermilion and blue pigments,
interlaced with painted patterns,
adorned with white jade,
and engraved with yellow gold.
Their shapes resembled dragons and snakes,
and their colorful patterns radiated light.
He then sent Dàfū Zhòng to present them to the King of Wú.
He said:
"The humble servant Gōujiàn, the laborer of the Eastern Sea, sends his servant Zhòng,
venturing through your subordinates
to be heard by your attendants:
Relying on the Great King’s power,
I privately built a small hall.
Since there were leftover materials,
I respectfully bow twice to present them to the Great King."
The King of Wú was greatly pleased.
Zǐxū remonstrated, saying:
"The King must not accept them!
In the past, Jié built the Líng Tower,
and Zhòu built the Lù Tower.
Yin and Yang were thrown out of harmony,
cold and heat came out of season,
the five grains did not ripen,
Heaven sent down disasters,
the people were exhausted and the state was transformed,
until they finally met their destruction.
If the Great King accepts these,
he will certainly be destroyed by the King of Yuè."
The King of Wú did not listen,
and he subsequently accepted them to build the Gūsū Tower.
For three years he gathered materials,
and it was completed in five years;
its height could be seen from two hundred *lǐ*.
People traveling on the roads
died on the paths and wept in the alleys,
and the sounds of sighs and groans never ceased.
The commoners were weary and the soldiers suffered;
the people could not make a living.
The King of Yuè said:
"Excellent!
This is the second strategy."
In the eleventh year,
the King of Yuè contemplated deeply and long;
wanting only to attack Wú,
he then requested a plan from Jì Ní, asking:
"I wish to attack Wú,
but I fear I cannot defeat them.
I wish to raise an army early,
so I ask you."
Jì Ní replied:
"To raise an army and mobilize troops,
one must first store the five grains within,
fill the coffers with gold and silver,
make the storehouses and treasuries full,
and sharpen the armor and weapons.
Regarding these four things,
one must observe the *qì* of Heaven and Earth,
trace them back to Yin and Yang,
be clear about 'solitary and void,'
and examine survival and destruction;
only then can one measure the enemy."
The King of Yuè said:
"As for the survival and destruction of Heaven and Earth,
what is the essence of it?"
Jì Ní said:
"In the *qì* of Heaven and Earth,
all things have life and death.
Tracing back to Yin and Yang
means knowing the dearness or cheapness of things;
being clear about 'solitary and void'
means knowing the points of convergence;
examining survival and destruction
means distinguishing truth from falsehood."
The King of Yuè said:
"What do you mean by 'life and death' and 'truth and falsehood'?"
Jì Ní said:
"In spring, one plants the eight grains;
in summer, they grow and are nurtured;
in autumn, they mature and are gathered;
in winter, they are stored and kept.
If the season of Heaven brings life but one does not provide the seeds,
that is the first 'death.'
If they should grow in summer but there are no sprouts,
that is the second 'death.'
If they should mature in autumn but there is no gathering,
that is the third 'death.'
If they should be stored in winter but there is no accumulation,
that is the fourth 'death.'
Though one may have the virtue of Yáo and Shùn,
there is nothing that can be done.
When the season of Heaven brings life,
if the diligent are old
and the workers are few,
yet one aligns with the *qì* and responds to the cycles
without losing the proper principles,
that is the first 'life.'
Paying close attention and observing,
diligently removing weeds from the sprouts,
so that weeds are eliminated and the sprouts flourish,
is the second 'life.'
Preparing equipment beforehand,
so that when the harvest arrives it is collected,
the state having no delinquent taxes
and the people losing no ears of grain,
is the third 'life.'
When the granaries are already sealed and coated,
getting rid of the old and bringing in the new,
the ruler is happy and the ministers are joyful,
and men and women act with trust,
that is the fourth 'life.'
As for Yin and Yang,
in the year where Tàiyīn resides,
if one waits and rests for three years,
the high and low prices will be manifest.
As for 'solitary and void,'
it refers to the Gate of Heaven and the Portal of Earth.
Survival and destruction
are found in the ruler’s Way and Virtue."
The King of Yuè said:
"How is it that your years are fewer than the long duration of these things?"
Jì Ní said:
"A man of excellence
is not restricted by being old or young."
The King of Yuè said:
"Excellent
is your Way!"
He then looked up to observe the celestial patterns,
gathered and examined the planetary positions and stars,
recorded the images of the four seasons,
and moving from the low to the high,
he set up eight empty granaries.
Following the Yin, he gathered and stored,
and looking to the Yang, he sold the grain.
Planning with his ultimate strategy,
in three years his wealth increased fivefold,
and the state of Yuè became intensely wealthy.
Gōujiàn sighed and said:
"I shall become a Hegemon!
Excellent
is the strategy of Jì Ní!"
In the twelfth year,
the King of Yuè said to Dàfū Zhǒng:
"I have heard that the King of Wú is licentious and fond of beauty,
deluded and immersed in indulgence,
and neglecting the affairs of government.
If we plot because of this,
is it possible?"
Zhǒng said:
"He can be defeated.
Since the King of Wú is licentious and fond of beauty,
and Zǎi Pǐ is sycophantic and sways his heart,
if we go and present beautiful women,
he will certainly accept them.
Your Majesty should choose two beautiful women and present them."
The King of Yuè said:
"Excellent."
He then sent physiognomists throughout the kingdom
and found the daughters of firewood sellers at Zhùluó Shān named Xī Shī and Zhèng Dàn.
Adorning them with fine silks and gauze,
teaching them graceful movements and steps,
having them practice at Tǔchéng,
and having them appear in the capital's alleys,
after three years of learning their manners and attire, they were presented to Wú.
He then sent Xiàngguó Fàn Lǐ to present them, saying:
"The King of Yuè, Gōujiàn, privately has two neglected women;
as the state of Yuè is lowly and hard-pressed,
he does not dare to detain them,
and respectfully sends his servant Lǐ to present them to the Great King.
Disregarding their lowly and humble appearance,
he wishes to offer them for domestic service."
The King of Wú was greatly pleased
and said:
"That Yuè contributes two women
is proof of Gōujiàn's complete loyalty to Wú."
Zǐxū remonstrated, saying:
"This is not permissible;
Your Majesty must not accept them.
I have heard that the five colors make one blind
and the five sounds make one deaf.
In the past, Jié treated Tāng lightly and was destroyed;
Zhòu treated Wénwáng lightly and perished.
If the Great King accepts them,
there will surely be calamity later.
I have heard that the King of Yuè reads in the morning without fatigue
and recites through the dark of the night;
moreover, he has gathered tens of thousands of soldiers prepared to die.
If this man does not die,
he will certainly achieve his ambition.
The King of Yuè practices sincerity and acts with benevolence,
listening to advice and promoting the worthy.
If this man does not die,
he will certainly establish his reputation.
The King of Yuè wears fur coats in summer
and thin linen in winter;
if this man does not die,
he will certainly become an adversary.
I have heard:
Worthy men
are the treasures of a state;
beautiful women
are the ruin of a state.
Xià perished because of Mòxǐ,
Yīn perished because of Dájǐ,
Zhōu perished because of Bāosì."
The King of Wú did not listen
and consequently accepted the women.
The King of Yuè said:
"How excellent!
This is the third strategy."
In the thirteenth year,
the King of Yuè said to Dàfū Zhòng:
"I have received your strategies;
what was planned was auspicious,
and has never failed to align.
Now I wish to plot against Wú again;
what should be done?"
Zhòng said:
"Your Majesty should personally state that the state of Yuè is humble and lowly
and the harvest has failed.
I wish Your Majesty to request to buy grain to test their intent;
if Heaven abandons Wú,
they will surely grant Your Majesty's request."
Yuè then sent Dàfū Zhòng as an envoy to Wú,
and through Zǎipǐ he sought an audience with the King of Wú,
saying:
"The state of Yuè is low-lying,
and floods and droughts have been irregular.
The harvest has failed,
the people are hungry and destitute,
and the roads are filled with the starving.
We wish to request to buy grain from the Great King;
next year we will return it to the Great Granary.
We only hope the Great King will save us from our dire straits."
The King of Wú said:
"The King of Yuè is faithful and keeps to the Way,
harboring no double-mindedness.
Now that he is in distress and comes to appeal,
how could I be stingy with wealth and treasures
and deny his wish?"
Zǐxū remonstrated, saying:
"It must not be!
It is not that Wú will possess Yuè,
but that Yuè will surely possess Wú.
If good fortune goes there, calamity will come here;
this is nurturing a living enemy and destroying the state.
Giving to them will not create kinship,
and not giving will not yet create a deep grudge.
Moreover, Yuè has a sage minister, Fàn Lǐ,
who is brave and skilled in strategy;
he will refine their tactics for attack and battle
to watch for our weaknesses.
Looking at the envoy sent by the King of Yuè to request grain,
it is not because the state is poor and the people are in distress that they request it.
It is to enter our state
and watch for our King's weaknesses."
The King of Wú said:
"I have humbled and subdued the King of Yuè,
and I possess his people
and embrace his state,
making Gōujiàn feel ashamed.
Gōujiàn's spirit is subdued;
he drove my carriage
and walked backward in front of my horse.
None of the feudal lords have failed to hear of this.
Now I have allowed him to return to his country,
to serve his ancestral temple
and restore his state;
how could he dare to have a heart of rebellion against me?"
Zǐxū said:
"I have heard that when a scholar is in distress, it is not hard for him to suppress his heart and humble himself before others,
but afterward, there will be a look of provocation.
I have heard that the King of Yuè is starving
and the people are in dire straits;
we should take this opportunity to destroy them.
Now, instead of using the Way of Heaven
and following the principles of Earth,
you transport food to them,
following the King's command.
This is like a fox and a pheasant playing together.
The fox humbles its body,
and the pheasant trusts it.
Thus the fox achieves its goal,
and the pheasant must die.
Can one not be careful?"
The King of Wú said:
"Gōujiàn's state is in sorrow,
and I provide them with grain.
Kindness goes and righteousness comes;
his virtue is manifest.
What is there to worry about?"
Zǐxū said:
"I have heard that the cubs of wolves have wild hearts,
and enemies cannot be befriended.
A tiger cannot be sated with food,
and a viper must not be allowed to follow its whims.
Now the Great King throws away the fortune of the state
to enrich a useless enemy,
discarding the words of a loyal minister
to satisfy the desires of an enemy.
I will surely see Yuè destroy Wú;
wild beasts and deer will roam on the Gūxū zhī Tái,
and thorns and brambles will overspread the palace gates.
I wish the King to look at the matter of Wǔ Wáng attacking Zhòu."
Tàizǎi Pǐ from the side replied:
"Wǔ Wáng was not Zhòu's minister;
he led the feudal lords to attack his lord.
Even though he defeated Yīn, can it be called righteousness?"
Zǐxū said:
"Wǔ Wáng established his name."
Tàizǎi Pǐ said:
"Personally slaying one's lord to make a name—
I cannot bear it."
Zǐxū said:
"He who steals a state is enfeoffed as a marquis,
but he who steals gold is executed.
If Wǔ Wáng lost his principles,
then why would Zhōu be the model for the Three Houses?"
Tàizǎi Pǐ said:
"Zǐxū, as a minister,
merely wishes to interfere with the King's goodwill
and oppose the King's heart
to satisfy himself.
King, why do you not see his error?"
Zǐxū said:
"Tàizǎi Pǐ certainly wishes to seek their favor;
previously he released the prisoner of the Shíshì
and accepted their gifts of treasures and women.
Externally he colludes with the enemy state,
and internally he deceives the King.
Great King, investigate this;
do not be insulted by a group of petty men.
Now the Great King is like someone bathing an infant;
though it cries, do not listen to Zǎipǐ's words."
The King of Wú said:
"Zǎipǐ is right.
Have you not heard my words?
This is not the way of a loyal minister;
it is like that of a slanderer and flatterer."
Tàizǎi Pǐ said:
"I have heard that when a neighboring state is in trouble,
one gallops a thousand li to save them;
this is what a kingly ruler does.
