Enfeoffing the descendants of a fallen state
was how the Five Hegemons assisted those whose lines were cut off."
The King of Wú then gave Yuè ten thousand shí of grain
and commanded him, saying:
"I have gone against the advice of my ministers to transport this to Yuè;
when the harvest is plentiful, return it to me."
Dàfū Zhòng said:
"I shall carry out my mission and return to Yuè;
when the harvest is in, we will surely return Wú's loan."
Dàfū Zhòng returned to Yuè,
and all the ministers of the state of Yuè shouted "Long Live!"
They immediately used the grain to reward the ministers
and distributed it to all the people.
In the second year,
the King of Yuè's grain ripened;
he selected the finest grain and steamed it
to return it to Wú.
He returned the same number of measures
and also sent Dàfū Zhòng to return it to the King of Wú.
When the King received the Yuè grain,
he sighed deeply
and said to Tàizǎi Pǐ:
"The land of Yuè is fertile,
and its seeds are very excellent.
They can be kept for my people to plant."
Thereupon, Wú planted the Yuè grain.
The seeds were killed and none sprouted;
the people of Wú suffered a great famine.
The King of Yuè said:
"They are now in dire straits;
they can be attacked."
Dàfū Zhòng said:
"Not yet.
The state has only just become poor;
loyal ministers are still there.
The signs of Heaven are not yet seen;
one must wait for the right time."
The King of Yuè also asked Chancellor Fàn Lǐ:
"I have a plan for revenge.
For water battle, one uses boats;
for land travel, one uses carriages.
The advantages of carriages and boats
are more effective than weapons and crossbows.
Now you plan matters for me;
has nothing gone wrong?"
Fàn Lǐ replied:
"I have heard that the sage kings of old all practiced war and used troops.
However, the matters of formations, ranks, and drums—
success or failure depends on their mastery.
Now I hear there is a maiden in Yuè
coming from Nánlín;
the people of the state praise her skills.
I wish Your Majesty to invite her;
she can be seen immediately."
The King of Yuè then sent an envoy to invite her,
to ask about the arts of the sword and halberd.
The maiden was going north to see the King,
and on the road met an old man
who called himself Yuán Gōng.
He asked the maiden:
"I hear you are skilled with the sword;
I wish to see it once."
The girl said:
"I dare not hide anything;
only please try me, Sir."
Thereupon,
Yuán Gōng then took up a línáng bamboo staff.
The bamboo tip rose and fell without hitting the ground.
The maiden immediately caught its tip.
Yuán Gōng then flew up into a tree
and transformed into a white gibbon.
He then departed,
and she went to see the Yuè Wáng.
Yuè Wáng asked:
"What is the way of the sword like?"
The maiden said:
"I was born in the deep forests
and grew up in the uninhabited wilds.
I have not studied any specific discipline.
Unknown to the feudal lords,
I secretly loved the way of striking
and practiced it without end.
I did not receive it from any person
but suddenly came to possess it myself."
Yuè Wáng asked:
"How is its way?"
The maiden said:
"The way is very subtle and easy,
its meaning very obscure and deep.
The way has gates and doors,
and also has Yīn and Yáng.
Open the gate and close the door;
Yīn declines and Yáng rises.
In the way of hand-to-hand combat,
internally solidify the spirit
and externally show a calm demeanor.
Appearing like a gentle woman,
but seizing like a startled tiger.
Distribute the form and wait for the Qì,
moving together with the spirit.
Obscure like the sun,
swift as a leaping rabbit.
Chase the form and pursue the shadow,
light like a flickering phantom.
Breathing in and out,
beyond the reach of laws and prohibitions.
Horizontal, vertical, against, or with,
straight or returning, unheard.
With this way,
one person can face a hundred,
and a hundred people can face ten thousand.
If the King wishes to try it,
the proof will be seen immediately."
Yuè Wáng then gave the maiden a title,
calling her:
"Yuè Nǚ".
He then ordered the five officers including Duò, Cháng, and Gāo to study it and teach the soldiers.
In that age, the sword of Yuè Nǚ was supreme.
Thereupon Fàn Lǐ introduced an expert archer, Chén Yīn.
Yīn
was a person of Chǔ.
Yuè Wáng invited Yīn and asked:
"I heard you are good at shooting;
from where did the way originate?"
Yīn said:
"I
am a rustic person of Chǔ
and have practiced the art of shooting,
yet I cannot fully know its way."
Yuè Wáng said:
"Even so,
I wish for you to explain it in detail."
Yīn said:
"I heard that the crossbow came from the bow,
the bow came from the pellet-bow,
and the pellet-bow arose from the filial sons of old."
Yuè Wáng asked:
"What about the pellet-bow of the filial sons?"
Yīn said:
"In ancient times,
people were simple and honest.
When hungry, they ate birds and beasts;
when thirsty, they drank mist and dew.
When they died, they were wrapped in white thatch
and cast into the wilds.
Filial sons could not bear to see their parents eaten by birds and beasts,
so they made pellet-bows to guard them
and put an end to the harm from birds and beasts.
Thus the song says:
'Cut the bamboo, join the bamboo;
fly the clay, chase away the harm.'
Then the Emperor Shén Nóng bent wood into a bow
and sharpened wood into arrows.
With the utility of the bow and arrow,
he overawed the four directions.
After Huáng Dì,
there was Hú Fù in Chǔ.
Hú Fù
was born in Jīng Shān of Chǔ.
He never saw his parents.
When he was a child,
he practiced using the bow and arrow,
and nothing he shot at escaped.
He passed his way to Yì,
Yì passed it to Féng Méng,
and Féng Méng passed it to Qín Shì of Chǔ.
Qín Shì believed the bow and arrow were not enough to overawe the world.
At that time,
the feudal lords were attacking each other
and weapons were clashing;
the power of the bow and arrow could not subdue them.
Qín Shì then placed the bow horizontally on a stock,
added a mechanism and a trigger,
and applied mechanical force.
Only then could the lords be subdued.
Qín Shì passed it to the three lords of Chǔ,
namely Gōu Dān, È, and Zhāng,
known to the people as Mí Hóu, Yì Hóu, and Wèi Hóu.
From the three lords of Chǔ, it was passed down to Líng Wáng.
Chǔ claimed it for many generations,
using peach-wood bows and thorn-wood arrows to prepare against neighboring states.
Since the time of Líng Wáng,
the way of shooting has branched off.
Though many talented people use it,
none have obtained its true essence.
My ancestors received it in Chǔ,
and it has been five generations down to me.
Although I am not fully enlightened in its way,
I ask the King to test it."
Yuè Wáng asked:
"What is the form of the crossbow modeled after?"
Chén Yīn said:
"The frame is the walled city;
it represents the defending subjects.
The trigger represents the ruler;
it is from where orders arise.
The tooth is the law;
it governs the officials and soldiers.
The nut is the central general;
it manages the internal affairs.
The lock is the defense;
it controls stopping and going.
The side-plates are the attendants;
they listen to the ruler.
The stock is the road;
it connects to where one is sent.
The bow is the general;
he bears the heavy burden.
The string is the military advisor;
he controls the warriors.
The arrow is the flying guest;
he carries out the primary mission.
The metal tip is the solid enemy;
it goes and does not stop.
The fletching is the deputy envoy;
it corrects the path.
It also receives instructions
to know if things are possible or not.
The binding is the colonel;
he holds the left and right sides.
Facing the enemy with a hundred deaths,
one must not be startled.
Birds have no time to fly,
beasts have no time to run;
wherever the crossbow points,
none fail to die.
Such is the extent of my humble
knowledge of the way."
Yuè Wáng said:
"I wish to hear the way of correct shooting."
Chén Yīn said:
"I have heard that the way of correct shooting
is diverse and subtle.
The sages of old
could name the target they would hit before the crossbow was even fired.
I cannot be like the sages of old,
but I ask to explain its essentials:
In the way of shooting,
the body should be as if supporting a board,
the head as if holding an egg.
The left foot steps forward and the right foot is horizontal.
The left hand is like leaning on a branch,
the right hand is like cradling a child.
Lift the crossbow and gaze at the enemy,
concentrate the mind and swallow the breath.
Release together with the breath,
achieving its harmony.
When the spirit is settled, think of the release;
going and stopping must be distinct.
The right hand releases the trigger,
while the left hand is unaware of it.
One body with different functions—
how much more so for the male and female elements?
This is the way of holding the crossbow for correct shooting."
"I wish to hear the way of sighting the enemy and the flight of the arrows."
Chén Yīn said:
"In the way of shooting,
sight the enemy from the markings,
align them with the three-point connection.
The crossbow has its tension,
and the arrow has its weight.
If the weight is precisely measured,
the calculations will be balanced.
Far, near, high, or low—
seek them through minute measurements.
The essence of the way lies here."
"...and I have no further words to leave behind."
Yuè Wáng said,
"Excellent.
Having fully mastered your Way,
I wish for you to teach all of it to the people of my state."
Yīn said,
"The Way originates from Heaven,
but its practice lies with man.
That which a person practices,
there is nothing that does not become divine."
Thereupon,
he then sent Chén Yīn to teach the soldiers archery outside of Běijiāo.
In three months,
the soldiers were all able to master the skill of the bow and crossbow.
When Chén Yīn died,
Yuè Wáng mourned him,
buried him to the west of the capital,
and named his burial place Chén Yīn Shān.
In the fifteenth year of Gōujiàn,
he planned to attack Wú.
He said to Dàfū Zhòng:
"I used your strategies,
escaped the punishment of Heaven’s cruelty,
and returned to my state.
I have sincerely explained this to the people of the state,
and the people are joyful.
Previously, you said:
'When the signs of Heaven arrive, come and report them.'
Are there now any such responses?"
Zhòng said:
"The reason Wú is strong
is because of Wǔ Zǐxū.
Now Wǔ Zǐxū has died for his loyal admonitions;
this is the sign of Heaven appearing beforehand as evidence of a falling state.
I wish for my lord to apply his mind and intent fully to please the people of the state."
The King of Yuè said:
"Listen to the words I used to address the people:
'I did not know my strength was insufficient,
and in seeking revenge against a great power,
I exposed the bones of the common people on the central plains.
This is my crime.
I sincerely change my methods.'
Thereupon,
he buried the dead and inquired after the wounded,
condoled with those in sorrow,
congratulated those with joy,
saw off those departing and welcomed those arriving,
and removed what harmed the people.
Then he served Fūchāi humbly,
and sent three hundred men to serve as officials in Wú.
Wú enfeoffed me with several hundred lǐ of land.
Thus I made a pact with the elders, brothers, and kinsmen of the state and swore to them, saying:
'I have heard that the virtuous rulers of antiquity
were sought by the people of the four quarters as water flows downward.
Now I cannot govern effectively;
I will lead you all, husbands and wives, to act as my protective fence.'
He ordered that young men should not marry old wives,
and old men should not marry young wives.
If a girl was seventeen and not yet married,
her parents were guilty of a crime.
If a man was twenty and had not yet married,
his parents were guilty of a crime.
Those about to give birth reported to me,
and I ordered physicians to attend them.
If two boys were born,
I rewarded them with a jar of wine and a dog.
If two girls were born,
I rewarded them with a jar of wine and a piglet.
If three children were born,
I provided a wet nurse.
If two children were born,
I provided one caregiver.
If the eldest son died,
I remitted government obligations for three years;
if the youngest son died,
I remitted government obligations for three months.
I would surely weep and bury them as if they were my own children.
He ordered that for orphans, widows, the chronically ill, and the poor and sick,
their children be taken into government care.
For those who wished to serve in office,
he assessed their dwellings,
improved their clothing,
satiated them with food,
and selected the sharpest among them.
To all the scholars who came from the four quarters,
he would surely grant them an audience and treat them with ritual propriety.
He carried rice and soup to travel throughout the state.
When he met young children playing in the state,
he fed them and gave them drink,
bestowing love upon them,
and asking their names.
If it was not my food, I did not eat;
if it was not my wife’s handiwork, I did not wear it.
For seven years, no taxes were collected in the state,
and every household had three years' worth of provisions.
Men sang and played music,
and women laughed together.
Now the elders and brothers of the state daily request of me, saying:
'In the past, Fūchāi humiliated our lord and king before the feudal lords,
making us long a laughingstock to the world.
Now the state of Yuè is prosperous and abundant,
and our king is frugal.
We request that we may avenge this humiliation.'
I declined, saying:
'In the past, the humiliation was mine;
it was not the fault of you all,
but my own crime.
As for someone like me,
how would I dare to toil the people of my state
to satisfy my long-standing grievance?'
The elders and brothers requested again, saying:
'Within the four borders of Yuè,
all are our lord's children.
A son avenges a father's enemy,
and a subject resolves a lord's grievance.
How could anyone dare not to exert their full effort?
We request to fight again
to remove our king's long-standing grievance.'
I was pleased and granted it."
Zhòng said:
"I observe that the King of Wú has had his way with Qí and Jìn;
he believes he can then cross into our land
and approach our borders with troops.
Now his army is weary and his soldiers are resting;
for a year they have not been tested,
and so they have forgotten about us.
We must not be idle.
I shall divine it from Heaven.
The people of Wú are already exhausted by military service
and distressed by fighting.
There is no accumulation of red rice in the markets,
and the state granaries are empty.
Its people will surely have thoughts of migrating,
seeking shelter among the rushes and shellfish on the shores of the Eastern Sea.
Signs and human affairs
are also seen in divination.
If the King raises an army
for an advantageous assembly
to invade the borders of Wú,
he should not yet go.
Although the King of Wú has no intention of attacking us,
he may yet be moved to anger.
It is better to investigate the situation
to know his intentions."
The King of Yuè said:
"I did not wish to have the intention of campaigning,
but the people of the state have requested to fight for three years now,
and I cannot but follow the desires of the people.
Now I hear Dàfū Zhòng’s warnings of difficulty."
The elders and brothers of Yuè again admonished, saying:
"Wú can be attacked.
If we win, we destroy their state;
if we do not win, we exhaust their troops.
If Wú seeks peace,
the King can make a covenant with them,
and his achievements and fame will be known among the feudal lords."
The King said:
"Good."
Thereupon,
he held a grand assembly of all ministers and ordered them, saying:
"Whoever dares to advise against attacking Wú
will be punished without pardon."
Lǐ and Zhòng said to each other:
"Our advice is no longer in accord,
yet we must still obey the King's command."
The King of Yuè assembled the army and marshaled the troops, giving a grand warning to the multitude,
and swore to them, saying:
"I have heard that the virtuous rulers of antiquity
did not worry about the insufficiency of their numbers,
but worried about the lack of shame in their conduct and will.
Now Fūchāi has one hundred and thirty thousand men clad in water-rhino armor;
he does not worry about the lack of shame in their conduct and will,
but worries about the insufficiency of his numbers.
Now I shall assist the majesty of Heaven.
I do not want the petty courage of a common man.
I want my soldiers to think of rewards when advancing
and to avoid punishment when retreating."
Thereupon, the fathers of Yuè encouraged their sons,
and brothers urged their younger brothers,
saying:
"Wú can be attacked!"
The King of Yuè again summoned Fàn Lǐ and said to him:
"Wú has already killed Zǐxū,
and flatterers are many.
The people of my state also urge me to attack Wú;
can it be attacked?"
Fàn Lǐ said:
"Not yet.
You must wait until the spring of next year before it is possible."
The King said:
"Why?"
Fàn Lǐ said:
"I observe that the King of Wú is meeting the feudal lords in the north at Huángchí.
His elite troops have followed the King,
and the state is empty.
The old and weak are left behind,
and the Crown Prince remains to guard.
The troops have only just left the borders and are not far away.
If they hear that Yuè is attacking their empty state,
it would not be difficult for the troops to return.
It is better to wait until next spring."
In the sixth month of that summer, on the day of Bǐngzǐ,
Gōujiàn asked again.
Lǐ said:
"They can be attacked."
Thereupon, he dispatched two thousand trained mariners, forty thousand elite soldiers, six thousand gentlemen of the guard, and one thousand attendants,
and on the day of Yǐyǒu, they fought with Wú.
On the day of Bǐngxū, they eventually captured and killed the Crown Prince.
On the day of Dīnghài, they entered Wú
and burned the Gūxū Terrace.
Wú reported the emergency to Fūchāi.
Fūchāi was just then meeting the feudal lords at Huángchí.
Fearing that the world would hear of it,
he immediately kept it secret and did not let it leak.
Having already made the covenant at Huángchí,
he then sent someone to request peace from Yuè.
Gōujiàn assessed for himself that he was not yet able to destroy them.
Thereupon they made peace with Wú.
In the twenty-first year,
in the seventh month,
the King of Yuè again mobilized all the soldiers in the state to attack Wú.
It happened that Chǔ sent Shēn Bāoxū on a mission to Yuè,
and the King of Yuè then asked Bāoxū, saying:
“Can Wú be attacked?”
Shēn Bāoxū said:
“I am unworthy in strategy and planning,
and am not sufficient to divine the outcome.”
The King of Yuè said:
“Wú has acted without principles,
ravaged our state altars,
leveled our ancestral temples,
turning them into flat plains,
so that the blood sacrifices were stopped.
I wish to seek Heaven’s justice against them;
although chariots, horses, weapons, armor, and troops are ready,
I have no way to set them in motion.
Truly, having heard of your reputation in warfare,
what do you consider feasible?”
Shēn Bāoxū said:
“In my foolishness, I cannot know.”
The King of Yuè persistently asked him,
and so Bāoxū said:
“Now, Wú
is a formidable state,
capable of winning over the feudal lords.
I dare to ask what your Majesty intends to use to fight them?”
The King of Yuè said:
“Among those at my side,
when drinking wine or eating meat,
I never fail to share it.
For my own food and drink, I do not seek exquisite flavors;
when listening to music, I do not listen to its full sound;
seeking only to repay the debt to Wú.
I wish to fight using this.”
Bāoxū said:
“Good as it may be,
it is not yet enough to fight.”
The King of Yuè said:
“Within the state of Yuè,
I practice universal love and treat people like my children,
and nurture them with loyalty and kindness.
I cultivate decrees and lenient punishments,
desire what the people desire,
remove what the people hate,
praise their goodness,
and cover their faults,
seeking only to repay Wú.
I wish to fight using this.”
Bāoxū said:
“Good as it may be,
it is not yet enough to fight.”
The King said:
“Within the state of Yuè,
the wealthy I make secure,
the poor I give to,
rescuing them in their need,
and reducing the excess,
so that the poor and the rich do not lose their benefit,
seeking only to repay Wú.
I wish to fight using this.”
Bāoxū said:
“Good as it may be,
it is not yet enough to fight.”
The King said:
“To the south, my state borders Chǔ,
to the west it is close to Jìn,
and to the north it looks toward Qí;
in spring and autumn, I offer currency, jade, silk, and maidens as tribute to them,
never daring to cease,
seeking only to repay Wú.
I wish to fight using this.”
Bāoxū said:
“Excellent!
Nothing can be added to this,
and yet you still cannot fight.
For the way of war,
knowledge is the beginning,
followed by benevolence,
and decided by courage.
If your Majesty lacks knowledge,
then you will lack stratagems for change
to distinguish between the numbers of many and few.
Without benevolence,
then you cannot share the conditions of hunger and cold with the three armies,
nor share the joy of hardship and pleasure.
Without courage,
then you cannot resolve doubts about whether to go or stay,
or decide on discussions of what is possible or not.”
Thereupon,
the King of Yuè said:
“I respectfully obey your command.”
In the tenth month of winter,
the King of Yuè then consulted the eight grandees, saying:
“Formerly, Wú acted without principles,
ravaged our ancestral temples,
leveled our state altars,
turning them into flat plains,
and stopping the blood sacrifices.
I wish to seek Heaven’s justice against them;
weapons and armor are now ready,
but I have no way to set them in motion.
I asked Shēn Bāoxū,
and he has already instructed me.
I venture to ask you grandees,
what should be done?”
Grandee Yè Yōng said:
“If rewards are certain, then one can fight.
Be careful with rewards,
make trust clear;
those without merit should not be reached,
and those with merit must be rewarded,
then the soldiers will not be idle.”
The King said:
“Sage-like!”
Grandee Kǔ Chéng said:
“If punishments are certain, then one can fight.
If punishments are certain, the soldiers will look up to you and fear them,
and not dare to disobey orders.”
The King said:
“Valiant!”
Grandee Wén Zhòng said:
“If matters are scrutinized, then one can fight.
If matters are scrutinized, right and wrong will be distinguished;
when right and wrong are clearly examined,
no one can be deceived.”
The King said:
“Discerning!”
Grandee Fàn Lǐ said:
“If preparation is scrutinized, then one can fight.
If preparation is scrutinized, one does not fail to guard
in order to await the unexpected;
with preparations established and defenses firm,
one can surely respond to difficulties.”
The King said:
“Prudent!”
Grandee Gāo Rú said:
“If reputation is scrutinized, then one can fight.
Be careful with reputation
to distinguish the clear from the turbid.
By ‘clear and turbid,’
I mean that our lord’s name
is heard in the Zhōu royal house,
and the feudal lords outside do not bear resentment.”
The King said:
“Insightful!”
Grandee Fú Tóng said:
“If grace is broadened and roles are understood, then one can fight.
Broaden grace to give widely,
and understand roles without external interference.”
The King said:
“Divine!”
Grandee Jì Ní said:
“Observe Heaven and examine the Earth,
and coordinate responses to their changes,
then one can fight.
When heavenly changes, earthly responses, and human paths are all favorable,
and these three appear before you,
then it is possible.”
The King said:
“Enlightened!”
Thereupon,
Gōujiàn withdrew to fast and then ordered the people of the state, saying:
“I shall have a deliberation regarding an unexpected matter,
from the near to the far,
none shall not hear of it.”
He then again ordered the officials and the people of the state, saying:
“Those who follow orders will be rewarded.
Everyone must meet at the state gate at the appointed time;
for those who do not follow the order,
I will have them publicly executed.”
Gōujiàn feared the people would not trust him,
so he made it known that he was punishing the unrighteous,
letting it be heard by the Zhōu royal house,
and ensuring the feudal lords outside would not bear resentment.
He ordered within the state:
“Within five days,
you shall be my good people.
Past five days,
you shall not be my people,
and I will also subject you to execution.”
After the instructions and orders were issued,
he went in to give orders to his wife.
The King stood with his back to the screen,
and his wife stood facing the screen.
The King said:
“From this day forth,
internal affairs shall not go out,
and external affairs shall not come in.
Each shall keep to their duty
to fulfill their trustworthiness.
If anyone within the palace is disgraced,
it is your responsibility.
If anyone within a thousand li outside the borders is disgraced,
it is my responsibility.
I see you here
as a clear warning.”
The King left the palace,
The Lady saw the King off, not going beyond the screen.
The King then turned and closed the door,
and filled it with earth.
The Lady removed her hairpins,
sat on the edge of the mat,
maintained a calm heart without adornment,
and did not sweep for three months.
When the King went out, he stood with his back against the wall;
the Grand Masters faced the wall in respect.
The King then commanded the Grand Masters, saying:
“The distribution of land’s produce is uneven,
the soil is not cultivated,
causing me to suffer shame within the state;
this is your fault.
Facing the enemy and not fighting,
the soldiers not being willing to die,
suffering shame before the feudal lords,
and achievements being ruined before the world;
this is my responsibility.
From now on,
internal affairs shall not go out,
and external affairs shall not enter.
I have thus cautioned you.”
The Grand Masters respectfully received the order.
The King then departed.
The Grand Masters saw him off outside the wall,
turned and closed the outer gate of the palace,
and filled it with earth.
The Grand Masters sat on the edge of their mats,
did not partake of the five flavors,
and did not respond to persuasion.
Gōujiàn gave orders to his Lady and the Grand Masters, saying:
“The state has those who guard and defend it.”
He then sat upon an open-air altar,
arranged the drums and sounded them.
The army formed into ranks.
He immediately executed three guilty men,
paraded them through the army,
and ordered:
“Those who do not follow my orders shall be like this.”
The next day,
he moved the army to the suburbs,
executed three guilty men,
and paraded them through the army,
ordering:
“Those who do not follow my orders shall be like this.”
The King then gave orders to those in the capital who were not going,
taking his leave and telling them:
“Stay peacefully on your land and keep your duties.
I am now going to strike and punish the enemy of my ancestral temple,
to apologize to you all.”
He ordered the people of the state to each see off their sons and brothers at the outskirts.
The soldiers each took their leave of their fathers and brothers;
the people of the state felt sorrow,
and all composed songs of parting and separation,
saying:
“Vigorous and eager to destroy the long-standing evil,
lifting halberds and wielding spears.
We depart without surrender,
to vent our King’s spirit and bring revival.
Once the three armies swoop down,
all before us shall perish.
If one soldier resolves to die,
he can match a hundred men.
The Way protects the virtuous,
and the soldiers of Wú shall slaughter themselves.
We wash away our King’s long-standing shame,
our majesty shaking the eight regions.
The ranks of the army cannot be changed,
our momentum is like that of brave beasts.
Move on, move on, let each man exert himself,
Alas, oh alas!”
Thereupon,
none of the onlookers were not moved to grief.
The next day,
he moved the army to the border,
executed three guilty men,
and paraded them through the army,
saying:
“Those who do not follow orders shall be like this.”
Three days later,
he moved the army to Zuìlǐ,
executed three guilty men,
and paraded them through the army,
saying:
“Those with dissolute hearts or hidden conduct, who do not face the enemy, shall be like this.”
Gōujiàn then ordered the officials to make a grand proclamation to the army,
saying:
“Those who have parents but no brothers,
come and tell me.
I have a great undertaking;
you are leaving the care of your parents and the love of your elderly kin
to hasten to the state’s emergency.
While you are among the soldiers and enemies,
if your parents or brothers are in a place of illness,
I shall regard them as my own parents’ or brothers’ illness.
If any should die,
I shall bury and conduct the funeral rites for them,
just as if it were the death and burial of my own parents or brothers.”
The next day,
he again proclaimed to the army,
saying:
“If a soldier is ill
and cannot follow the army or join the battle,
I shall give him medicine,
provide him with rice porridge,
and eat together with him.”
The next day,
he again proclaimed to the army,
saying:
“Those whose strength is not enough to bear armor and weapons,
or whose will and conduct are not enough to obey the King’s commands,
I shall lighten their burdens
and balance their duties.”
The next day,
he led the army to the south of the river,
again displayed strict laws,
and again executed five guilty men,
proclaiming:
“I love my soldiers;
even my own son could not exceed this love.
But when it comes to committing a crime that warrants execution,
even my own son could not escape it.”
Fearing the soldiers might dread the law and not be usable,
and feeling he had not yet obtained the soldiers’ utmost effort unto death,
he saw a frog on the road puffing out its belly in anger,
as if it had the spirit of battle;
he immediately bowed to it from the carriage rail.
His soldiers asked the King:
“Why does our Lord respect a mere frog and bow to it from the carriage rail?”
Gōujiàn said:
“I have longed for the soldiers’ martial rage for a long time,
but none have yet matched my wish.
Now this frog, a mindless creature,
shows an angry spirit when it sees an enemy;
therefore I bowed to it.”
Thereupon,
when the soldiers heard this,
none did not harbor the heart to happily die for him,
each man being ready to give his life.
The officials and generals made a grand proclamation throughout the army, saying:
“Each squad shall command its unit,
each unit shall command its soldiers.
If told to return but you do not,
if told to stay but you do not,
if told to advance but you do not,
if told to retreat but you do not,
if told to go left but you do not,
if told to go right but you do not,
those who do not follow orders
shall be beheaded.”
Thereupon,
Wú deployed all its troops on the north of the river,
and Yuè stationed its army on the south of the river.
The King of Yuè split his army in half to form the left and right armies,
all wearing rhinoceros-hide armor;
he also ordered the people of Ānguǎng to carry stone-tipped arrows,
draw the crossbows of Lúshēng,
and personally led a central formation of six thousand elite gentleman-soldiers.
The next day,
as they were about to fight on the river,
at dusk he ordered the left army
to hold gags in their mouths and go five lǐ upriver,
to wait for the Wú troops.
He then ordered the right army
to hold gags in their mouths and go ten lǐ downriver,
to also wait for the Wú troops.
At midnight,
he made the left and right armies cross the river and beat their drums,
staying in the middle of the water to wait for Wú to move.
The Wú army heard this
and was greatly terrified.
They said to one another:
“Now the Yuè army has split into two divisions
and will attack us from both sides.”
They also split their own army in the darkness of the night
to surround the Yuè.
The King of Yuè secretly had the left and right armies feign battle with Wú from a distance,
letting the sound of the drums be heard.
He kept his six thousand personal elite soldiers in ambush,
who held gags in their mouths and attacked Wú without drums.
The Wú army was soundly defeated.
The left and right armies of Yuè then attacked them,
defeating them soundly at Yòu.
They defeated them again in the suburbs,
and again at the ferry.
In this way, after three battles and three retreats,
they went straight to Wú
and besieged Wú at the western city.
The King of Wú was greatly terrified
and fled by night.
The King of Yuè pursued the fleeing enemy,
attacked the Wú troops,
and entered Jiāngyáng and Sōnglíng.
Wishing to enter the Xū Gate,
they arrived within six or seven lǐ.
Looking toward the southern city of Wú,
they saw the head of Wǔ Zǐxū,
as large as a chariot wheel,
his eyes like flashing lightning,
His beard and hair bristled in all directions,
and his eyes shot beams for ten li.
The Yuè army was greatly terrified
and halted their troops to ask for passage.
That same day at midnight,
a violent wind and torrential rain broke out,
thunder roared and lightning flashed,
flying stones and swirling sand
were as swift as arrows from a crossbow.
The Yuè army was broken and defeated,
retreating from Sōnglíng;
soldiers fell dead and stiff,
the masses were scattered and disorganized,
and nothing could be done to save or stop it.
Fàn Lǐ and Wén Zhòng then kowtowed with bared torsos,
bowing in apology to Wǔ Zǐxū,
begging for passage.
Wǔ Zǐxū then appeared in a dream to Zhòng and Lǐ,
saying:
"I know that Yuè must inevitably enter Wú;
therefore, I asked for my head to be placed at the Nánmén
to watch your destruction of Wú.
My only desire was to bring ruin to Fūchāi.
Yet when it came to your entering my country,
my heart could not bear it,
so I created the wind and rain to turn back your army.
However, Yuè's campaign against Wú
is indeed the will of Heaven.
How could I stop it?
If Yuè wishes to enter,
change your route to the Dōngmén;
I shall open the way and pierce the city walls for you
to clear your path."
Thereupon,
the next day the Yuè army changed course and set out from the river,
entering Hǎiyáng at the Zháishuǐ of the three routes;
they then broke through the southeast corner to reach their destination,
and the Yuè army subsequently besieged Wú.
After maintaining the siege for one year,
the Wú forces were repeatedly defeated,
and they finally cornered the King of Wú on Gūxū Shān.
Wú sent Wángsūn Luò to crawl forward with a bared torso on his knees,
requesting peace from the King of Yuè,
saying:
"Your humble servant Fūchāi
dares to lay bare his heart.
On a former day, I offended you at Kuàijī,
yet Fūchāi did not dare to defy Fate
and allowed you, Great King, to conclude a treaty and return home.
Now that you, Great King, have raised an army to punish your humble servant,
I shall only obey your commands.
I wonder if you might treat today at Gūxū
as that former day at Kuàijī?
If I might receive the grace of Heaven
and be pardoned from the death penalty,
then Wú wishes to serve as your subjects and concubines forever."
Gōujiàn could not bear his words
and was about to grant him peace.
Fàn Lǐ said:
"Regarding the matter at Kuàijī,
Heaven bestowed Yuè upon Wú,
but Wú did not take it.
Now Heaven bestows Wú upon Yuè;
can Yuè defy Fate?
Moreover, you, Great King, have gone to court early and retired late,
gnashing your teeth and engraving this in your bones,
planning this for over twenty years;
was this not all for the sake of this one morning?
If you attain it today only to cast it away,
can such a plan be right?
When Heaven offers and one does not take,
one will in turn suffer the consequences.
How can you forget the disaster at Kuàijī?"
Gōujiàn said:
"I wish to follow your words,
but I cannot bear to face his messenger."
Fàn Lǐ then beat the drums and advanced the troops,
saying:
"The King has already entrusted the government to the officials;
messenger, leave quickly,
lest you soon meet with punishment."
The Wú messenger left weeping.
Gōujiàn took pity on him
and sent someone to go in and tell the King of Wú:
"I shall place you in Yǒngdōng,
providing for you and your wife along with over three hundred people
to live out your days;
would that be acceptable?"
The King of Wú declined, saying:
"Since Heaven has brought disaster upon the state of Wú,
it was not sooner or later
but precisely during my reign,
I who have lost and destroyed the ancestral temple and the altars of state.
The land and subjects of Wú
are already possessed by Yuè.
I am old
and cannot serve you as a subject."
He then fell upon his sword and committed suicide.
Once Gōujiàn had destroyed Wú,
he led his army north across the Jiāng and Huái rivers,
meeting with the lords of Qí and Jìn at Xúzhōu,
and sent tribute to Zhōu.
Zhōu Yuán Wáng sent an envoy to grant favors to Gōujiàn.
Having received his mandate and title,
he left to return south of the Jiāng.
He gave the land above the Huái to Chǔ,
returned the land Wú had seized from Sòng,
and gave one hundred li east of the Sì River to Lǔ.
At this time,
the Yuè army moved freely across the Jiāng and Huái rivers,
and the feudal lords all offered their congratulations.
The King of Yuè returned to Wú
and, upon his return, asked Fàn Lǐ:
"Why is it that your words align so well with Heaven?"
Fàn Lǐ said:
"This is the Way of the Sùnǚ;
a single word can align with the Great King's affairs.
If the King asks how it is done,
the essentials of the Jīn Kuì truly lie in the balance of the upper and lower."
The King of Yuè said:
"Excellent.
I shall not call myself a King arrogantly.
Can this be fully explained?"
Lǐ said:
"It cannot.
Formerly when Wú called itself King,
it usurped the title of the Son of Heaven;
Heaven changed above,
and the sun was eclipsed by the moon.
Now if you continue to usurp the title without returning to your proper place,
I fear heavenly portents will appear again."
The King of Yuè returned to Wú
and held a banquet at Wéntái,
where the ministers made merry.
He then ordered music to be composed, the "Song of Conquering Wú."
The music master said:
"I have heard that one composes a tune upon an event
and creates music when success is achieved.
The Great King exalts virtue
and instructs the states that possess the Way,
punishes the unrighteous,
avenges grievances and wipes away shame;
your majesty extends over the lords,
and you have achieved the merit of a Hegemon King.
Your merit can be depicted in paintings,
your virtue can be carved in metal and stone,
your voice can be entrusted to strings and pipes,
and your name can be preserved on bamboo and silk.
I ask to take up the qín and play it."
He then composed the Zhāngchàng lyrics, saying:
"In hardship,
now wishing to attack Wú,
is it possible yet?"
The Grandees Zhòng and Lǐ said:
"Wú killed the loyal minister Wǔ Zǐxū;
if we do not attack Wú now,
what use are men?"
Grandee Zhòng stepped forward to offer a toast,
and his words were:
"August Heaven grants aid,
our King receives blessings.
Good ministers gather their counsel,
it is our King's virtue.
The ancestral temple assists in governance,
the ghosts and gods provide support.
The lord does not forget his subjects,
and the subjects exhaust their strength.
The high heavens are vast and blue,
they cannot be obstructed.
Two pints of wine in this cup,
may ten thousand blessings be without end."
Thereupon,
the King of Yuè remained silent and said nothing.
Grandee Zhòng said:
"Our King is wise and benevolent,
harboring the Way and embracing virtue.
Having destroyed the enemy and broken Wú,
he does not forget to return to his own state.
He is not stingy with rewards,
and all evils are blocked.
Lord and subject are in harmony,
with a hundred billion blessings.
Two pints of wine in this cup,
may ten thousand years never end."
The ministers on the terrace were greatly pleased and laughed,
but the King of Yuè had no joy on his face.
Fàn Lǐ knew that Gōujiàn loved the land
and did not care if his ministers died;
because his plans had succeeded and the state was settled,
he would surely no longer need those of merit upon returning to the state;
therefore, the King's face showed worry and he was not pleased.
Fàn Lǐ wished to depart from Wú,
but fearing that Gōujiàn had not yet returned
and he might fail in the duty of a minister,
he followed him into Yuè.
On the way, he said to Wén Zhòng:
"You should leave now;
the King of Yuè will surely execute you."
Zhòng did not believe his words.
Lǐ again wrote a letter to leave for Zhòng, saying:
“I have heard that Heaven has its four seasons,
giving life in spring and harvesting in winter.
Humans have their peaks and declines;
when prosperity reaches its limit, misfortune must follow.
To know when to advance and when to retreat, when to persist and when to perish, without losing one’s integrity—
is this not only for the virtuous?
Although Lǐ is untalented,
I clearly understand when to advance and retreat.
When the high-flying birds have dispersed,
the good bow is put away.
When the cunning rabbits are exhausted,
the good hound is cooked.
The King of Yuè is a man with a long neck and a bird’s beak,
with the eyes of a hawk and the stride of a wolf;
he is one with whom one can share hardships but cannot share in pleasures.
One can walk with him through danger,
but one cannot dwell with him in peace.
If you do not leave,
it will surely bring harm to you,
this is clear.”
Wén Zhòng did not believe his words.
The King of Yuè hatched a secret plot,
and Fàn Lǐ discussed his desire to leave,
seeking a way out.
In the twenty-fourth year,
on the day of Dīngwèi in the ninth month,
Fàn Lǐ took his leave of the King, saying:
“I have heard that when the lord is worried, the official toils;
when the lord is humiliated, the official dies.
This is the single principle of righteousness.
Now I serve Your Majesty;
in the past, I could not extinguish the buds of trouble before they sprouted,
and later, I could not save you from the calamity of downfall.
Even so,
I ultimately desired to make my lord a hegemon and the state powerful,
thus I did not refuse any trial of life or death.
I privately reflected on myself,
and so I was sent to Wú.
At Your Majesty’s shame and humiliation,
the reason Lǐ did not die
was truly for fear of being slandered by the Grand Chancellor Pǐ
and bringing about a fate like that of Wǔ Zǐxū.
Therefore I did not dare to die earlier,
and lived for a short while longer.
The heart’s sense of shame must not be allowed to grow great,
and the embarrassment that brings sweat cannot be endured.
Fortunately, relying on the divine spirits of the ancestral temple
and Your Majesty’s majestic virtue,
defeat was turned into success.
Just as Tāng and Wǔ overcame Xià and Shāng to achieve their royal enterprise,
establishing merit and washing away disgrace,
this is why I have occupied my seat for so long.
I now beg to take my leave.”
The King of Yuè was moved with sorrow,
tears fell and dampened his clothes,
and he said:
“The scholar-officials of the state depend on you,
the people of the state depend on you,
and I have entrusted my own person and title to await your orders.
Now you say you are leaving
and desire to depart.
This is Heaven abandoning Yuè and destroying me;
I shall have nothing to rely upon.
I have these words to say:
If you stay in your position,
I will divide the state to share it with you;
if you leave,
your wife and children will be executed.”
Fàn Lǐ said:
“I have heard that a gentleman waits for the right time;
a plan is not plotted multiple times,
one does not face death with doubt,
and one does not deceive oneself internally.
Since I am departing,
what law would apply to my wife and children?
May Your Majesty exert yourself;
I take my leave from here.”
He then boarded a small boat,
exited through the Sānjiāng,
and entered the Wǔhú,
and no one knew where he went.
After Fàn Lǐ had gone,
the King of Yuè’s expression changed with sorrow,
and he summoned Grand Master Zhòng, saying:
“Can Lǐ be pursued?”
Zhòng said:
“He cannot be reached.”
The King said:
“What can be done!”
Zhòng said:
“When Lǐ left,
he drew six Yin lines
and three Yang lines;
the gods before the sun could not control him.
With Xuánwǔ and Tiānkōng in majestic motion,
who would dare to stop him?
He crossed the Tiānguān,
waded through the Tiānliáng,
then entered the Tiānyī,
with divine light shielding him in front.
Those who speak of him will die;
those who look for him will go mad.
I wish for Your Majesty not to pursue him again.
Lǐ will never return.”
The King of Yuè then took Fàn Lǐ’s wife and children,
enfeoffed them with a territory of a hundred lǐ,
and decreed that if anyone dared to encroach upon them,
they would be punished by High Heaven.
Thereupon,
the King of Yuè ordered skilled craftsmen to cast a golden image in the form of Fàn Lǐ,
placed it beside his seat,
and discussed politics with it morning and night.
From this time onward,
Jì Ní feigned madness.
Men like Grand Masters Yè Yōng, Fú Tóng, and Gāo Rú
became increasingly distant each day
and were not close to the court.
Grand Master Zhòng was troubled internally and did not attend court;
someone slandered him to the King, saying:
“Wén Zhòng gave up the position of Chancellor
and enabled the King to become hegemon over the feudal lords;
but now his office has not been promoted
nor has his position or fief been increased.
Thus he harbors a heart of resentment and grievance,
which erupts with indignation within
and changes his expression without;
therefore he does not attend court.”
On another day,
Zhòng remonstrated, saying:
“The reason I came to court but retired late as if I were suffering from an illness
was only for the sake of Wú.
Now that it has been destroyed,
what worry does the King have?”
The King of Yuè remained silent.
At that time, Duke Āi of Lǔ was distressed by the Sānhuán
and wished to use the feudal lords to attack them.
The Sānhuán were also distressed by Duke Āi’s anger,
and for this reason, the lord and ministers caused trouble for each other.
Duke Āi fled to Xíng,
and the Sānhuán attacked Duke Āi.
The Duke fled to Wèi,
and then fled to Yuè.
The State of Lǔ was left empty,
and the people of the state grieved for him,
coming to welcome Duke Āi
and returning together with him.
Gǒujiàn was worried that Wén Zhòng would not plan for it,
and therefore he did not attack the Sānhuán for Duke Āi.
In the twenty-fifth year,
at dawn on the day of Bǐngwǔ,
the King of Yuè summoned the Minister of State and Grand Master Wén Zhòng and asked him:
"I have heard that knowing others is easy,
but knowing oneself is difficult.
What kind of person does the Minister know himself to be?"
Wén Zhòng said:
"How tragic!
Your Majesty knows my courage,
but does not know my benevolence.
You know my loyalty,
but do not know my trustworthiness.
I have indeed repeatedly urged you to reduce your indulgence in music and women,
to eliminate excessive pleasures,
and with strange theories and unusual arguments,
I have spoken fully and exhausted my loyalty,
even to the point of offending Your Majesty,
going against your heart and being harsh to your ears,
which must surely result in my punishment.
I do not dare to love my life and remain silent,
but to speak and then die;
Wǔ Zǐxū was like this in Wú in the past.
When Fūchāi was being executed,
he said to me:
'When the cunning rabbits are dead,
the good hounds are cooked.
When the enemy states are destroyed,
the strategists perish.'
Fàn Lǐ also had these words.
Why did Your Majesty ask about the eighth level of the Yùmén?
I see Your Majesty's intent."
The King of Yuè remained silent and did not respond,
and the Grand Master also withdrew.
He chewed his own ear to satisfy the malice of others.
His wife said:
"My lord is behaving so meanly!
As the minister of a whole state,
do you lack the salary of the king?
When facing food you do not eat,
and why do you chew on your ear with such malice?
With wife and children by your side,
you have the ability of an ordinary man.
Having attained the position of Minister of State yourself,
what more can you hope for?
Is it perhaps out of greed?
Why is your mind so unsettled like this?"
Wén Zhòng said:
"How sad,
you do not understand.
Since our King escaped from disaster and hardship
and wiped out the shame in Wú,
I moved my entire household and threw myself into the land of death.
I exhausted the strategies of the Nine Arts;
there I was a flatterer,
but for the lord I was loyal.
The King does not perceive this.
Instead he says:
'Knowing others is easy,
knowing oneself is difficult.'
My answer had no other words,
which is proof of an ominous omen.
I will enter the palace again,
but I fear I will not return.
I bid you a long farewell,
and we shall seek each other in the underworld."
His wife said:
"How do you know this?"
Wén Zhòng said:
"When I saw the King,
it was precisely the eighth level of the Yùmén.
The hour Chén overcomes the day Rì,
the superior harms the inferior;
this is a sign of disorder and ugliness,
and will surely harm the virtuous.
Today the day overcomes the hour,
the superior's harm to the inferior stops,
but my life is but a moment away."
The King of Yuè summoned the Minister of State again
and said to him:
"You have secret strategies and military arts
to overthrow enemies and seize states.
Of the strategies of the Nine Arts,
now three have been used
to break the powerful Wú.
The other six are still with you.
I wish for you to use the remaining arts on my behalf to plot against the ancestors of Wú before my late kings in the underworld."
Thereupon Wén Zhòng looked up to the sky and sighed, saying:
"Alas!
I have heard that great kindness is not repaid
and great merit is not returned;
does it refer to this?
I regret not following Fàn Lǐ's plan
and instead being slaughtered by the King of Yuè.
I did not consume good words,
therefore I chew on the malice of men."
The King of Yuè then bestowed upon Wén Zhòng the sword Shǔlú.
When Wén Zhòng received the sword,
he sighed again, saying:
"The Governor of Nányáng has been captured by the King of Yuè."
He laughed to himself and said:
"At the end of a hundred generations,
loyal ministers will surely use me as a metaphor."
Then he fell upon the sword and died.
The King of Yuè buried Wén Zhòng on the West Mountain of the capital.
More than three thousand soldiers from the tower-ships
built a tripod-foot tomb path,
and some entered below the Three Peaks.
A year after the burial,
Wǔ Zǐxū came from the sea, bored through the side of the mountain, and took Wén Zhòng away,
and together they floated in the sea.
Therefore, the one in the front tide who is Pānhòu
is Wǔ Zǐxū.
The one in the back in the heavy waters
is Grand Master Wén Zhòng.
After the King of Yuè had executed the loyal minister,
he became hegemon east of the Pass.
At Lángyá he built a viewing tower,
the tower being seven lǐ in circumference,
to gaze at the Eastern Sea,
with eight thousand suicide warriors
and three hundred halberd ships.
Not long after,
he personally sought out worthy scholars.
Kǒngzǐ heard of this
and followed by his disciples, brought the elegant zithers and the rites and music of the former kings to play for Yuè.
The King of Yuè then put on the armor of Tángyí,
wore the sword Bùguāng,
held the spear Qūlú,
and sent out three hundred suicide warriors to form an array below the pass.
After a while Kǒngzǐ arrived in Yuè.
The King of Yuè said:
"Indeed, indeed,
what does the Master have to teach us?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"I, Qiū, can transmit the Way of the Five Emperors and Three Kings,
therefore I play the elegant zither to present it to Your Majesty."
The King of Yuè let out a long sigh and said:
"The nature of the Yuè people is brittle and foolish;
they travel by water and live on mountains.
They use boats as carriages
and oars as horses.
They go like the wind,
and when they leave, it is hard to follow them.
They delight in arms and dare to die;
this is the constant nature of Yuè.
What theory does the Master have that he wishes to teach us?"
Kǒngzǐ did not answer,
so he took his leave and departed.
The King of Yuè sent people to Mùkè Shān
to take the remains of Yǔncháng,
intending to move the burial to Lángyá.
They dug into Yǔncháng's tomb three times,
but from the tomb arose blazing winds and flying sand and stones to strike people,
so that no one could enter.
Gōujiàn said:
"Does my former lord not wish to be moved?"
So he left it and departed.
Gōujiàn then sent envoys to command Qí, Chǔ, Qín, and Jìn
to all assist the Zhōu house,
and they departed after a blood oath.
Duke Huán of Qín did not follow the King of Yuè's command,
so Gōujiàn selected generals and soldiers of Wú and Yuè
to cross the river to the west to attack Qín.
The soldiers suffered from this.
It happened that Qín was terrified,
and preemptively took the blame upon themselves,
so Yuè returned its army.
The soldiers were joyful
and then composed the "Poem of the Héliáng,"
saying:
"Crossing the Héliáng, oh, crossing the Héliáng,
raising troops to punish and attack the King of Qín.
In the tenth month of early winter, there is much snow and frost,
the severe cold on the roads is truly hard to bear.
Before the arrayed troops crossed, the Qín army surrendered,
the feudal lords were terrified and in great fear.
Our fame spreads within the seas, our majesty to distant states,
becoming hegemons like Mù of Qín, Huán of Qí, and Zhuāng of Chǔ.
The world is at peace and life is long,
sadly we return, why is there no bridge?"
From the time Yuè destroyed Wú,
all the Central States feared it.
In the twenty-sixth year,
the King of Yuè took the Zhūzǐ captive and brought him back because he was lawless,
and established his crown prince Hé.
In winter,
Duke Āi of Lǔ came to flee for refuge because of the pressure from the Sān Huán families.
The King of Yuè wished to attack the Sān Huán for him,
but because the ministers of the feudal lords would not follow orders,
it did not come to pass.
In the twenty-seventh year,
in winter,
Gōujiàn was bedridden with illness.
As he was about to die,
he said to the Crown Prince Xīngyí:
"I am a descendant of Yǔ,
and having inherited the virtue of Yǔncháng,
and received the protection of the spirits of heaven and the blessings of the gods of the earth,
starting from the remote land of Yuè
and relying on the vanguard of Chǔ
to destroy the weapons of the King of Wú.
Crossing the Jiāng and wading the Huái,
reaching the lands of Jìn and Qí,
my achievements and virtues are lofty.
Having attained this myself,
can I not be sincere?
The descendants of a hegemon
find it difficult to maintain their position for long;
you must be cautious!"
He then died.
Xīngyí died after one year on the throne,
and his son was Wēng.
Wēng died,
and his son was Bùyáng.
Bùyáng died,
and his son was Wúqiáng.
Wúqiáng died,
and his son was Yù.
Yù died,
and his son was Zūn.
Zūn died,
and his son was Qīn.
From Gōujiàn to Qīn,
the eight rulers who passed were all called hegemons,
totaling two hundred and twenty-four years.
Qīn lost the support of the people,
left Lángyé,
and moved to Wú.
From Huángdì to Shàokāng,

From when Yǔ received the abdication to when Shàokāng ascended the throne,
there were six generations,
being one hundred and forty-four years.
The interval from Zhuānxū to the accession of Shàokāng
was four hundred and twenty-four years.
